It was the last thing the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, enjoined upon his community. In Allah’s Book, it is singled out for particular mention after a general statement, as in His words, Exalted is He:

“And those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer.”

And His words:

“Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish prayer.”

It is also coupled with patience, zakat, sacrifice, and jihad in various passages of Allah’s Book, as in His words, Exalted is He:

“And seek help through patience and prayer.”

And His words:

“And establish prayer and give zakat.”

And His words:

“Indeed, my prayer and my sacrifice.”

And His words:

“Forceful against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating.”

And His words:

“And when you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a group of them stand with you, taking their weapons. When they have prostrated, let them go behind you, and let another group, which has not yet prayed, come forward and pray with you, taking their precautions and their weapons.”

Continuing to His words:

“And when you are secure, establish prayer. Indeed, prayer has been prescribed for the believers at appointed times.”

---

## Page 13662

And its importance is too great to be fully encompassed; those in authority must therefore give it greater attention than any other duty. For this reason, the Commander of the Faithful, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, used to write to his officials:

“The most important of your duties in my eyes is prayer. Whoever upholds it and observes it faithfully safeguards his religion; whoever neglects it will neglect other duties even more.”

This was narrated by Mālik and others.

The muhtasib must enjoin Friday and congregational prayers, truthfulness in speech, and the faithful discharge of trusts. He must forbid wrongdoing, including lying, betrayal of trust, and everything these encompass, such as giving short measure or weight and practising deception in crafts, sales, religious affairs, and the like. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“Woe to those who give short measure, who take their full measure when receiving from others, but give less when measuring or weighing for them.”

And He says in the account of Shuʿayb:

“Give full measure, and do not be among those who cause loss. Weigh with an even balance. Do not deprive people of what is rightfully theirs, and do not spread corruption in the land.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“Indeed, Allah does not love anyone who is treacherous and sinful.”

And He says:

“And Allah does not bring the schemes of the treacherous to success.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Hakīm ibn Hizām reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The buyer and seller have the option of withdrawing from the sale so long as they have not parted. If they are truthful and make matters clear, their transaction will be blessed; but if they conceal facts and lie, the blessing of their transaction will be erased.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah reported:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came upon a heap of food and put his hand into it

---

## Page 13663

and his fingers felt moisture. He asked, ‘What is this, owner of the food?’ The man replied, ‘Rain fell on it, O Messenger of Allah.’ He said, ‘Why did you not put it on top of the food so that people could see it? Whoever cheats us is not one of us.’” Another version reads:

“Whoever cheats me is not one of me.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus stated that a person who cheats does not fall under the unqualified designation of people of religion and faith. Likewise, he said:

“No adulterer commits adultery while he is a believer; no thief steals while he is a believer; and no one drinks wine while he is a believer.”

He thus denied such a person the reality of faith by which one merits reward and deliverance from punishment, even though he retains the foundation of faith that distinguishes him from the disbelievers and through which he will be brought out of the Fire.

Cheating occurs in sales through concealing defects and deceptively presenting goods—for example, when the goods appear better on the outside than they are within, as with the man whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, encountered and rebuked. It also occurs in crafts: among those who prepare foods such as bread, cooked dishes, lentils, roasted meat and other things; those who make clothing, such as weavers, tailors and the like; and those who manufacture other goods. They must be forbidden to engage in cheating, betrayal of trust and concealment.

Among these are the “alchemists,” who adulterate coins, gems, perfumes and other things. They manufacture gold, silver, ambergris, musk, gems, saffron, rose water and other things, imitating Allah’s creation thereby. Yet Allah has not created anything

---

## Page 13664

that His servants can create as He does. Rather, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, as His Messenger related from Him:

“Who does greater wrong than one who sets out to create as I create? Let them create a tiny ant; let them create a mosquito.”

Thus, manufactured things, such as cooked foods, clothing and dwellings, are created only through human agency. Allah Most High says:

“And a sign for them is that We carried their descendants in the laden ship, and We created for them others like it on which they ride.”

And He says:

“Do you worship what you carve, when Allah created you and what you make?”

Natural creations—minerals, plants and animals—are beyond human beings’ ability to manufacture. They merely produce imitations for fraudulent purposes. This is the true nature of alchemy: it consists of imitations. This is an extensive subject on which experts have written works that cannot be discussed here.

Practices to be condemned also include contracts forbidden by Allah and His Messenger, such as contracts involving usury and gambling; sales involving uncertainty; habal al-habala sales; sales concluded by touching or tossing the goods; and usury involving deferment or unequal exchange. Likewise, they include artificial bidding—when someone raises the price of goods without intending to buy them—leaving a dairy animal unmilked to exaggerate its apparent milk yield, and all other forms of deceptive concealment.

The same applies to usurious transactions, whether between two parties or three, when their overall purpose is to exchange a sum of dirhams for a greater sum payable at a later date.

Two-party transactions are those conducted between two people, such as combining a loan with a sale, a lease, an orchard-tending partnership or a crop-sharing agreement. It is authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

---

## Page 13665

said:

“It is not lawful to combine a loan with a sale, to impose two conditions in a sale, to profit from something for which one has assumed no liability, or to sell what one does not have.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is an authentic hadith.”

Another example is selling someone a commodity on deferred payment and then buying it back from him. In Sunan Abī Dāwūd, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Whoever concludes two sales in one may take the lower of the two prices, or else incur usury.”

Three-party transactions include bringing in an intermediary to make usury appear lawful. The usury-taker buys the commodity from this intermediary, then sells it on deferred payment to the usury-payer, who sells it back to its original owner at a price reduced by an amount that the intermediary gains.

Some of these transactions are forbidden by the consensus of the Muslims: for example, those in which such an arrangement is stipulated; those in which the commodity is sold before possession has been taken as required by Islamic law, or without fulfilling the conditions required by Islamic law; and those in which an insolvent debtor’s debt is rolled over at an increase. An insolvent debtor must be granted time to pay, and, by the consensus of the Muslims, it is impermissible to increase what he owes through a transaction or otherwise. Some scholars have disagreed over other forms of these transactions, but what is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Companions and the Successors is that all of them are forbidden.

Practices to be condemned also include intercepting goods before they reach the market. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited this because it involves misleading the seller: he does not know the market price, so the buyer purchases from him for less than the goods are worth. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, granted the seller the right to rescind the sale once he reaches the market.

There is no doubt that he has this right when he has been underpaid. Whether he has it without having been underpaid, however, is disputed among the scholars. Two opinions are reported from Ahmad: the first recognizes this right, which is also the position of al-Shāfiʿī; the second does not

---

## Page 13666

recognize it when there has been no underpayment. Mālik, Ahmad and others hold that a buyer who does not bargain has the right to rescind a sale if overcharged. Market traders may not sell to someone who bargains at one price, then charge a higher price to someone who does not bargain or does not know the market price. This is among the practices for which sellers must be reproved.

It is reported in a hadith:

“Overcharging someone who does not bargain is usury.”

This is comparable to intercepting goods before they reach the market, since the arriving seller does not know the market price. Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited a town-dweller from selling on behalf of a Bedouin, saying:

“Leave people to trade with one another; Allah provides for some through others.”

Ibn ʿAbbās was asked: “What does his statement, ‘A town-dweller must not sell on behalf of a Bedouin,’ mean?” He replied: “He must not act as his broker.” This is prohibited because it harms buyers. When a resident acts as an agent for an arriving seller in selling goods that people need, while that seller does not know the market price, this harms the buyer. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Leave people to trade with one another; Allah provides for some through others.”

The same applies to hoarding goods that people need. Muslim narrated in his Sahīh, on the authority of Maʿmar ibn ʿAbd Allāh, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“None but a sinner hoards.”

A hoarder deliberately buys food that people need, then withholds it from them, seeking to raise its price against them. He thereby wrongs those who buy it. For this reason, the ruler may compel people to sell what they possess at its fair market value when people are in dire need of it—for example, someone who possesses food he does not need while the people are in

---

## Page 13667

famine. He must therefore be compelled to sell it to the people at its fair market value. For this reason, the jurists have said:

Anyone in dire need of another person’s food may take it without the owner’s consent, paying its fair market value. Even if the owner refuses to sell it for anything less than a price above its market value, he is entitled only to its market value.

This makes clear that some price-setting is unjust and impermissible, while some is just and permissible. If it involves wronging people by compelling them, without right, to sell at a price they do not accept, or preventing them from doing what Allah has permitted them, it is forbidden. But if it establishes justice among people—for example, by compelling them to make the exchanges required of them at a fair market price, and preventing them from unlawfully demanding more than fair compensation—then it is permissible; indeed, obligatory.

An example of the former is what Anas narrated:

“Prices rose during the time of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The people said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, if only you would set prices!’ He replied, ‘Allah is the One who withholds, grants abundance, provides sustenance, and sets prices. I hope to meet Allah with no one seeking redress from me for any wrong I have done him concerning blood or property.’”

This was narrated by Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it authentic.

If people sell their goods in the customary manner, without wrongdoing on their part, and prices rise either because goods are scarce or because the population has increased, then this is a matter left to Allah. Compelling people to sell at a specified price is coercion without right.

An example of the latter is when the owners of goods refuse to sell them despite people’s dire need

---

## Page 13668

for them, unless they are paid more than the customary price. In such a case, they must sell them at their fair market value. Price-setting means nothing more than requiring them to accept that value, so they must abide by what Allah has required of them.

An even stronger case is where people have agreed that only certain designated individuals may sell food or other goods: those goods are sold only to them, and they then resell them. If anyone else sells such goods, he is prevented from doing so—either unjustly, for the sake of a levy collected from the seller, or justifiably, because of the harm involved. Here, prices must be set for these dealers so that they neither sell goods nor buy people’s property except at fair market value. No scholar has any hesitation on this point. For if others have been prevented from selling or buying that type of goods, allowing these dealers to sell or buy at whatever prices they choose would wrong people in two ways: it would wrong those wishing to sell such goods, and it would wrong those buying from these dealers.

When not all injustice can be prevented, the duty is to prevent as much of it as possible. Price-setting in such circumstances is therefore obligatory, without dispute. In essence, it means requiring them to sell or buy only at a fair market price. This is obligatory in many situations under Islamic law.

Just as compelling someone to sell is impermissible without a rightful basis, it is permissible when there is a rightful basis, as when property is sold to discharge a debt that must be paid or to provide obligatory maintenance. Likewise, compelling someone to sell only at a fair market price is impermissible without a rightful basis, but is permissible in certain cases, such as that of someone in dire need of

---

## Page 13669

food belonging to someone else, or plantings and buildings on another person’s land, which the landowner may acquire at their fair market value, but not for more. There are many similar examples. The same applies to the extension of manumission to the remaining shares in a slave, as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“Whoever frees his share in a slave and has enough wealth to cover the slave’s price must have the slave fairly valued, neither undervalued nor overvalued. He must then pay his co-owners their shares, and the slave is freed at his expense. Otherwise, only the share he has freed is free.”

Likewise, anyone obliged to purchase something for an act of worship—such as equipment for Hajj, a slave to be freed, or water for ritual purification—must purchase it at its fair market value. He may not insist on buying only at a price of his own choosing.

The same applies to the food or clothing he must provide for those whose maintenance is his responsibility. If food or clothing customarily considered suitable for them is available at its fair market price, he may not resort to something inferior while waiting for the suitable item to be offered to him at a price of his own choosing. There are many similar examples.

For this reason, a number of scholars, including Abū Hanīfah and his companions, prohibited those who divide real estate and other property for a fee from forming partnerships when people need their services and their fees would thereby rise. It is therefore all the more justified to prohibit sellers from colluding to sell only at a price they have fixed. Likewise, if buyers collude to join forces and share in whatever any one of them purchases in order to depress the prices of people’s goods, prohibiting them is also all the more justified.

---

## Page 13670

Thus, if a group buying or selling a particular kind of goods colludes to depress the value of what they buy, purchasing it below its recognized fair market price, while raising the price of what they sell above the customary price, and increasing what they purchase, this is a greater transgression than intercepting goods before they reach the market, a townsman selling on behalf of a desert dweller, or bidding up prices without intending to buy. They have thereby agreed to wrong people, forcing them to sell their goods and purchase them at more than their fair market value, even though people need these goods and need to purchase them. Whatever the public needs to buy and sell must be sold only at its fair market price, when the need to buy and sell it is general.

This includes people’s need for the work of particular trades, such as farming, weaving, and building. People must have food to eat, clothes to wear, and homes to live in. If sufficient clothing is not brought into their town—as it used to be brought into the Hijaz during the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him)—they need people to weave clothing for them. Clothing was brought to the Hijaz from Yemen, Egypt, and Syria, whose inhabitants were unbelievers; the Muslims wore what unbelievers had woven without washing it.

They must also have food, either brought in from elsewhere or grown in their own land, which is generally the case. Likewise, they must have homes to live in and therefore need builders. For this reason, a number of jurists among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, as well as others, stated:

---

## Page 13671

such as Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī, and others: practicing these trades is a communal obligation, for people’s welfare cannot be secured without them. Likewise, jihad is a communal obligation unless it becomes an individual obligation, as when an enemy advances upon a town or the ruler calls someone to arms.

Acquiring religious knowledge is also a communal obligation, except where it becomes an individual duty. For example, each person must learn what Allah has commanded and forbidden him; this is an individual obligation. As reported in the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“Whoever Allah intends good for, He grants him understanding of the religion.”

Everyone for whom Allah intends good must therefore be granted understanding of the religion. Whoever is not granted understanding of the religion is someone for whom Allah has not intended good. The religion is what Allah sent His Messenger with: what a person must believe and put into practice. Everyone must affirm the truth of what Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) has conveyed and obey what he has commanded, with a general commitment to belief and obedience. Then, when a particular report from him is established as authentic, one must believe that report specifically. Likewise, when a particular command applies to a person in a given respect, he must obey him in that specific matter.

Similarly, washing the deceased, shrouding them, offering the funeral prayer over them, and burying them are communal obligations. Enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is likewise a communal obligation.

---

## Page 13672

All religious offices—such as leadership of the believers and the offices beneath it, including kingship, ministerial office, and administrative posts, whether concerned with official correspondence or accounting for revenues collected and funds disbursed as stipends to soldiers or others; likewise military command, the judiciary, oversight of public conduct, and the subordinate branches of these offices—were instituted solely to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

In his city of Medina, the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) personally undertook all the duties of those in authority, while appointing officials in places distant from him. Thus, he appointed ‘Attāb ibn Asīd over Mecca, ‘Uthmān ibn Abī al-‘Ās over al-Tā’if, and Khālid ibn Sa‘īd ibn al-‘Ās over the villages of ‘Urayna. He also sent ‘Alī, Mu‘ādh, and Abū Mūsā to Yemen.

He likewise appointed commanders over military expeditions and sent collectors to collect zakat. They would collect it from those obliged to pay it and distribute it to the eligible recipients whom Allah named in the Quran. A collector would then return to Medina with nothing but his whip, bringing nothing to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) if he had found eligible recipients among whom to distribute it.

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) also required his officials to render a full account, examining what they had collected and what they had disbursed. Thus, in the two Sahīh collections, Abū Humayd al-Sā‘idī reported:

“The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) appointed a man from al-Azd, called Ibn al-Lutbiyya, to collect zakat. When he returned, the Prophet called him to account. The man said, ‘This is for you

---

## Page 13673

and this was given to me as a gift.’ The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, ‘What is the matter with a man whom we appoint to carry out some of the duties Allah has entrusted to us, who then says, “This is for you, and this was given to me as a gift”? Why did he not sit in his father’s and mother’s house and see whether he would receive any gifts? By Him in whose hand is my soul, any man whom we appoint to carry out some of the duties Allah has entrusted to us, and who misappropriates anything from it, will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying it on his neck: if it is a camel, it will be bellowing; if a cow, it will be lowing; and if a sheep, it will be bleating.’ Then he raised his hands towards heaven and said, ‘O Allah, have I conveyed the message? O Allah, have I conveyed the message?’ He said this twice or three times.”

The point here is that these duties, which are collective obligations, become an individual obligation upon a person when no one else undertakes them, especially if others are incapable of doing so. Thus, when people need a group’s farming, weaving, or building services, that work becomes obligatory. If they refuse, the ruler compels them to undertake it for the customary remuneration. He does not allow them to demand more than the customary remuneration from people, nor does he allow people to wrong them by paying them less than their due. For example, if troops assigned to jihad need their land cultivated, he requires those whose occupation is farming to cultivate it for them. The troops are required not to wrong the farmer, just as the farmer is required to cultivate the land for the troops.

Sharecropping is permissible according to the sounder of the two scholarly opinions, and it was the practice of the Muslims during

---

## Page 13674

the time of their Prophet and his Rightly Guided Caliphs. It was practised by the families of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, and ʿAlī, as well as other households among the Emigrants. Its permissibility was upheld by leading Companions such as Ibn Masʿūd. It is also the position of the jurists of hadith, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī, al-Bukhārī, Muhammad ibn Ishāq ibn Khuzayma, Abū Bakr ibn al-Mundhir, and others. It is likewise the position of al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Ibn Abī Laylā, Abū Yūsuf, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and other Muslim jurists.

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) had arranged for the people of Khaybar to receive half the fruit and crops yielded by its land until his death. That arrangement continued until ʿUmar expelled them from Khaybar. He had stipulated that they cultivate it at their own expense, and they supplied the seed, not the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). Thus, the sounder of the two scholarly opinions is that the cultivator may supply the seed. Indeed, a group of the Companions held that the seed must be supplied by the cultivator alone.

The Prophet’s (peace and blessings be upon him) prohibition of sharecropping and leasing land has been explained as referring to their practice of stipulating that the landowner receive the crops from a particular plot. Such a condition is invalid according to the revealed text and scholarly consensus. It is like stipulating, in a profit-sharing investment partnership, that the provider of capital receive a specified sum of dirhams: this is impermissible by agreement. Such dealings are founded on justice, and these arrangements are forms of partnership. A partnership exists only when each of the two partners has an undivided share

---

## Page 13675

such as a third or a half. If either partner is assigned a fixed amount, that is not justice but injustice. Some scholars have regarded these partnerships as hiring contracts with unspecified remuneration. They therefore said that legal analogy requires their prohibition. Some of them prohibited sharecropping in orchards and fields but permitted profit-sharing investment partnerships by juristic preference on grounds of need, since dirhams cannot be leased. This is Abū Hanīfa’s position.

Others permitted orchard sharecropping, either without restriction, as in Mālik’s position and al-Shāfiʿī’s earlier position, or only for date palms and grapevines, as in al-Shāfiʿī’s later position, because trees, unlike land, cannot be leased. They also permitted such agricultural sharecropping as was needed as an adjunct to orchard sharecropping. Thus, they permitted agricultural sharecropping as an adjunct to orchard sharecropping when the land predominated, as in al-Shāfiʿī’s position, or limited it to one-third, as in Mālik’s position.

The majority of the early generations and the jurists of the major centres, however, said that these arrangements are partnerships, not hiring contracts in which the labour itself is the object. What each party seeks is the resulting fruit and crops. They are partners: one contributes his labour and the other his property, just as in a profit-sharing investment partnership.

For this reason, the sounder of the two scholarly opinions is that when these partnerships are invalid, the customary share is due, not the customary wage. Thus, a third or a half of the profit or increase is due, according to the customary practice in comparable arrangements. A fixed payment is not due, for it could consume the entire capital and several times its amount. Rather, in an invalid arrangement, what is due

---

## Page 13676

is comparable to what is due under a valid contract. What is due under a valid contract is not a specified wage, but a specified, undivided share of the profit. Something comparable is therefore due under an invalid contract. Agricultural sharecropping is more clearly lawful than leasing and more consistent with justice and the principles of the law, for both parties share in gain and loss. Leasing is different: the landowner receives the rent, while the tenant may or may not obtain a crop. Scholars differ over the permissibility of each arrangement, but the correct view is that both are permissible.

This applies whether the land has been allotted or not. I know of no Muslim scholar—whether belonging to the four schools or otherwise—who has said that leasing allotted land is impermissible. Muslims have continued to lease allotted land from the time of the Companions down to our own day. Some people of our time, however, have introduced this novel opinion. They argue that the allotment-holder does not own the right to use the land and is therefore like a borrower who leases out land lent to him. This analogy is mistaken for two reasons.

First, the borrower had no entitlement to the use of the land; rather, the lender granted it to him gratuitously. As for lands belonging to the Muslims, the right to use them belongs to the Muslims. The ruler distributes their entitlements among them; he is not making a gratuitous grant to them as a lender does. The allotment-holder enjoys the use of the land by virtue of his entitlement, just as the beneficiary of an endowment enjoys its benefits—indeed, with even greater entitlement. If the beneficiary of an endowment may lease the endowed property, even though he may die and the lease would then terminate upon his death according to the sounder of the two scholarly opinions, then it should be permissible for the allotment-holder to lease the allotted land

---

## Page 13677

even if the lease terminates upon his death or for some other reason—all the more so.

Second, if the lender permits the property to be leased, the lease is valid. The same applies to leasing allotted land: the ruler permits allotment-holders to lease it, and he allotted it to them precisely so that they could benefit from it, whether through agricultural sharecropping or leasing. Whoever prohibits benefiting from it through leasing and sharecropping undermines the Muslims’ religious and worldly affairs. For the allotment-holder can benefit from premises such as shops, houses, and the like only by leasing them out. As for farmland and orchards, the usual ways of benefiting from them are leasing, agricultural sharecropping, and arrangements in which orchards are tended in return for a share of their produce. The murāba'a arrangement is a form of agricultural sharecropping. The only alternative to these arrangements is for him to hire someone to work the land for him at a fixed wage. Very few people do this, because he may lose his money and receive nothing in return. A partnership, by contrast, allows both parties to share in gain and loss, and is therefore closer to justice. This is why sound human dispositions prefer it. These matters can be discussed in greater detail elsewhere.

The point here is that if the ruler compels those engaged in trades to provide the work people need, such as farming, weaving, and building, he is to set their wages at the rate paid for comparable work. He must not allow the employer to reduce the worker’s wage below that rate, nor allow the worker to demand more than it when he is personally obliged to perform the work. This is a form of obligatory price regulation.

Likewise, if people need someone to make equipment for jihad, such as weapons, bridges for warfare, and the like, those workers are to be employed at the rate paid for comparable work; neither

---

## Page 13678

may the employers be allowed to wrong them, nor may the workers demand more than their due when their services are needed. This is price regulation in the sphere of labour.

As for property, if people need weapons for jihad, those who possess them must sell them at a fair market price. They must not be allowed to withhold the weapons until the enemy gains the upper hand or they are paid whatever sum they choose. If the ruler assigns particular fighters to jihad, it becomes their individual duty, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“When you are called upon to go forth, then go forth.”

This is reported in the two Sahīh collections. It is also reported from him in the Sahīh that he said:

“A Muslim must listen and obey in hardship and ease, whether willing or reluctant, and even when others are given preference over him.”

If he is obliged to strive in jihad with his person and his wealth, how could he not be obliged to sell what is needed for jihad at a fair market price? Someone unable to participate in jihad personally must support it with his wealth, according to the sounder of the two scholarly opinions. This is also one of the two positions reported from Ahmad. Allah has commanded striving in jihad with wealth and person in several places in the Quran. Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

This is reported in the two Sahīh collections. Thus, someone unable to participate in jihad physically is not relieved of the obligation to support it financially, just as someone unable to support it financially is not relieved of the obligation to participate physically. As for anyone who requires a physically incapacitated person to pay from his wealth for someone else to perform Hajj on his behalf, and regards Hajj as obligatory for someone who has the financial means, his position is

---

## Page 13679

plainly self-contradictory.

This also applies when people need someone to grind grain and bake bread for them because they cannot grind and bake in their homes as the people of Medina did in the time of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him. They had no one who ground grain or baked bread for payment, nor anyone who sold flour or bread. Rather, they bought grain and ground it and baked it in their homes. They therefore had no need for price regulation. Those who brought grain would sell it, and people would buy it from these suppliers. Hence the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The supplier is granted provision, while the hoarder is accursed.”

He also said:

“None but a sinner hoards.”

Muslim reported this in his Sahīh.

As for the report narrated from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that “he prohibited the miller’s qafīz (measure),” it is a weak hadith—indeed, a baseless one. There was no miller or baker in Medina, since its people had no need for such services. Likewise, when the Muslims conquered the lands, all the farmers were unbelievers, because the Muslims were occupied with jihad.

For this reason, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, conquered Khaybar, he entrusted it to the Jews to cultivate, because the Companions were unable to farm it themselves. Doing so would have required them to live there. Those who conquered it were the participants in the Pledge of Divine Pleasure, who had pledged allegiance beneath the tree. They numbered approximately fourteen hundred and were joined by those aboard Jaʿfar’s ship. These were the people among whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, divided the land of Khaybar. Thus, had there remained

---

## Page 13680

a group of these men there to cultivate it, the affairs of the religion that only they could attend to would have been neglected. Later, in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, when lands had been conquered and the Muslims had grown numerous, they no longer needed the Jews and expelled them. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, had said:

“We shall allow you to remain there as long as we wish”—or, according to another narration, “as long as Allah allows you to remain.”

At the time of his death, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, ordered their expulsion, saying:

“Expel the Jews and Christians from the Arabian Peninsula.”

For this reason, some scholars, such as Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī, held that unbelievers may remain in Muslim lands on payment of jizya only when the Muslims need them. Once the Muslims no longer need them, they are to expel them, as happened to the people of Khaybar. There is disagreement on this issue, but this is not the place to discuss it.

The point here is that when people need millers and bakers, this takes one of two forms:

First, they may need their services, as in the case of those who grind grain and bake bread for households. Such workers are entitled to payment, but when people need them, they may demand no more than the customary fee for comparable work, just like other craftsmen.

Second, people may need both production and sale: someone to buy wheat and grind it, and someone to bake it and sell it as bread, because people need to

---

## Page 13681

buy bread in the markets. If these traders were allowed to buy the wheat brought to market for the people and sell flour and bread at whatever price they wished, despite people’s need for that wheat, this would cause great harm. These are merchants who must pay zakat on their merchandise according to the four imams and the majority of Muslim scholars. The same obligation applies to anyone who buys something intending to resell it at a profit, whether or not he does any work on it, and whether he buys food, clothing or livestock. It applies equally to a travelling merchant who transports goods from one town to another, one who holds goods until demand is brisk, and one who continually buys and sells, like a shopkeeper. All these must pay zakat on their merchandise.

If they are obliged to produce flour and bread because people need them, they are compelled to do so, as explained above. Alternatively, they may voluntarily undertake to supply what people need, without any particular individual being compelled. In either case, prices are set for their flour and wheat: they may sell wheat and flour only at the customary price for comparable goods, allowing them a reasonable profit without harming either themselves or the public.

Scholars have differed over price regulation in two cases.

The first is when there is a prevailing price and some people wish to sell above it. According to Mālik’s school, they are prevented from doing so in the market. But are they also prevented from selling below it? There are two opinions within the school.

As for al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad’s followers, such as Abū Hafs al-ʿUkbarī and Judge

---

## Page 13682

Abū Yaʿlā, al-Sharīf Abū Jaʿfar, Abū al-Khattāb, Ibn ʿAqīl and others—they did not permit this.

Mālik cited as evidence the report he related in his Muwattaʾ from Yūnus ibn Yūsuf, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb passed by Hātib ibn Abī Baltaʿah while he was selling raisins in the market. ʿUmar told him, “Either raise your price or withdraw from our market.”

Al-Shāfiʿī and those who agreed with him responded with the report he related, saying:

“Al-Darāwardī narrated to us from Dāwūd ibn Sālih al-Tammār, from al-Qāsim ibn Muhammad, from ʿUmar, that he passed by Hātib in the market at the prayer ground. Before him were two sacks containing raisins. He asked him their price, and Hātib quoted two mudds per dirham. ʿUmar told him, ‘I have been told of a caravan approaching from al-Tāʾif carrying raisins, and they will take your price as their benchmark. Either raise your price or take your raisins home and sell them however you wish.’

“When ʿUmar returned, he reconsidered what he had done. He then visited Hātib at his home and said, ‘What I told you was neither a binding command nor a judgment. I merely intended to benefit the people of the town. Sell wherever you wish and however you wish.’”

Al-Shāfiʿī said: “The import of this report does not contradict what Mālik related. Rather, he related only part of the report—or the person who transmitted it from him did so—whereas this version gives the report from beginning to end. This is the view I adopt, for people have authority over their property. No one may take it, or any part of it, without the freely given consent of

---

## Page 13683

their owners, except where they are obliged to part with it; this is not one of those cases.”

I say:

Regarding Mālik’s view, Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī said: “The price that someone who undercuts it is ordered to match is the price charged by the majority. If one person or a small number of people alone lower their prices, they are ordered to match the majority’s price, since it is the majority’s situation that is taken into account, and their price determines the valuation of goods.”

Ibn al-Qāsim related from Mālik: “The traders are not to be expelled for the sake of five.”

He said: “In my view, the size of the markets must be considered in this matter. Is someone who increases what he offers in the market—that is, the quantity sold for a dirham, for example—to be expelled just as someone who reduces it is expelled?”

Abū al-Hasan Ibn al-Qassār al-Mālikī said: “Our scholars differed over Mālik’s words, ‘But one who lowers a price.’ The Baghdad scholars said that he meant someone who sells five for a dirham while others sell eight. Some of the Egyptian scholars said that he meant someone who sells eight while others sell five.”

He said: “In my view, both practices are prohibited. Someone who sells eight while others sell five disrupts the business of the market traders, and this may lead to disturbances and disputes. There is therefore a benefit in prohibiting both.”

Abū al-Walīd said: “There is no disagreement that this is the rule governing the market traders. As for someone bringing goods from elsewhere, Muhammad’s book states: ‘Such a trader is not prevented from selling in the market at a lower price than others.’

“Ibn Habīb said: ‘Goods other than wheat and barley may be sold only at the prevailing price; otherwise, those selling them must withdraw.’ He said: ‘As for someone bringing wheat and barley, he may sell as he wishes;

---

## Page 13684

except that, among themselves, they are subject to the rules governing market traders: if some of them lower their prices, they are left alone; but if many do so, the remainder are told, ‘Either sell at their prices or withdraw.’’

Ibn Habīb said: ‘This applies to goods sold by measure or weight, whether foodstuffs or otherwise, but not to goods sold by neither measure nor weight, since their prices cannot be fixed owing to their lack of uniformity.’”

Abū al-Walīd said: “He means when the goods sold by measure or weight are of equal quality. If their quality differs, the seller of superior goods is not ordered to sell them at the price of inferior goods.”

I say:

The second issue on which scholars differed regarding price regulation concerns the rule that no limit should be set for market traders beyond which they may not go, so long as people are fulfilling their obligations. Such price fixing was prohibited by the majority of scholars, including Mālik himself according to the well-known position reported from him. Its prohibition was also reported from Ibn ‘Umar, Sālim, and al-Qāsim ibn Muhammad. Abū al-Walīd reported that Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, Rabī‘a ibn Abī ‘Abd al-Rahmān, and Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd permitted it, but he did not quote their words.

Ashhab related from Mālik, concerning the market supervisor’s fixing prices for butchers—one-third of a ratl of mutton or half a ratl of camel meat, failing which they must leave the market—that he said: “If he fixes their prices in accordance with his assessment of their purchase costs, there is no harm in it. But I fear that they may leave the market.”

Those who held this view argued that this serves the public interest by preventing the raising of

---

## Page 13685

prices charged to them, without causing them any harm.

They said:
“People are not compelled to sell; they are merely prevented from selling at any price other than that set by the ruler, according to what he considers beneficial to both seller and buyer. The seller is neither denied a profit nor permitted a profit that harms people.”

The majority, however, cited the previously mentioned hadith of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. It was also narrated by Abū Dāwūd and others through al-‘Alā’ ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān, from his father, from Abū Hurayra, who said:

“A man came to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, fix prices for us.’ He replied, ‘Rather, pray to Allah.’ Then another man came and said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, fix prices for us.’ He replied, ‘Rather, Allah raises and lowers prices, and I certainly hope to meet Allah with no one having a claim against me for any injustice.’”

They said:
“Furthermore, compelling people to make a sale they are not obliged to make, or preventing them from doing what is lawful under Islamic law, is an injustice to them, and injustice is forbidden.”

As for how price regulation should be carried out according to those who permit it, Ibn Habīb said:
“The ruler should assemble the leading traders in the commodity concerned, with others present as a check on their truthfulness. He should ask them, ‘How do you buy, and how do you sell?’ He should then negotiate with them towards an arrangement that serves both their interests and those of the public, until they agree. Price regulation must not be imposed upon them by force, but by their consent.”

He said:
“It was on this basis that those who permitted it did so.”

Abū al-Walīd said:
“The rationale is that this makes it possible to ascertain the interests of sellers and buyers, and to allow sellers, in

---

## Page 13686

such transactions, enough profit to sustain them without imposing undue hardship on the public. If prices are imposed on them without their consent at a level that leaves them no profit, this leads to market disruption, the concealment of food supplies, and the loss of people’s wealth.”

I say:

This, then, is the matter over which the scholars disagreed.

But if people refuse to sell what they are obliged to sell, they are ordered to fulfil their obligation and punished for failing to do so. Likewise, if someone who is obliged to sell at the prevailing market price refuses to sell except at a higher price, he is undoubtedly ordered to fulfil his obligation and punished for failing to do so.

Whoever prohibits price regulation unconditionally, citing the words of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him,

“Allah is the One who sets prices, withholds, and grants abundance, and I certainly hope to meet Allah with none of you holding a claim against me for any injustice involving blood or property,”

has erred. This concerns a particular case; it is not a statement of general application. Nothing in it indicates that anyone had refused to make a sale or perform work that was obligatory upon him, or had demanded more than the customary compensation for it.

It is well known that if an owner offers an item for sale in the customary manner, but people seek to outbid one another for it and thus drive up its price, no price is to be fixed for them. As we have mentioned, most of the food sold in Medina was brought in from elsewhere, though some produce grown there might also be sold. The only crop grown there was

---

## Page 13687

barley. The sellers and buyers were not a fixed group of individuals, nor was there any particular person whose services or property people needed such that he could be compelled to work or sell. Rather, all the Muslims stood on the same footing: they all fought in Allah’s cause. Every adult Muslim capable of fighting took part in military expeditions. Each went on campaign in person, supported by his own wealth, by what he received from charitable funds or public revenues, or by equipment provided by someone else. Compelling sellers to sell their goods only at a specified price would therefore have been unjustified coercion. If compelling them to sell in the first place was impermissible, compelling them to accept a fixed price was likewise impermissible.

As for someone who is personally obliged to sell, an example is the person whose selling price the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, determined, thereby imposing a price upon him. Thus, it is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever frees his share in a slave and possesses enough wealth to cover the slave’s price shall have the slave fairly valued, without undervaluation or overvaluation. He shall then pay his partners their shares, and the slave shall become wholly free at his expense.”

Here, since the co-owner was obliged to enable his partner to emancipate the remaining share, so that the slave could become entirely free, his compensation was fixed by having the whole slave fairly valued, without undervaluation or overvaluation, and paying him his proportion of that value. According to the great majority of scholars, including Mālik, Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad, the co-owner is entitled to half the total value, not the value of a half-share.

For this reason, these scholars said: Anything that cannot be divided is to be sold and its price divided if one of the co-owners requests this;

---

## Page 13688

and any co-owner who refuses is compelled to sell. Some Mālikī scholars have reported a consensus on this, because the co-owner is entitled to half the total value, as this authentic hadith indicates, and he cannot receive that amount unless the whole property is sold. If the Lawgiver requires an owner to relinquish his property for fair compensation because his co-owner needs to emancipate the slave, and the owner may not demand more than half its value, then how much more compelling is the case of someone whose need is greater than the need to emancipate that share—for example, someone desperately in need of food, clothing or other necessities?

The Prophet’s command, peace and blessings be upon him, to assess the whole property at its fair value is precisely a form of price-setting. Likewise, a co-owner may exercise his right of pre-emption to take the half-share from its purchaser at the same price the purchaser paid, without any increase, to avoid the harm arising from joint ownership and partition. This is established by the widely transmitted Sunnah and scholarly consensus. The transaction is thus imposed at that price, without any increase, to secure the benefit of consolidating ownership in one person. How much stronger, then, is the case where a greater benefit is at stake? The purchaser is not entitled to sell it to the co-owner at whatever price he wishes. Rather, he may not demand from the co-owner anything above the price he paid for it.

This is, in fact, a form of resale at cost: the purchaser transfers the goods to someone else for the same price he paid for them. This goes further than requiring a sale at the fair market price. Nevertheless, the purchaser cannot be compelled to sell it to an outsider who is not a co-owner except at a price of his own choosing, since the latter has no need to

---

## Page 13689

buy it to the same extent as the co-owner. If, however, people are compelled by necessity to take shelter in someone’s house, finding no other place where they can shelter, he must accommodate them. Likewise, if they need him to lend them clothes to keep warm against the cold, or implements for cooking, building, or drawing water, he is to make these available free of charge.

If they need him to lend them a bucket to draw water, a pot to cook in, or an axe to dig with, is he obliged to make it available at the customary hire charge, without demanding more? Scholars of Ahmad’s school and others hold two views on this. The correct view is that these things must be made available free of charge if their owner has no need of either their use or payment for it, as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah. Allah Most High says:

“So woe to those who pray,
 yet are heedless of their prayer;
 those who show off
 and withhold small acts of kindness.”

In the Sunan collections, Ibn Masʿūd said: “We used to understand ‘small acts of kindness’ as lending a bucket, a pot, or an axe.”

In the two Sahih collections, it is reported that when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, spoke of horses, he said:

“For one man they are a source of reward, for another a protection, and for another a burden of sin. As for the man for whom they are a source of reward, he keeps them to be self-sufficient and refrain from begging, and does not forget Allah’s due concerning them and their use as mounts.”

In the two Sahih collections, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The rights due concerning camels include lending their bucket and allowing their male to mate.”

It is also authentically established that he, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade charging for a male animal’s mating services. And in the two Sahih collections, it is reported that he

---

## Page 13690

said:

“No neighbour should prevent his neighbour from inserting a beam into his wall.”

Ahmad and others hold that allowing this use is obligatory.

If someone needs to channel water through another person’s land without harming its owner, may the owner be compelled to allow it? Scholars hold two views on this, both reported from Ahmad. Reports to this effect have been transmitted from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, who said to the man who refused permission: “By Allah, we shall make it flow, even over your belly!”

A number of the Companions and Successors held that the zakat due on jewellery consists in lending it. This is one of two positions within the school of Ahmad and others.

The uses of property that must be made available are of two kinds. Some are a right due on the property itself, as mentioned concerning horses, camels and the lending of jewellery. Others must be made available because people need them.

Likewise, making one’s services available is obligatory when needed, as with teaching religious knowledge, issuing fatwas, giving testimony, adjudicating disputes, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, jihad, and other personal services. There is therefore no impediment to requiring that the use of property be made available to those in need. Allah Most High says:

“Let not the witnesses refuse when they are called upon.”

And He says:

“Let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him.”

The jurists hold four views on accepting payment for testimony, corresponding to four positions within the school of Ahmad and others:

The first is that it is not permissible under any circumstances.

The second is that it is not permissible except in cases of need.

---

## Page 13691

The third is that it is permissible unless giving testimony becomes his individual duty.

The fourth is that it is permissible. If he receives payment for the work, he may not also receive payment for delivering the testimony. These questions are discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that, since the Sunnah has established in certain cases that an owner must sell his property at a specified price—either the fair market price or the price at which he purchased it—setting prices cannot be categorically forbidden. Furthermore, the price set by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for purchasing the co-owner’s share when the other owner emancipates his share of a slave serves to complete the slave’s emancipation. This is a right due to Allah. Likewise, where people have a general need, the right involved belongs to Allah. Hence scholars classify these matters as rights and prescribed penalties belonging to Allah Most High, as distinct from those belonging to individuals. Examples include the rights of mosques, fay’ revenues (property acquired without fighting), charitable funds, endowments for the needy and for public benefit, and similar matters, as well as the prescribed penalties for armed robbery, theft, unlawful sexual intercourse and drinking wine.

Someone who kills a person to take his wealth must be executed, according to scholarly consensus, and the victim’s heirs have no right to pardon him. This differs from someone who kills another for a personal reason, such as a dispute between them. In that case, the right belongs to the victim’s next of kin: they may have him executed or pardon him, as they wish, by the consensus of the Muslims.

The Muslims’ need for food, clothing and other matters of public welfare involves no right belonging exclusively to any particular individual. Requiring someone who is obliged to sell to charge the fair market price is therefore even more warranted than setting a price to complete a slave’s emancipation. However, completing that emancipation is obligatory upon the co-owner who emancipated his share; if no price were set, he would suffer harm from the demands of

---

## Page 13692

the other co-owner for whatever price he wished. Here, the public must purchase food and clothing for themselves; if those whose goods they need were allowed to sell only at whatever price they wished, the harm to the public would be greater.

For this reason, the jurists have said that when someone is compelled by necessity to obtain another person’s food, its owner must make it available to him at the fair market price. A distinction must therefore be drawn between someone who is obliged to sell and someone who is not. Of the imams, al-Shāfiʿī is the least inclined to require an exchange or fix its price. Nevertheless, he requires someone whose food another person needs out of necessity to provide it at the fair market price. His followers disagreed over whether prices may be set when the public is in need; there are two opinions within his school on this question.

The followers of Abū Hanīfah said:

The ruler should not set prices for people unless the public’s right to protection from harm is involved. When a hoarder’s case is brought before the judge concerning the sale, at the prevailing price, of whatever exceeds his own and his family’s food requirements, the judge forbids him to hoard. If the merchant is brought before him a second time over the same matter, he imprisons him and imposes a discretionary punishment as he sees fit, to deter him or protect people from harm. If food merchants act unjustly and charge prices grossly exceeding the goods’ value, and the judge cannot safeguard the Muslims’ rights except by setting prices, he should then set them in consultation with people of sound judgment and insight. If anyone transgresses after this has been done, the judge compels him to comply.

This is clear according to Abū Hanīfah’s position, since he does not recognize placing a free person under legal interdiction. The same holds according to the two, namely Abū

---

## Page 13693

Yūsuf and Muhammad, unless the legal interdiction applies to specific individuals. If any of them sells at the price fixed by the ruler, the sale is valid, since he is not compelled to make it. May the judge sell a hoarder’s food without his consent?

One view is that this falls under the familiar disagreement concerning the sale of a debtor’s property. Another is that the judge may sell it in this case by agreement, because Abū Hanīfah recognizes legal interdiction to prevent harm to the public.

When prices rose during the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and people asked him to set prices but he declined, there is no mention of anyone possessing food and refusing to sell it. Rather, most food sellers were traders bringing food into town, who sold it upon reaching the market.

However, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade a town-dweller to sell on behalf of a desert-dweller: he forbade him to act as his broker, saying:

“Leave people alone; Allah provides for some through others.”

This is authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through several chains of transmission. He thus forbade a town-dweller familiar with prices to act as an agent for a desert-dweller bringing goods to market. If he acted as his agent, his knowledge of people’s need for the goods would enable him to raise the price charged to the buyer. He therefore forbade him to act as the seller’s agent—even though agency is generally permissible—because this would raise prices for people.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also forbade intercepting traders bringing goods to market. This too is authentically reported through several chains of transmission. The seller was granted the option to rescind the sale upon reaching the market. Hence, most jurists held that he prohibited this practice because it harmed the seller, who would receive less than the fair market price and be shortchanged. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, therefore granted the option to rescind to this

---

## Page 13694

seller. Is this option to rescind established unconditionally, or only if he has been shortchanged? Scholars hold two views, both reported from Ahmad. The stronger view is that he has this option only if he has been shortchanged. The second is that he has it unconditionally, which is the apparent position of al-Shāfiʿī’s school.

Another group held that the prohibition was instead due to the harm caused to the buyer when someone intercepts the trader, purchases his goods, and then resells them. In sum, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited forms of buying and selling that are lawful in principle until the seller knows the price—that is, the fair market price—and the buyer knows the goods.

Someone employing faulty analogical reasoning says: “The buyer may buy wherever he wishes, and he has bought from the seller,” just as he says: “The desert-dweller may appoint a town-dweller as his agent.” Yet the Lawgiver took the public interest into account. When a trader bringing goods to market does not know the prevailing price, he is ignorant of the fair market price, and the buyer thus deceives him. For this reason, Mālik and Ahmad extended the same ruling to every trusting party to a transaction.

A trusting party is someone who does not haggle, or someone who does not know the value of the item sold. Such a person is in the same position as traders bringing goods to market who do not know the prevailing price. It thus becomes clear that one must sell to such people only at the prevailing price, namely the fair market price—even if they have no need to buy from that particular seller. This is because they do not know the value, or because they place their trust in the seller without haggling with him. Consent is essential to a sale, and consent depends on knowledge. Someone who does not know that he is being overcharged may consent, or he may not

---

## Page 13695

consent. If he learns that he has been overcharged and consents, there is nothing wrong with that. But if he is dissatisfied with the fair market price, his dissatisfaction is disregarded. For this reason, the Lawgiver established the option to rescind for someone who was unaware of a defect or deceptive concealment. The presumption in a sale is that the goods are sound and that their actual condition matches their outward appearance. When someone buys on that basis, his consent is known only to extend to that condition. If the goods prove to involve deception or a defect, this is like describing them as having a particular quality when they turn out otherwise: he may consent, or he may not. If he consents, the sale stands; otherwise, he rescinds it.

In the two Sahīh collections, Hakīm ibn Hizām reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The buyer and seller each have the option to rescind so long as they have not parted. If they are truthful and disclose the relevant facts, their transaction will be blessed. If they lie and conceal them, the blessing of their transaction will be erased.”

The Sunan collections relate:

“A man owned a tree on another man’s land. The landowner suffered harm from the tree owner entering his property, so he complained to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He instructed the tree owner to accept something in exchange for it from the landowner, or to give it to him freely. When he refused, he permitted the landowner to uproot it and told the tree owner: ‘You are only causing harm.’”

Here, he required him to sell the tree if he would not give it freely. This indicates that selling becomes obligatory when the buyer needs the item. Yet how does this man’s need compare with the general public’s need for food?

The same applies to those who trade in food through milling and baking. Likewise, it applies to the operator of an inn, a market hall, or a bathhouse when people need to use these facilities and he has taken them on only as a commercial venture. If he were to refuse people entry unless they paid whatever he demanded, while they

---

## Page 13696

needed these facilities, he would not be permitted to do so and would be required to make them available at the customary rate. Likewise, someone who buys wheat and mills it for trade, or buys flour and bakes it for trade, is obliged to supply what people need from him. Indeed, requiring him to sell it at the fair market price is all the more appropriate and warranted. If he refuses to bake or mill, thereby causing people harm, he must be compelled to do so, as explained earlier. If their producing enough for everyone would meet people’s needs, allowing purchases to be made at the customary price, there is no need to set prices. But if people’s needs cannot be met except through fair price-setting, fair prices must be set for them, with neither undervaluation nor excess.

Section

As for fraud and deception in “religious matters,” these include innovations in speech and action that contradict the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations of the Ummah, such as publicly engaging in whistling and clapping in Muslim mosques.

They also include reviling the general body of the Companions and of Muslims, or reviling the Muslims’ imams, shaykhs, and rulers who are widely known throughout the Ummah for their goodness; denying the hadiths of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which the scholars have accepted; transmitting fabricated hadiths falsely attributed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; and going to extremes in religion

---

## Page 13697

by elevating human beings to the rank of God. Other examples include regarding departure from the law of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as permissible; deviating from the truth concerning Allah’s names and signs; distorting words from their proper meanings; denying Allah’s predestination; and invoking His decree and predestination to oppose His commands and prohibitions.

They also include displaying magical trickery, sleight of hand employing natural means, and similar practices that imitate the miracles granted to prophets and the extraordinary wonders granted to Allah’s righteous servants, in order to turn people away from Allah’s path or make them think well of someone who does not deserve it. This is a vast subject that would take a long time to describe.

Anyone who openly commits any of these wrongs must be stopped and punished—if he has not repented by the time he is apprehended—in accordance with what Islamic law prescribes, whether execution, flogging, or some other punishment. As for the official charged with enjoining right and forbidding wrong, he must impose discretionary punishment on anyone who openly engages in such things in word or deed, and prevent gatherings where there are grounds for suspicion. Punishment may be imposed only for a proven offense. Preventive restrictions and precautions, however, may be taken on the basis of suspicion, just as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, forbade boys to gather with anyone suspected of sexual misconduct. This is akin to taking care not to accept the testimony of someone suspected of lying, entrust anything to someone suspected of dishonesty, or do business with someone suspected of stalling on payment.

---

## Page 13698

Section

“Enjoining right and forbidding wrong” cannot be fully accomplished without the punishments prescribed by Islamic law, for Allah restrains through governing authority those whom He does not restrain through the Quran. Enforcing the prescribed punishments is a duty incumbent upon those in authority. This is accomplished by punishing the neglect of obligations and the commission of prohibited acts. Some punishments are fixed, such as giving the slanderer eighty lashes and amputating the thief’s hand. Others are not fixed and may be called “discretionary punishment.” Their severity and form vary according to the gravity of the sins, the offender’s circumstances, and how infrequently or frequently the offense occurs.

“Discretionary punishment” takes various forms: verbal reprimand and rebuke, imprisonment, banishment from one’s homeland, and beating.

If beating is imposed for neglecting an obligation—for example, failing to pray or to discharge binding obligations, such as repaying a debt despite being able to do so, returning wrongfully seized property, or restoring something entrusted to one to its rightful owners—the offender is beaten repeatedly until he fulfills the obligation, with the beatings spread out over successive days.

If, however, the beating is imposed for a past sin, as recompense for what he has done and as a deterrent from Allah to him and others, only as much as is needed is administered. There is no fixed minimum.

---

## Page 13699

As for the maximum discretionary punishment, there are three opinions within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. The first sets it at ten lashes. The second sets it below the lowest prescribed punishment: either thirty-nine or seventy-nine lashes. This is the view of many followers of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad.

The third holds that it is not restricted to these limits. This is the view of Mālik’s followers and some followers of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad, and it is one of the two positions reported from Ahmad. However, where discretionary punishment concerns an offense for which a fixed punishment is prescribed, it must fall short of that punishment. Thus, discretionary punishment for theft below the minimum value requiring amputation must not extend to amputation; punishment for rinsing the mouth with wine must fall short of the prescribed punishment for drinking it; and punishment for slanderous accusations other than accusations of unlawful sexual intercourse must fall short of the prescribed punishment for the latter.

This is the most equitable of these opinions, supported by the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the practice of his rightly guided caliphs:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered that a man whose wife had given him permission to have intercourse with her slave woman be given one hundred lashes, but averted the prescribed punishment on grounds of doubt.”

Abū Bakr and Umar ordered that a man and a woman found together under one cover be given one hundred lashes each. He also ordered one hundred lashes for the man who had made an engraving on his signet ring and taken money from the public treasury. He then had him given another hundred lashes on the second day and another hundred on the third. He also gave Sabīgh ibn Isl a severe beating, which he did not repeat, because of the religious innovation he observed in him.

Anyone whose corruption in the land cannot be stopped except by execution is to be executed, such as one who divides

---

## Page 13700

the Muslim community and one who calls people to religious innovations. Allah Most High says:

“For that reason We decreed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a person—unless in retribution for murder or for spreading corruption in the land—it is as though he had killed all mankind.”

In the Sahīh, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“If allegiance is pledged to two caliphs, execute the latter of them.”

He also said:

“Whoever comes to you while you are united under one man, seeking to divide your community, strike his neck with the sword, whoever he may be.”

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered the execution of a man who had deliberately attributed a lie to him.”

“Ibn al-Daylamī asked him about those who would not desist from drinking wine. He replied: ‘Whoever does not desist from it, execute him.’”

For this reason, Mālik and a group of Ahmad’s followers held that executing a spy is permissible. Mālik and those followers of al-Shāfiʿī who agreed with him also held that a propagator of religious innovations should be executed. This brief treatise is not the place to discuss that, for the public inspector has no authority to execute or amputate.

Forms of discretionary punishment include banishment and exile. Umar ibn al-Khattāb would impose banishment to Khaybar as a discretionary punishment for drinking wine. He also banished Sabīgh ibn Isl to Basra and sent Nasr ibn Hajjāj away to Basra when women became infatuated with him.

Section

“Discretionary punishment through financial penalties” is also sanctioned in specific cases

---

## Page 13701

according to the well-known position in Mālik’s school, and in Ahmad’s school in certain cases concerning which reports from him agree, and others concerning which they differ. It is also one of al-Shāfiʿī’s opinions, although they disagree over the details. This is demonstrated by examples from the Sunnah, such as “the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, permitting anyone who discovered someone hunting in the sanctuary of Medina to take that person’s belongings,” and his ordering wine jars to be broken and wineskins to be slit open. Another example is “his ordering Abd Allah ibn Amr to burn his two safflower-dyed garments. He asked him, ‘Should I wash them?’ He replied, ‘No, burn them.’”

Another is “his ordering them, on the day of Khaybar, to break the vessels containing donkey meat. Then, when they sought his permission to pour out their contents instead, he permitted it. When he saw the pots boiling with donkey meat, he ordered them to be broken and their contents poured out. They asked, ‘May we not pour out their contents and wash them?’ He replied, ‘Do so.’” This indicates that either course was permissible, since punishment in this manner was not obligatory.

Other examples include his demolition of the mosque built to cause harm; Moses’ burning of the calf that had been taken as a god; “his doubling, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the financial liability of someone who stole property that was not kept in a secure place”; the reports concerning the burning of the belongings of someone who misappropriated war booty, and depriving a combatant of the spoils of the man he had slain because he had transgressed against the commander; Umar ibn al-Khattāb’s and Ali ibn Abī Tālib’s orders to burn down premises where wine was sold; taking half the wealth of someone who withheld zakat; Uthmān ibn Affān’s burning of Quran manuscripts that differed from the standard codex; Umar ibn al-Khattāb’s burning of the books of the ancients; and his order to burn down the palace that Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās had built when he wished

---

## Page 13702

to seclude himself from the people. Umar therefore sent Muhammad ibn Maslamah with orders to burn down Saʿd’s palace; he went and burned it down. All these incidents are authentically reported and well known to scholars versed in such matters, and there are numerous similar cases.

Anyone who claims that financial punishments have been abrogated and attributes this unqualified position to the followers of Mālik and Ahmad has misrepresented their schools. Whoever makes this sweeping claim, whatever his school, speaks without evidence. Nothing whatsoever has been reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, indicating that he prohibited all financial punishments. Indeed, the fact that the Rightly Guided Caliphs and his senior Companions continued to apply them after his death demonstrates that they remain in force and have not been abrogated. Explicit rulings on most of these cases are transmitted from Ahmad, Mālik and his followers, while some are also positions held by al-Shāfiʿī, based on the hadiths that reached him.

The position of Mālik, Ahmad and others is that financial punishments, like corporal punishments, fall into two categories: those that accord with Islamic law and those that contravene it. Neither Mālik nor Ahmad regards financial punishment as abrogated. Those who claim abrogation have no evidence for it from either the Quran or the Sunnah. Such is the practice of many who oppose authentic texts and the established Sunnah without any proof beyond the mere assertion of abrogation. Yet when asked to identify the abrogating text, they have no proof

---

## Page 13703

for ceasing to act upon certain texts, other than the notion that his own school’s position of not acting upon them constitutes consensus, and that consensus is evidence of abrogation. There is no doubt that, if consensus is established, it indicates that the text has been abrogated, for the Muslim community does not agree upon error. Yet no consensus to cease acting upon a text is known without the abrogating text also being known. Thus, when the claims of those who allege that texts have been abrogated on the basis of a supposed consensus are closely examined, the consensus they claim usually proves unfounded. At most, they are unaware of any disagreement. Indeed, in some such cases, most scholars hold a position contrary to that of their fellow adherents, but they themselves are unfamiliar with the scholars’ views.

Furthermore, the obligations prescribed by Islamic law that constitute rights owed to Allah fall into three categories: acts of worship, such as prayer, zakat and fasting; punishments, whether prescribed or discretionary; and expiations. Each category of obligations is further divided into those involving the body, those involving wealth, and those combining both.

Acts of worship involving the body include prayer and fasting; those involving wealth include zakat; and those combining both include Hajj.

Expiations involving wealth include feeding others; those involving the body include fasting; and those combining both include offering and slaughtering a sacrificial animal.

Corporal punishments include execution and amputation; financial punishments include destroying wine vessels.

---

## Page 13704

and those combining both include flogging a thief who steals property that was not securely kept and requiring him to pay double compensation, as well as killing unbelievers and taking their property.

Just as corporal punishments sometimes serve as retribution for past acts, such as amputating a thief’s hand, and sometimes serve to avert future harm, such as executing a murderer, so too do financial punishments. Some of these fall under the elimination of wrongdoing. Like corporal punishments, they are divided into destruction, alteration, and transfer of ownership to another.

As for the first category, unlawful objects and attributes may be eliminated by destroying the material embodying them. For example, since the forms of idols worshipped besides Allah are unlawful, the material from which they are made may be destroyed. Thus, if they are made of stone, wood, or similar materials, they may be smashed and burned. Likewise, instruments of entertainment, such as the tanbūr, may be destroyed according to most jurists. This is Mālik’s position and the better-known of the two positions reported from Ahmad.

The same applies to wine vessels: they may be broken and punctured. A shop in which wine is sold may also be burned down. Ahmad explicitly stated this, as did Mālikī jurists and others.
