He said, “Peace be upon you, hired worker!”

They said, “Say, ‘Peace be upon you, commander!’”

He said, “Peace be upon you, hired worker!”

Muʿāwiyah said, “Leave Abū Muslim alone, for he knows best what he is saying.”

Abū Muslim then said, “You are only a hired worker whom the owner of these sheep has hired to tend them. If you apply tar to those afflicted with mange, treat the sick, and hold back those at the front until those at the rear catch up, their master will pay you your wages in full. But if you do not apply tar to those afflicted with mange, do not treat the sick, and do not hold back those at the front until those at the rear catch up, their master will punish you.”

This is clear upon reflection: people are Allah’s servants, rulers are Allah’s deputies over His servants, and they are the servants’ agents acting on their behalf, in the position of one of two partners in relation to

---

## Page 13843

the other; thus, they combine the roles of authority and agency. If a guardian or agent appoints someone to act on his behalf, passing over another who is better suited to handling trade or property, and sells goods at a price when he can find someone willing to pay more, he has betrayed his principal—especially if he is bound by friendship or kinship to the person he has favoured. His principal will resent and blame him, considering that he has betrayed him and shown undue favour to his relative or friend.

Section

Once this is understood, he is required only to appoint the most suitable person available. There may be no one available who is ideally suited to that office, so he must choose the best available candidate for each position according to its particular requirements. If he does so after exercising his utmost judgment and undertaking the office with due regard for its obligations, he has discharged the trust and fulfilled his duty in this matter. In this respect, he becomes one of the just and equitable leaders in Allah’s sight, even if some matters go awry because of someone else, provided that no better course was possible. For Allah says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And He says:

“Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.”

Concerning striving in Allah’s cause, He says:

“So fight in the cause of Allah; you are responsible only for yourself. And encourage the believers.”

And He says:

“O you who believe, take care of yourselves. Those who go astray will not harm you if you are rightly guided.”

Whoever fulfils the duty within his ability has thus followed right guidance. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If I command you to do something, then do

---

## Page 13844

as much of it as you can.” This was recorded in the two Sahīh collections. However, if he falls short without necessity or betrays his trust, he is punished for that.

He should know who is most suitable for each office, for authority rests on two pillars: capability and trustworthiness. As Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy.”

The ruler of Egypt said to Joseph, peace be upon him:

“Today you are established in position and trusted among us.”

And Allah Most High says, describing Gabriel:

“Indeed, this is the word of a noble messenger, possessed of strength, secure in rank with the Lord of the Throne, obeyed there and trustworthy.”

The capability required for each office varies according to its nature. In military command, it consists of courage, experience in warfare and its stratagems—for war is deception—and proficiency in the various forms of combat: shooting, thrusting, striking, riding, charging, retreating, and the like. As Allah Most High says:

“And prepare against them whatever strength you can muster and warhorses, to terrify thereby the enemy of Allah and your enemy.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Practise archery and horsemanship; I prefer that you practise archery rather than horsemanship. Whoever learns archery and then forgets it is not one of us.”

In another narration:

“It is a blessing he has denied.”

Reported by Muslim.

Capability in judging between people consists of knowing the justice taught by the Quran and the Sunnah, and having the ability to enforce judgments. Trustworthiness rests on fearing Allah and not selling His revelations for a paltry price

---

## Page 13845

and not fearing people. These are the three qualities Allah has required of everyone who judges between people, in His words, Most High:

“So do not fear people, but fear Me, and do not exchange My verses for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed—it is they who are the disbelievers.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Judges are of three kinds: two are in the Fire and one is in Paradise. A man who knows the truth but judges contrary to it is in the Fire. A man who judges between people in ignorance is in the Fire. A man who knows the truth and judges according to it is in Paradise.”

Reported by the compilers of the Sunan collections. The term ‘judge’ applies to everyone who decides and passes judgment between two people, whether a caliph, sultan, deputy, governor, someone appointed to judge according to Islamic law, or that person’s deputy. It even includes someone who judges children’s handwriting when they compete with one another. This is how the Companions of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, described it, and this is evident.

Section

Capability and trustworthiness are seldom combined in one person. For this reason, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say:

“O Allah, I complain to You of the wicked man’s vigor and the trustworthy man’s incapacity.”

Thus, every office must be entrusted to the person best suited to its particular requirements. If the choice is confined to two men, one more trustworthy and the other more capable, preference is given to whichever of them is more beneficial to that office and less

---

## Page 13846

harmful in that office. Thus, in military command, a capable, courageous man—even if he is wicked—is given preference over a weak, ineffectual man, even if the latter is trustworthy.

Imam Ahmad was asked about two men commanding military expeditions, one capable but wicked, the other righteous but weak: “With which of them should one go on campaign?”

He replied: “As for the capable but wicked man, his words benefit the Muslims, while his wickedness harms himself. As for the righteous but weak man, his righteousness benefits himself, while his weakness harms the Muslims. One should therefore go on campaign with the capable but wicked man.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, Allah supports this religion through a wicked man.”

Another version reads: “Through people who have no share in goodness.”

If he is not wicked, he has an even stronger claim to military command than someone more righteous in religion, if the latter cannot perform as effectively as he does.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appointed Khālid ibn al-Walīd to military command from the time he embraced Islam, and said:

“Indeed, Khālid is a sword Allah has drawn against the polytheists.”

Yet Khālid sometimes did things of which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, disapproved. On one occasion, he stood up, raised his hands towards heaven, and said:

“O Allah, I declare before You that I am free of responsibility for what Khālid has done.”

This was when he sent him to Banū Jadhīmah, and Khālid killed people among them and seized their property on the basis of a certain misapprehension. This was not permissible, and some of the Companions accompanying him objected to his actions. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, subsequently paid blood money for those killed and compensated them for their property. Nevertheless, he continued to give Khālid precedence in military command, because he was better suited to this role than others, and had acted as he did on the basis of a particular interpretation.

---

## Page 13847

Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, surpassed Khālid in trustworthiness and truthfulness. Yet the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to him:

“O Abū Dharr, I see that you are weak, and I wish for you what I wish for myself. Do not assume command over even two people, nor take charge of an orphan’s property.”

Reported by Muslim.

He forbade Abū Dharr from assuming command or public office because he considered him weak, despite the report:

“The sky has never sheltered, nor the earth borne, anyone more truthful in speech than Abū Dharr.”

On one occasion, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appointed ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs to command the expedition of Dhāt al-Salāsil over men who were superior to him, seeking thereby to win over the relatives of ʿAmr to whom he had sent him. He also appointed Usāmah ibn Zayd to command in order to avenge his father. Thus, he would appoint a man to secure an overriding benefit, even though others serving under that commander might surpass him in knowledge and faith.

Likewise, Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, the successor to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, continued to employ Khālid in the war against the apostates and in the conquests of Iraq and Syria. Khālid committed some lapses, acting on the basis of a particular interpretation, and it was reported to Abū Bakr that personal desire had played a part in them. Nevertheless, he did not dismiss him on their account, but rebuked him for them, because the benefit of retaining him outweighed the harm, and no one else could fill his place. For when the chief ruler’s temperament inclines towards gentleness, his deputy’s temperament should incline towards sternness; whereas if his temperament inclines towards sternness, it is appropriate that

---

## Page 13848

his deputy’s temperament should incline towards gentleness, so that a balance is maintained. This is why Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, preferred to appoint Khālid as his deputy, whereas ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, preferred to dismiss Khālid and appoint Abū ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrāh, may Allah be pleased with him. Khālid was stern like ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, while Abū ‘Ubaydah was gentle like Abū Bakr. For each of them, appointing the man he chose was the most fitting course, ensuring that his governance remained balanced. In this way, he would be among the successors of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, whose character was truly balanced. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I am the Prophet of mercy; I am the Prophet of battle.”

He also said:

“I am the cheerful one, the warrior.”

His community likewise follows a middle course. Allah Most High said of them:

“Firm against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure.”

And He Most High said:

“Humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers.”

Thus, when Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, assumed authority, they became fully accomplished as rulers. The tendencies towards opposite extremes for which they had been known during the Prophet’s lifetime—the gentleness of one and the sternness of the other—became balanced. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, even said of them:

“Follow those who come after me: Abū Bakr and ‘Umar.”

In fighting the apostates and others, Abū Bakr displayed such courage of heart that he surpassed ‘Umar and all the other Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all.

When the need for trustworthiness in an office is greater, the trustworthy person should be given preference, as in

---

## Page 13849

safeguarding funds and similar responsibilities. Collecting and safeguarding them, however, requires both strength and trustworthiness. A strong supervisor should therefore be appointed to collect them through his strength, alongside a trustworthy accountant who safeguards them through his expertise and integrity. Likewise, in military command, when the commander orders consultation with people of knowledge and religious commitment, he combines both benefits. The same applies to all other offices: if one man cannot fully serve the public interest, several should be appointed together. Thus, the most suitable candidate must be given preference, or several people appointed when one fully qualified individual does not suffice.

For judicial office, preference should be given to the most knowledgeable, the most scrupulous, and the most capable. If one candidate is more knowledgeable and the other more scrupulous, the more scrupulous should be preferred in matters where the ruling appears clear but there is a risk of bias. In matters where the ruling is subtle and confusion is feared, the more knowledgeable should be preferred.

A hadith reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah loves penetrating discernment when ambiguities arise, and He loves sound judgment when desires assail.”

Both should be preferred over the more capable candidate if the judge enjoys full support from the military governor or the general public. The more capable candidate should be preferred if administering justice requires strength and assistance for the judge more than it requires additional knowledge and scrupulousness. A judge with unrestricted jurisdiction must be knowledgeable, upright, and capable.

Indeed, the same applies to everyone who holds authority over Muslims: any deficiency in one of these qualities produces a corresponding failing. Such capability is secured either through coercion and fear,

---

## Page 13850

or through benevolence and incentives. In reality, both are indispensable.

One scholar was asked: “If the only candidates available for judicial appointment are a learned but morally corrupt man and a devout man lacking knowledge, which should be preferred?”

He replied: “If the need for religious integrity is greater because corruption is widespread, the devout man should be preferred. If the need for knowledge is greater because the cases are difficult to resolve, the learned man should be preferred.”

Most scholars give preference to the person of religious integrity, for the leading scholars agree that the appointee must be upright and qualified to give testimony. They differ, however, over the requirement of knowledge. Must he be qualified to exercise independent legal reasoning? May he instead follow the legal opinions of others? Or is the obligation to appoint the best available candidate, then the next best, as circumstances permit? These are three positions. This matter has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Although necessity permits appointing someone who does not meet the qualifications when he is the best available candidate, one must nevertheless genuinely strive to improve conditions, so that people possess all that they need in matters of public office, leadership, and the like. Similarly, an insolvent debtor must strive to repay his debt, even though, for the time being, he is required to do only what he can. Likewise, preparations for jihad must be made by mustering strength and keeping horses ready, even when incapacity suspends the obligation to fight. Whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation is itself obligatory. This differs from acquiring the means to perform Hajj and similar conditions: one is not required to acquire them, because the obligation itself arises only when they are present.

---

## Page 13851

Section

What matters most in this regard is identifying the person best suited to an office. This requires knowing the purpose of that office and the means of achieving it. Once the ends and means are known, the matter is settled. Thus, when worldly aims rather than religion came to dominate the concerns of most kings, they appointed those who would help them achieve those aims. Anyone seeking authority for himself preferred to appoint those who would uphold his authority.

The Sunnah was for the military commanders—the ruler’s deputies in charge of the troops—to lead the Muslims in Friday and congregational prayers and deliver sermons to them. Thus, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appointed Abū Bakr to lead the prayer, the Muslims appointed him to leadership in war and other affairs.

Whenever the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, dispatched a commander on a military expedition, he also appointed him to lead his companions in prayer. The same applied whenever he appointed a man as his deputy over a town, as when he appointed Attāb ibn Asīd over Mecca, Uthmān ibn Abī al-Ās over al-Tā’if, Alī, Mu‘ādh, and Abū Mūsā over Yemen, and Amr ibn Hazm over Najrān: his deputy was the one who led them in prayer and enforced

---

## Page 13852

the prescribed punishments among them and discharged the other duties of a military commander. The same was true of his successors, the caliphs, and the Umayyad rulers and some Abbasid rulers who came after them. This is because the most important matters of religion are prayer and jihad.

For this reason, most hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concern prayer and jihad. Whenever he visited a sick person, he would say:

“O Allah, heal Your servant so that he may attend prayer for You and inflict harm on an enemy for Your sake.”

When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent Mu‘ādh to Yemen, he said: “O Mu‘ādh, the most important of your duties in my eyes is prayer.”

Likewise, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, would write to his officials:

“The most important of your duties in my eyes is prayer. Whoever observes it diligently and safeguards it safeguards his religion; whoever neglects it will be even more neglectful of his other duties.”

This is because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Prayer is the pillar of religion.”

Thus, when the officeholder upholds the pillar of religion, prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing and helps people perform other acts of obedience, as Allah Most High said:

“Seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is difficult except for the humbly submissive.”

And He, glorified and exalted, said:

“O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.”

And He said to His Prophet:

“Enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in maintaining it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you. And the best outcome is for those who fear Allah.”

And He said

---

## Page 13853

Most High:

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

“I seek no provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me.”

“Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of Power, the Almighty.”

The obligatory purpose of public office is therefore to put people’s religious affairs in order—for if they lose their religion, they suffer a manifest loss, and whatever comforts they enjoyed in this world will avail them nothing—and to put in order those worldly affairs without which religion cannot be maintained. These fall into two categories: distributing wealth among those entitled to it, and punishing transgressors. As for those who do not transgress, their religious and worldly affairs are put in order.

For this reason, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb used to say:

“I have only sent my officials to you to teach you the Book of your Lord and the Sunnah of your Prophet, and to distribute your public revenues among you.”

When the subjects changed in some respects and the rulers in others, affairs fell into disorder. If a ruler strives, to the best of his ability, to put their religious and worldly affairs in order, he is among the best people of his time and among the best of those who strive in Allah’s cause. It has been reported:

“One day of a just ruler’s rule is better than sixty years of worship.”

In Imam Ahmad’s Musnad, it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The most beloved of creation to Allah is a just ruler, and the most hated of them to Him is an unjust ruler.”

In the two Sahih collections, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Seven are those whom Allah will shade in His shade on the Day when there will be no shade but His: a just ruler; a young man who grows up in obedience to Allah; a man whose heart remains attached to the mosque from the time he leaves it until he returns; two men who love one another for Allah’s sake, meeting and parting on that basis; a man who remembers Allah in solitude and tears well up

---

## Page 13854

in his eyes; a man whom a woman of rank and beauty invites to sin, but who says, ‘I fear Allah, Lord of all worlds’; and a man who gives charity so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends.”

In Sahīh Muslim, ‘Iyād ibn Himār, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The people of Paradise are of three kinds: a just ruler; a man who is merciful and tenderhearted towards every relative and every Muslim; and a wealthy man who is chaste and gives charity.”

In the Sunan collections, it is reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“One who collects charity justly is like one who strives in Allah’s cause.”

When commanding fighting in His cause, Allah Most High said:

“Fight them until there is no more fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked:

“O Messenger of Allah, a man fights out of bravery, another out of partisan zeal, and another for show. Which of these is in Allah’s cause?”

He replied:

“Whoever fights so that Allah’s word may be supreme is fighting in Allah’s cause.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded this in their Sahīh collections.

The aim, then, is that religion should be entirely for Allah and that Allah’s word should be supreme. “Allah’s word” is a comprehensive term encompassing His words contained in His Book. Likewise, Allah Most High said:

“We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance, so that people may uphold justice.”

The purpose of sending the messengers and revealing the Scriptures is therefore that people should uphold justice concerning both the rights of Allah and the rights of His creation. Then Allah Most High said:

---

## Page 13855

“And We sent down iron, in which is great strength and benefits for people, so that Allah may know those who support Him and His messengers though they do not see Him.”

Whoever departs from the Book is set right by iron. Thus, religion is upheld by the Quran and the sword. It is reported that Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh, may Allah be pleased with them both, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded us to strike with this—meaning the sword—whoever departs from this—meaning the Quran.”

Since this is the objective, it should be pursued through the means that come closest to achieving it, in order of priority. Of two candidates, whichever is better suited to achieving that objective should be appointed. If, for example, the office consists solely of leading the prayer, preference should be given to the person whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave precedence when he said:

“The people should be led in prayer by the one most proficient in reciting the Book of Allah. If they are equal in recitation, then by the one most knowledgeable about the Sunnah. If they are equal in knowledge of the Sunnah, then by the one who emigrated earliest. If they are equal in emigration, then by the oldest. No man should lead another in prayer within the latter’s sphere of authority, nor sit in his place of honour in his house, except with his permission.”

Muslim recorded it.

If two men are equally qualified and it is unclear which is more suitable, lots should be drawn between them. Thus, Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās drew lots among the people on the day of al-Qādisiyyah when they disputed over giving the call to prayer, following the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“If people knew what reward there is in the call to prayer and the first row, and could find no way to obtain them except by drawing lots, they would draw lots.”

When precedence is thus determined by Allah’s command where the proper choice is clear, and by His action—namely, the choice He determines through drawing lots when the matter is unclear—the appointing authority has discharged the trusts of public office by entrusting them to those entitled to them.

---

## Page 13856

Section

The Second Category of Trusts: Property

Allah Most High says concerning debts:

“If one of you entrusts another, let the one entrusted discharge his trust, and let him fear Allah, his Lord.”

This category includes property and debts, both private and public: returning deposits for safekeeping; returning a partner’s property or property held under an agency or profit-sharing arrangement; and returning the property of those in one’s care, such as orphans and beneficiaries of endowments, and the like. It also includes settling debts arising from purchases, repaying loans, paying women’s dowries, and paying fees for the use of property or services, and the like.

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, mankind was created anxious: distressed when evil touches him, and withholding when good touches him—except those who pray, who are constant in their prayer, and in whose wealth there is a known right for the beggar and the deprived.”

And later in the passage:

“And those who are faithful to their trusts and pledges.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth so that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you. And do not plead on behalf of the treacherous.”

That is, do not argue in their defence.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“The believer is one whom Muslims trust with their lives and wealth. The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand Muslims are safe. The emigrant is one who abandons what

---

## Page 13857

Allah has forbidden. The one who strives in Allah’s cause is one who strives against his own self for Allah’s sake.” This is an authentic hadith, parts of which appear in the Sahīh collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, and parts in Sunan al-Tirmidhī.

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“Whoever takes people’s wealth intending to repay it, Allah will repay it on his behalf; whoever takes it intending to squander it, Allah will bring him to ruin.”

Narrated by al-Bukhārī.

Since Allah has made it obligatory to return trusts lawfully received, this also indicates the obligation to restore property seized by force, stolen, or obtained through betrayal or similar wrongdoing. Borrowed property must likewise be returned.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, delivered a sermon during the Farewell Pilgrimage, in which he said:

“Borrowed property must be returned, property granted for use must be given back, debts must be repaid, and a guarantor is liable for payment. Allah has given everyone their due, so no bequest may be made to an heir.”

This category applies to both rulers and subjects: each must render to the other whatever is due. The ruler and his deputies responsible for disbursements must give everyone their due. Revenue collectors, such as the officials of the administrative bureaux, must deliver to the ruler whatever must be paid to him. The same applies to subjects who owe such dues.

Subjects have no right to demand from those administering public funds anything to which they are not entitled, thereby becoming like those of whom Allah Most High says:

“And among them are those who criticize you concerning the charitable funds. If they are given some, they are pleased; but if they are not given any, they become angry.”

“If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. To Allah alone we turn with hope.’”

Then He, glorified be He, explained who is entitled to these funds

---

## Page 13858

by saying:

“Charitable funds are only for the poor, the needy, those employed to administer them, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, freeing those in bondage, those in debt, Allah’s cause, and the stranded traveller—a duty ordained by Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

Nor may they withhold from the ruler any dues that must be paid to him, even if he is unjust. Thus, when the injustice of rulers was mentioned, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded:

“Give them what is due to them, for Allah will question them about what He entrusted to their care.”

In the Sahīh collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Children of Israel were governed by prophets. Whenever a prophet died, another prophet succeeded him. There will be no prophet after me, but there will be caliphs, and they will be many.”

They asked, “What, then, do you command us to do?”

He replied, “Honour your pledges of allegiance in the order in which they were given, and give them their due, for Allah will question them about what He entrusted to their care.”

Both collections also relate that Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“After me, you will see favouritism and things you disapprove of.”

They asked, “What do you command us to do, O Messenger of Allah?”

He replied, “Give them their due, and ask Allah for what is due to you.”

Those in authority have no right to distribute these funds according to their own desires, as an owner distributes his own property. They are merely trustees, deputies, and agents, not owners, as the Messenger of Allah said

---

## Page 13859

may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“By Allah, I neither give to anyone nor withhold from anyone; I am only a distributor, allocating as I have been commanded.”

Al-Bukhārī narrated it, and a similar report is related from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. Thus, the Messenger of the Lord of all worlds explained that withholding and giving were not matters of his own will and choice, as they are for an owner permitted to dispose of his property, or for kings who give to those they love and withhold from those they hate. Rather, he is Allah’s servant, distributing wealth at His command and allocating it wherever Allah Most High has commanded him.

Likewise, a man said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, “O Commander of the Faithful, why not allow yourself more generous expenditure from the funds of Allah Most High?”

ʿUmar replied, “Do you know what my position in relation to these people is like? It is like that of a group travelling together who pooled their money and entrusted it to one man to spend on their behalf. Would it be lawful for that man to favour himself over them with their money?”

On one occasion, a large sum from the one-fifth share was brought to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him. He said, “People who have faithfully discharged their trust in this are truly trustworthy.”

One of those present said to him, “You have faithfully discharged your trust towards Allah Most High, so they have faithfully discharged their trust towards you. Had you indulged yourself, they would have done likewise.”

It should be understood that those in authority are like a marketplace: whatever sells well there is brought to it. This is what ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, may Allah be pleased with him, said. If truthfulness, righteousness, justice and trustworthiness are in demand there, these will be brought there; but if falsehood and wickedness are in demand there

---

## Page 13860

and injustice and treachery, these will be brought there. Those in authority must acquire wealth through lawful means, allocate it where it rightfully belongs, and not withhold it from those entitled to it.

Whenever ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, heard that one of his deputies had committed an injustice, he would say:

“O Allah, I did not command them to wrong Your creation or neglect what is due to You.”

Section

Public revenues established in the Quran and Sunnah fall into three categories: war booty, alms, and fay.

War booty is wealth taken from the unbelievers through fighting. Allah mentioned it in Sūrat al-Anfāl (The Spoils of War), which He revealed during the Battle of Badr. He called it anfāl because it is an addition to the Muslims’ wealth. He said:

“They ask you about the spoils of war. Say, ‘The spoils of war belong to Allah and the Messenger.’”

Further on, He says:

“And know that whatever you take as spoils of war, one-fifth belongs to Allah, the Messenger, his near relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveller,” to the end of the verse.

He also said:

“So consume what you have taken as spoils of war, lawful and good, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, may Allah be pleased with them both, reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been given five things that no prophet before me was given: I have been granted victory

---

## Page 13861

through fear cast into my enemies’ hearts from a month’s journey away. The earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification for me, so let any man of my nation pray when the time for prayer comes. War booty has been made lawful for me, though it was not lawful for anyone before me. I have been granted intercession. Each prophet was sent specifically to his own people, whereas I have been sent to all humanity.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“I have been sent with the sword ahead of the Hour, so that Allah alone is worshipped, without any partner. My provision has been placed beneath the shade of my spear, and humiliation and abasement have been imposed upon whoever opposes my command. Whoever imitates a people is one of them.”

Ahmad narrated this in his Musnad from Ibn ‘Umar, and al-Bukhārī cited it as supporting evidence.

The obligation concerning war booty is to set aside one-fifth, distribute that fifth to those whom Allah Most High has mentioned, and divide the remainder among those who took part in the campaign. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “War booty belongs to those who were present at the battle.” These are those who attended for the purpose of fighting, whether or not they actually fought. It must be divided fairly among them, without favouring anyone because of his leadership, lineage, or merit, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his caliphs used to divide it.

Sahīh al-Bukhārī reports that Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās, may Allah be pleased with him, considered himself to have greater merit than those below him. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Are you granted victory and provision except through the weak among you?”

In Ahmad’s Musnad, Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās reported:

“I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, should a man who defends his people receive the same share as anyone else?’ He replied, ‘May your mother be bereaved of you, son of Umm Sa‘d! Are you granted provision and victory

---

## Page 13862

except through the weak among you?’”

War booty continued to be divided among those who took part in the campaigns under the Umayyad and Abbasid dynasties, when the Muslims fought the Byzantines, Turks, and Berbers.

However, the ruler may grant an additional share to those who distinguish themselves by inflicting greater harm upon the enemy: for example, a detachment sent out from the army, a man who scales a high fortress and captures it, or someone who charges the enemy commander and kills him, thereby routing the enemy, and similar cases. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his caliphs used to grant additional shares for such deeds. He would award a detachment one-quarter after the fifth had been deducted on the outward journey, and one-third after the fifth had been deducted on the return journey.

Regarding this additional award, scholars have said that it is taken from the fifth. Some have said that it is taken from one-fifth of the fifth, so that none of those entitled to the booty receives preferential treatment over the others. The correct view, however, is that it may be taken from the remaining four-fifths, even though this entails favouring some over others, provided this serves a religious interest rather than personal inclination, as the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did on more than one occasion.

This is the position of the jurists of Syria, Abū Hanīfa, Ahmad, and others. On this basis, one view holds that the ruler may award a quarter or a third with or without a prior stipulation, but may award more than that only through a prior stipulation—for example, by saying, “Whoever directs me to a fortress shall receive such-and-such,” or, “Whoever brings me a head shall receive such-and-such,” and similar statements.

Another view holds that he may not award more than a third, nor make an additional award except through a prior stipulation. These are two positions reported from Ahmad and others. Likewise—according to the correct view—

---

## Page 13863

the ruler may say, “Whatever anyone takes is his,” as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said during the Battle of Badr, if he considers the benefit of doing so to outweigh the harm.

If the ruler collects and distributes the spoils, no one may misappropriate anything from them:

“Whoever misappropriates anything will bring what he misappropriated on the Day of Resurrection.”

Misappropriation is a betrayal of trust. Nor is plundering permissible, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade it.

If the ruler forgoes collecting and distributing the spoils and gives lawful permission to take from them, whatever anyone takes without transgression becomes lawful for him once its fifth has been deducted. Anything that indicates permission constitutes permission.

If, however, the ruler gives no permission, or gives permission that is not lawful, a person may take the equivalent of what he would receive through distribution, taking care to act justly. Whoever forbids Muslims to collect the spoils under these circumstances, yet allows the ruler to do whatever he wishes with them, has adopted two positions at opposite extremes. Allah’s religion follows a middle course.

A just distribution is to allot one share to a foot soldier and three shares to a mounted fighter with an Arabian horse: one for the fighter and two for his horse. This is how the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, distributed the spoils at Khaybar.

Some jurists hold that a mounted fighter receives two shares. The former view, however, is supported by the authentic Sunnah, and also by the fact that a horse requires upkeep for itself and its groom—and a mounted fighter with his horse is of greater benefit than two foot soldiers.

Some of them hold that Arabian and mixed-breed horses are to be treated equally

---

## Page 13864

in this regard. Others hold that a mixed-breed horse receives only one share, as reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions.

A mixed-breed horse is one whose dam is Nabataean. It is called a birdhawn, and some call it a Tatar horse. It may be a stallion, a gelding—called an akdīsh—or a ramaka, meaning a mare. The early Muslims kept stallions for combat because of their strength and spirit; mares for raids and night attacks, because they do not give a neigh that would alert the enemy and put them on their guard; and geldings for travel, because of their greater endurance on journeys.

If captured property, whether land or movable possessions, previously belonged to Muslims, and its owner is identified before distribution, it must be returned to him, by Muslim consensus.

There are transmitted reports and scholarly opinions concerning the detailed questions and rulings on spoils. Muslims agree on some of these and disagree on others. This is not the place to discuss them; the purpose here is merely to state the comprehensive principles.

Section

As for zakat, it belongs to those whom Allah Most High has named in His Book. It is reported that a man asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for some zakat, and he replied:

“Allah has not left the apportionment of zakat to a prophet or anyone else; rather, He has divided it into eight portions. So if

---

## Page 13865

you belong to one of those categories, I will give you some.”

The poor and the needy share a common need for sufficient provision. Zakat is therefore not lawful for a wealthy person or for someone strong and able to earn a living.

(And those employed to administer it) are those who collect it, safeguard it, keep its records, and perform similar duties.

(And those whose hearts are to be reconciled) we shall discuss, if Allah Most High wills, under fay’ revenues.

(And for freeing those in bondage) includes assisting slaves who have contracted to purchase their freedom, ransoming captives, and freeing slaves. This is the strongest opinion concerning this category.

Those in debt are people who have debts they cannot repay. They are given enough to discharge their debts, even if the amount is large, unless they incurred them in disobedience to Allah Most High; in that case, they are not given anything until they repent.

(And in the cause of Allah) refers to fighters who are not given enough from Allah’s funds to meet the needs of their campaigns. They are given what they need to campaign, or enough to make up the shortfall, whether in horses, weapons, expenses, or wages. Hajj also falls within the cause of Allah, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said.

(And the wayfarer) is someone travelling from one land to another.

Section

As for fay’, its basis is what Allah Most High mentioned in Sūrat al-Hashr, which He revealed concerning the expedition against Banū al-Nadīr after Badr, beginning with His words:

“Whatever Allah bestowed upon His Messenger from them—you spurred neither horses nor camels to obtain it, but Allah gives His messengers power

---

## Page 13866

over whom He wills. And Allah has power over all things.”

“Whatever Allah has bestowed upon His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah, the Messenger, his close relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer, so that wealth may not circulate solely among the rich among you. Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.”

“It is for the poor Emigrants who were driven from their homes and possessions, seeking Allah’s bounty and pleasure and supporting Allah and His Messenger. They are the ones who are true.”

“And those who had made their home in the city and embraced the faith before their arrival love those who migrate to them. They feel no resentment in their hearts over what the Emigrants have been given, and they give them preference over themselves, even though they too are in need. Those who are protected from their own souls’ stinginess—it is they who will be successful.”

“And those who come after them say, ‘Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and let there be no rancour in our hearts towards those who believe. Our Lord, You are indeed Most Kind, Most Merciful.’”

Thus Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the Emigrants, the Helpers, and those who came after them with the qualities He described. This third category therefore includes everyone who follows this course until the Day of Resurrection, just as they are included in His words, Most High:

“And those who believe afterwards, emigrate, and strive alongside you—they are of you.”

And in His words:

“And those who follow them in righteousness.”

And in His words:

“And others among them who have not yet joined them. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

As for His words:

“You spurred neither horses nor camels to obtain it,”

they mean: you did not

---

## Page 13867

urge on or drive any horses or camels.

For this reason, the jurists say that fay’ is wealth taken from the disbelievers without fighting, since spurring on horses and camels signifies fighting. It is called fay’ because Allah restored it to the Muslims—that is, returned it to them from the disbelievers. The underlying principle is that Allah Most High created wealth only to assist in His worship, just as He created His creatures only to worship Him. He therefore made lawful for His believing servants who worship Him the lives of the disbelievers, which they did not devote to His worship, and their wealth, which they did not use to assist them in His worship. He restored to the believers what was rightfully theirs, just as a man is given back what was wrongfully taken from his inheritance, even if he had never previously received it.

This includes the jizyah levied on Jews and Christians; money that the enemy agrees to pay under a peace settlement or presents to the Muslim ruler, such as payments sent from Christian lands and the like; the one-tenth levy collected from merchants from enemy territories; and the one-twentieth levy collected from merchants of protected non-Muslim communities when they trade outside their own lands. This was how ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, collected these levies. It also includes wealth taken from those among them who break their covenant, and the land tax originally imposed upon them, even if some of it has since come to be borne by some Muslims.

Furthermore, fay’ encompasses all state funds belonging to the Muslim treasury, such as property with no identifiable owner—for example, the estate of a Muslim who dies without an identifiable heir—and wrongfully seized property, articles lent for use, and deposits held in trust:

---

## Page 13868

whose owners could not be identified; and other Muslim property, whether immovable or movable. This and similar property belongs to the Muslims collectively. Allah Most High mentioned only fay’ in the Quran because, during the Prophet’s lifetime, peace and blessings be upon him, no one died without an identifiable heir, since the lineages of his Companions were well known.

On one occasion, a man from a tribe died, and the Prophet gave his estate to the most senior man of that tribe—that is, the one closest in descent to their common ancestor. A number of scholars adopted this position, including Ahmad, in one expressly recorded opinion, and others. Another man died, leaving only his freedman, and the Prophet gave his estate to that freedman. A number of Ahmad’s followers and other scholars adopted this position. He also gave a man’s estate to someone from the same village. He, peace and blessings be upon him, and his successors took a broad approach to giving a deceased person’s estate to someone related to him by descent, as we have mentioned.

He collected nothing from the Muslims except obligatory alms, and he commanded them to strive in Allah’s cause with their wealth and their lives, as Allah commanded in His Book.

During the time of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, there was no comprehensive register of funds received and distributed. Rather, funds were distributed as they came in. During the time of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, wealth increased, the territories expanded, and the population grew. He therefore established a register of stipends for the fighting men and others; and the military register—in our time—includes

---

## Page 13869

most of it; and that register is the most important of the Muslims’ registers. The provincial centres also had registers for land tax, fay’, and other revenues collected. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and his successors would audit their officials’ accounts of obligatory alms, fay’, and other funds.

Thus, in this period and earlier, revenues came to fall into three categories:

One category consists of funds that the ruler is entitled to collect according to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus, as we have mentioned. Another consists of funds whose collection is unanimously prohibited, such as levies collected from villagers for the public treasury because someone has been killed among them—even when the deceased has an heir—or payments exacted for an offense someone has committed that incurs a prescribed punishment, which is then waived in return. This also includes tolls whose imposition is unanimously held to be unlawful. A third category is subject to juristic judgment and disagreement, such as the estate of someone who has a blood relative who is neither a fixed-share heir nor a residuary heir, and similar cases.

Rulers and subjects frequently wrong one another in these matters: the former take what is unlawful, while the latter withhold what they are obliged to pay, just as soldiers and farmers may wrong one another. Likewise, some people neglect their obligations of striving in Allah’s cause, while rulers hoard wealth belonging to Allah that they are not permitted to hoard. The same applies to punishments used to enforce payment: punishments that are permissible or obligatory may be neglected, while unlawful punishments may be inflicted.

The underlying principle is that anyone obliged to hand over money or property—such as a man

---

## Page 13870

who holds a deposit, capital entrusted to him under a profit-sharing arrangement, partnership funds, his principal’s money, an orphan’s property, endowment funds, or money belonging to the public treasury, or who owes a debt that he can repay—is liable to punishment if he refuses to fulfil the obligation, whether by returning specific property or repaying a debt, and is known to be able to do so. He may be punished until he produces the property or discloses its whereabouts. If the property’s whereabouts are known and he endures imprisonment, what is due is recovered from that property, and there is no need to beat him. If he refuses both to disclose his property’s whereabouts and to pay, he is beaten until he pays what is due or allows it to be recovered. The same applies if he refuses to provide the maintenance obligatory upon him despite being able to afford it.

This is supported by the report of ‘Amr ibn al-Sharīd, from his father, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Delay by one who has the means to pay makes it lawful to censure and punish him.”

This was narrated by the compilers of the Sunan. He also said, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Delay in payment by one who can afford it is wrongdoing.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded this in their Sahīhs. “Delay” here means procrastination, and a wrongdoer deserves punishment and discretionary discipline.

This is an agreed-upon principle: anyone who commits a prohibited act or neglects an obligation deserves punishment. If the punishment is not fixed by Islamic law, it is discretionary, determined by the ruler’s judgment. Thus, a debtor who can afford to pay but procrastinates is punished with imprisonment. If he persists, he is punished by beating until he fulfils his obligation. Jurists among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others—may Allah be pleased with them—have explicitly stated this, and I know of no disagreement concerning it.

Al-Bukhārī also narrated in his Sahīh: “Ibn ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, reported that

---

## Page 13871

the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, after concluding a peace agreement with the people of Khaybar stipulating the surrender of their gold, silver, and weapons, questioned one of the Jews—Sa‘yah, the uncle of Huyayy ibn Akhtab—about Huyayy ibn Akhtab’s treasure. He replied, ‘Expenses and wars have consumed it.’ The Prophet said, ‘Only a short time has passed, and the wealth was too great for that.’ The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, then handed Sa‘yah over to al-Zubayr, who subjected him to torture. Sa‘yah said, ‘I saw Huyayy going around a ruin here.’ They went and searched, and found the leather container in the ruin.”

This man was a protected non-Muslim, and a protected non-Muslim may not lawfully be punished without just cause. Likewise, anyone who conceals something he is obliged to disclose, such as information he must provide, is punished for neglecting that obligation.

A just ruler may recover from officials and others whatever Muslim property they have taken unlawfully, including gifts they receive because of their office. Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, may Allah be pleased with him, said, “Gifts to public officials constitute misappropriation.” Ibrāhīm al-Harbī narrated in his Kitāb al-Hadāyā (Book of Gifts), from Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Gifts to governors constitute misappropriation.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded in their Sahīhs that Abū Humayd al-Sā‘idī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, appointed a man from al-Azd called Ibn al-Lutbiyyah to collect zakat. When he returned, he said, ‘This is for you, and this was given to me as a gift.’ The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, ‘Why is it that a man whom we appoint to carry out one of the duties that

---

## Page 13872

Allah has entrusted to us then says, “This is for you, and this was given to me as a gift”? Why did he not stay in his father’s or mother’s house and see whether he would be given gifts or not? By Him in whose hand is my soul, whatever he takes from it, he will bring on the Day of Resurrection, carrying it on his neck—whether a camel grunting, a cow lowing, or a sheep bleating.’ Then he raised his hands until we could see the pale skin of his armpits, and said, ‘O Allah, have I conveyed the message? O Allah, have I conveyed the message? O Allah, have I conveyed the message?’—three times.”

Likewise, preferential treatment shown to governors in transactions such as sales, leases, profit-sharing partnerships, orchard-tending partnerships, sharecropping, and the like is a form of gift. For this reason, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, took half the wealth of some of his officials, including men of merit and religious integrity who were not suspected of dishonesty. He did so only because of the preferential treatment and other advantages they had received on account of their office. The circumstances called for this, for he was a just ruler who distributed equally. When both ruler and subjects changed, however, each person was obliged to fulfill whatever obligations he could, refrain from what was forbidden to him, and not treat as forbidden what Allah had permitted him.

People may be afflicted with governors who refuse gifts and the like so that they can thereby fully exact their unjust demands from them, while neglecting the duty Allah has imposed on them to attend to people’s needs

---

## Page 13873

so they would prefer someone who takes payment from them for putting an end to an injustice and meeting a lawful need to such a governor. For the governor described earlier has sold his Hereafter for another’s worldly gain, and no one makes a more ruinous bargain than one who sells his Hereafter for another’s worldly gain.

Rather, the duty is to ward off injustice from them to the best of one’s ability and meet those needs essential to people’s welfare: conveying their needs to the ruler, informing him of their circumstances, directing him towards what benefits them, and turning him away from what harms them. This should be done through various means, gentle or otherwise, just as officials with personal interests, such as scribes and others, pursue their own ends.

In the hadith of Hind ibn Abī Hālah, may Allah be pleased with him, it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“Convey to me the needs of those unable to convey them themselves. Whoever conveys to a person in authority the need of someone unable to convey it himself, Allah will make his feet firm upon the Bridge on the Day when feet slip.”

Imam Ahmad and Abū Dāwūd, in his Sunan, narrated from Abū Umāmah al-Bāhilī, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever intercedes on behalf of his brother, then accepts a gift given to him for doing so, has entered a great gate among the gates of usury.”

Ibrāhīm al-Harbī narrated from ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: “Unlawful gain is when someone seeks to have a man’s need met, and when it is met, he is given a gift and accepts it.”

It is also reported from Masrūq that he spoke to Ibn Ziyād about an injustice, and Ibn Ziyād redressed it. The man concerned then gave Masrūq a young male slave as a gift, but he returned him, saying: “I heard Ibn Mas‘ūd say: ‘Whoever

---

## Page 13874

redresses an injustice suffered by a Muslim and takes anything from him in return, whether little or much, has acquired unlawful gain.’ I said, ‘O Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān, we thought unlawful gain meant only bribery in judgment.’ He replied, ‘That is disbelief.’”

But if the ruler exacts wealth from his officials intending to reserve it for himself and his relatives, neither side should be assisted, for both are wrongdoers. They are like a thief stealing from another thief, or two factions fighting out of partisan loyalty and rivalry for power. It is unlawful for anyone to assist in wrongdoing.

Cooperation is of two kinds:

The first is cooperation in righteousness and piety, such as jihad, enforcing the prescribed punishments, securing people’s rights, and giving those entitled to receive their due. This is something Allah and His Messenger have commanded. Whoever refrains from it for fear of becoming an accomplice of oppressors has abandoned an individual or communal obligation while imagining himself to be exercising religious scrupulousness. How often cowardice and faintheartedness are mistaken for scrupulousness, since both involve abstaining and holding back!

The second is cooperation in sin and aggression, such as helping to take a protected life, seize protected property, beat someone who does not deserve to be beaten, or the like. This is what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden. However, if wealth has been taken unjustly and returning it to its owners has become impossible—as is the case with much wealth held by rulers—then assisting in the disbursement of this

---

## Page 13875

wealth for the benefit of the Muslims—such as securing the frontiers, supporting the fighting forces, and similar purposes—constitutes cooperation in righteousness and piety. For when its owners cannot be identified and the wealth cannot be returned to them or their heirs, the ruler must spend it for the benefit of the Muslims, repenting as well if he was the wrongdoer.

This is the view of the majority of scholars, including Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, and Ahmad. It is also reported from several Companions and supported by the scriptural evidence, as explained elsewhere. If someone else took the wealth, he himself must dispose of it in this way. Likewise, if the ruler refuses to return it, helping to spend it for the benefit of its owners is preferable to leaving it in the hands of someone who will squander it, depriving both its owners and the Muslims of its benefit.

For the Sharia rests upon Allah’s words:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able,”

which explain His words:

“Fear Allah as He should be feared,”

and upon the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

This is recorded in the two Sahīh collections. It also rests upon the principle that benefits must be secured and enhanced, and harms prevented and reduced. When these considerations conflict, what is prescribed is to secure the greater of two benefits by foregoing the lesser, and to avert the greater of two harms while bearing the lesser.

The one who cooperates in sin and aggression is someone who helps an oppressor commit oppression. As for someone who

---

## Page 13876

helps an oppressed person lessen the injustice inflicted upon him or pay an unjust exaction is acting as the agent of the oppressed, not of the oppressor. He is like someone who lends the oppressed person money or undertakes to carry his money to the oppressor on his behalf.

For example, if an oppressor demands money from the guardian of an orphan or the administrator of an endowment, and, after exhausting his efforts to resist the demand, he strives to avert it by paying a smaller sum to the oppressor or to someone else, then he is doing good:

“There is no blame upon those who do good.”

The same applies to an owner’s agent—whether an auctioneer, a scribe, or someone else—who acts on owners’ behalf in concluding contracts, receiving payments, and paying what is demanded of them, rather than acting for the oppressors in collecting it.

Likewise, if an unjust levy is imposed on the people of a village, street, marketplace, or city, and a well-meaning man from among them intervenes to ward it off as far as possible, apportioning it among them according to their means, without favoring himself or anyone else and without accepting bribes, but instead acting on their behalf in resisting the demand and making payment, then he is doing good.

Usually, however, someone who becomes involved in this acts as an agent of the oppressors, showing favoritism, accepting bribes, shielding whomever he wishes, and taking money from whomever he wishes. Such a person is among the worst oppressors, who will be gathered in coffins of fire, together with their helpers and others like them, and then hurled into the Fire.

---

## Page 13877

Section: Expenditure

In distributing funds, priority must be given to the most important public interests of the Muslims, then to the next most important, such as providing stipends to those whose work benefits Muslims generally.

These include the fighting forces, who provide military support and wage jihad. They have the strongest claim to fay revenues, since these are obtained only through them. Indeed, the jurists have differed over whether fay revenues are reserved exclusively for them or may be allocated to all public interests. As for other state revenues, there is agreement that they serve all public interests, except for funds earmarked for particular categories, such as zakat and spoils of war.

Those entitled to receive funds also include people entrusted with the Muslims’ affairs, such as governors, judges, scholars, and officials responsible for collecting, safeguarding, and distributing funds, and similar duties. This extends to prayer leaders, muezzins, and others in comparable roles.

Funds may likewise be spent on purchases and wages for works of general benefit: securing frontier posts with mounts and weapons, maintaining public thoroughfares that require maintenance—including bridges and arched bridges—and waterways such as rivers.

Those entitled to receive funds also include people in need, for the jurists have differed over whether they should be given priority

---

## Page 13878

over others when allocating revenues other than zakat, such as fay and similar funds. There are two views on this in the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. Some hold that they should be given priority; others hold that entitlement to these funds rests on being Muslim, so Muslims share in them just as heirs share in an inheritance. The correct view is that those in need should be given priority, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to give them priority, as he did when distributing the wealth of Banū al-Nadīr. Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“No one has a greater right to this wealth than anyone else. What matters is a man’s precedence in Islam, the benefit he brings, the efforts he makes, and his need.”

Thus Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, divided them into four categories:

First: those with precedence in Islam, through whose early efforts the funds were acquired.

Second: those who serve the Muslims by securing benefits for them, such as rulers and scholars who bring them religious and worldly benefits.

Third: those who render valuable service in warding off harm from them, such as those who strive in Allah’s cause: soldiers, intelligence agents among emissaries and sincere advisers, and others like them.

Fourth: those in need.

If any of these people serves without payment, Allah has met the need through him. Otherwise, he is given enough to suffice him or an amount commensurate with his work. Once you understand that grants are made according to the benefit

---

## Page 13879

a man brings and his need, from funds for public welfare as well as from zakat, then he is entitled to anything beyond that only on the same basis as his peers—for example, when he shares in war booty or an inheritance.

The ruler may not give anyone something to which he is not entitled merely out of personal inclination, because of kinship, affection or the like. Still less may he give it in return for an unlawful service, as in payments to effeminate, beardless boys, whether free or enslaved, and others like them; to prostitutes, singers, jesters and the like; or to fortune-tellers, such as soothsayers, astrologers and others like them.

However, it is permissible—indeed, obligatory—to give money to win over those whose hearts need to be won over, even if it is not lawful for the recipient to accept it. Thus Allah Most High has permitted in the Quran that zakat be given to those whose hearts are to be won over. Likewise, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to give such people grants from fay and similar revenues. These were leaders whose tribes obeyed them. For example, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to give to al-Aqraʿ ibn Hābis, chief of Banū Tamīm; ʿUyaynah ibn Hisn, chief of Banū Fazārah; Zayd al-Khayr al-Tāʾī, chief of Banū Nabhān; and ʿAlqamah ibn ʿUlāthah al-ʿĀmirī, chief of Banū Kilāb. He also gave to leaders of Quraysh who had been granted amnesty, such as Safwān ibn Umayyah, ʿIkrimah ibn Abī Jahl, Abū Sufyān ibn Harb, Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, al-Hārith ibn Hishām and many others.

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, may Allah be pleased with him, reported:

---

## Page 13880

“While in Yemen, ʿAlī sent the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, a small piece of gold still mixed with its earth. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, divided it among four men: al-Aqraʿ ibn Hābis al-Hanzalī, ʿUyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazārī, ʿAlqamah ibn ʿUlāthah al-ʿĀmirī, chief of Banū Kilāb, and Zayd al-Khayr al-Tāʾī, chief of Banū Nabhān.

He said: “Quraysh and the Ansār became angry and said, ‘He gives to the chiefs of Najd and leaves us out!’ The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said, ‘I did that only to win their hearts.’ Then a man came with a thick beard, prominent cheekbones, deep-set eyes, a protruding forehead and a shaved head. He said, ‘Fear Allah, Muhammad!’ The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, replied, ‘Who would fear Allah if I disobeyed Him? Does He entrust me with the people of the earth, yet you do not trust me?’”

He said: “Then the man turned away, and one of those present asked permission to kill him—they believed it was Khālid ibn al-Walīd. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said, ‘From this man’s stock will come people who recite the Quran, but it will not go beyond their throats. They will kill the people of Islam and leave the idolaters alone. They will pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. If I encounter them, I shall surely slay them as ʿĀd were slain.’”

Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj, may Allah be pleased with him, reported:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, gave Abū Sufyān ibn Harb, Safwān ibn Umayyah, ʿUyaynah ibn Hisn and al-Aqraʿ ibn Hābis one hundred camels each. He gave ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās less than that, whereupon ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās said:

---

## Page 13881

‘Will you divide my share of the spoils and al-ʿUbayd’s
Between ʿUyaynah and al-Aqraʿ?
Neither Hisn nor Hābis
Surpassed Mirdās in the assembly.
Nor was I inferior to either man;
Whoever is lowered today will not be raised.’

He said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, then made his allotment up to one hundred.” Reported by Muslim. Al-ʿUbayd was the name of his horse.

Those whose hearts are to be won over are of two kinds: disbelievers and Muslims. A disbeliever may be given something in the hope of securing a benefit, such as his embracing Islam, or averting his harm if it cannot otherwise be averted. Giving to a Muslim who commands obedience may likewise bring an anticipated benefit: strengthening his commitment to Islam, bringing someone like him to Islam, collecting money from those who will pay only out of fear, inflicting losses on the enemy, or restraining him from harming the Muslims if he cannot otherwise be restrained.

Although this kind of giving may outwardly resemble the practice of kings—giving to leaders while leaving out the weak—deeds are judged by intentions. If the purpose is to serve the interests of the religion and its followers, it belongs to the same category as the giving of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and his caliphs. If the purpose is domination in the land and corruption, it belongs to the same category as Pharaoh’s giving.

It is only those whose religion is corrupt who object to this, such as Dhū al-Khuwaysirah, who objected to the Prophet’s doing so, peace and blessings be upon him, prompting him to say what he said about him. Likewise, his faction, the Khārijites, objected to the actions of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, through which he sought

---

## Page 13882

the common good through arbitration, the erasure of his name, and his refusal to take Muslim women and children captive. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded that these people be fought, because their religion is corrupt and brings neither worldly nor otherworldly well-being.

Misguided scrupulousness is often confused with cowardice and miserliness, since both involve refraining from something. Thus, avoiding wrongdoing out of fear of Allah Most High may be confused with neglecting the prescribed duties of jihad and spending out of cowardice and miserliness. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The worst qualities in a person are consuming greed and paralyzing cowardice.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “An authentic hadith.”

Likewise, someone may refrain from acting, believing or pretending that this is scrupulousness, when it is nothing but arrogance and a desire for supremacy. The Prophet’s saying, peace and blessings be upon him,

“Deeds are judged only by intentions,”

is comprehensive and complete. Intention is to a deed what the soul is to the body. After all, both someone prostrating to Allah and someone prostrating to the sun or moon place their foreheads on the ground: their outward forms are identical, yet one is among those nearest to Allah Most High, while the other is among those furthest from Him.

Allah Most High said:

“And urge one another to patience and urge one another to compassion.”

A transmitted report states:

“The best of faith is generosity and patience.”

Caring for people and governing them properly require generosity, meaning giving, and valour, meaning courage. Indeed, neither religious nor worldly affairs can be set right without them. Thus, whoever fails to uphold these two qualities is stripped of authority by [Allah] (1), who transfers it to someone else, as declared by

## Page 13883

Allah Most High:

“O you who believe, what is the matter with you that, when you are told, ‘Go forth in the cause of Allah,’ you cling heavily to the earth? Are you content with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? Yet the enjoyment of worldly life is but little compared with the Hereafter.”

“If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and replace you with another people. You will not harm Him at all, and Allah has power over all things.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Here you are, called upon to spend in the cause of Allah, yet some of you are miserly. Whoever is miserly is only miserly at his own expense. Allah is free of all need, while you are the needy. If you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“Those of you who spent and fought before the conquest are not equal to the others. They are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterwards. Yet Allah has promised the finest reward to them all.”

He thus linked the matter to spending, which is generosity, and fighting, which is courage. Likewise, Allah Most High said in more than one place:

“Strive with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah.”

He made clear that miserliness is among the major sins in His saying:

“Let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them. Rather, it is bad for them. On the Day of Resurrection, what they withheld will be fastened around their necks.”

And in His saying:

“Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the cause of Allah—give them tidings of a painful punishment,”

to the end of the verse. The same applies to cowardice, as in the saying of Allah Most High:

“Whoever turns his back to them on that day—unless maneuvering for battle or joining another group—has incurred the wrath of Allah, and his refuge is

---

## Page 13884

Hell—an evil destination.” And in His saying, Most High:

“They swear by Allah that they are indeed of you, but they are not of you; rather, they are people who are afraid.”

This is frequently addressed in the Quran and Sunnah, and it is something upon which people everywhere agree. They even say in their popular proverbs:

“He offers neither a spear-thrust nor a bowl of food.”

And they say:

“Neither a horseman nor a notable among the Arabs.”

Yet people have divided into three groups in this regard.

One group is dominated by a love of supremacy in the land and corruption. They give no thought to their ultimate fate in the Hereafter. They consider that authority cannot be maintained without giving, and that giving may be impossible without extracting wealth unlawfully. Thus they become lavish plunderers and lavish givers.

These people say that no one can govern others unless he takes for himself and gives to others. If a scrupulous man assumes office who neither takes nor gives, the leaders become displeased with him and remove him—if they do not also harm him personally or seize his wealth. These people attend to their immediate worldly interests while neglecting the longer-term consequences in both this world and the Hereafter. Their eventual outcome is therefore bad in both worlds, unless repentance or something similar sets their final affairs right.

Another group possesses fear of Allah Most High and religious commitment that restrains them from what they believe to be reprehensible: wronging people and committing forbidden acts. This is good and obligatory. Yet they may also believe that governance cannot be carried out without the forbidden practices of the first group, and so they abstain from it altogether. Their religious commitment may also be accompanied by cowardice, miserliness, or ill temper. Thus they sometimes neglect an obligation whose neglect is

---

## Page 13885

more harmful to them than certain forbidden acts. Or they forbid an obligation, thereby barring people from Allah’s path. They may be acting on an interpretation they believe to be correct. They may even believe that opposing such conduct is obligatory and can only be accomplished through fighting, so they fight the Muslims, as the Khawārij did. Such people cannot put worldly affairs in order or uphold religion in its entirety, though they may put many aspects of religion and some worldly affairs right. They may be pardoned for errors made in exercising independent judgment, and their shortcomings may be forgiven. Yet they may also be among those whose deeds bring the greatest loss—those whose efforts in this worldly life have gone astray while they think they are doing good.

This is the approach of someone who takes nothing for himself and gives nothing to others, and who does not believe in winning over unbelievers and evildoers through money or other benefits. He regards giving to those whose hearts are to be won over as a form of injustice and unlawful giving.

The third group:

The balanced community: those who follow the religion of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and of his successors in authority over people of all ranks until the Day of Resurrection. Their approach is to spend wealth and provide benefits to people—even leaders—as needed to put affairs right, uphold religion, and sustain the worldly affairs necessary for religion. They also exercise personal restraint, refraining from taking even money to which they are entitled. Thus they combine fear of Allah with doing good:

“Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who do good.”

Religious governance cannot be fully realized without this, and neither religious nor worldly affairs can be set right except

---

## Page 13886

through this approach. Such a person feeds people what they need, while eating only what is lawful and wholesome himself. Moreover, he can manage with less expenditure than the first type needs, for people have expectations of someone who takes for himself that they do not have of someone who exercises restraint. He also brings about improvements in people’s religious lives that the second type cannot, for restraint when one has power strengthens reverence for religion.

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Sufyān ibn Harb reported that Heraclius, emperor of the Byzantines, asked him about the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “What does he command you to do?” He replied: “He commands us to pray, speak truthfully, exercise restraint, and maintain ties of kinship.”
