A report states: “Allah revealed to Abraham, His close friend, peace be upon him: ‘Abraham, do you know why I took you as a close friend? Because I saw that giving was dearer to you than taking.’”

What we have discussed concerning provision and giving—generosity and conferring benefits—has its counterpart in patience and anger—courage and warding off harm.

People fall into three groups: those who become angry for their own sake and for their Lord’s sake; those who become angry neither for their own sake nor for their Lord’s sake; and the third, balanced group, who become angry for their Lord’s sake, not their own. Thus, in the two Sahīh collections, ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never struck with his hand any servant of his, any woman, any animal, or anything at all, except when fighting in Allah’s cause; nor

---

## Page 13887

did he ever retaliate for a wrong done to him, unless Allah’s sacred limits were violated. When Allah’s sacred limits were violated, nothing could withstand his anger until he had exacted retribution for Allah’s sake.”

As for those who become angry for their own sake but not their Lord’s, or take for themselves without giving to others, they constitute a fourth group: the worst of creation. Neither religious nor worldly affairs can be set right through them. By contrast, the righteous, who govern in the most complete manner, are those who fulfil their obligations and refrain from what is forbidden. They give whatever serves religion through its giving, take only what is lawful for them, become angry for their Lord’s sake when His prohibitions are violated, and forgo their own rights. Such was the character of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in giving and warding off harm. This is the most perfect conduct, and the closer a person comes to it, the better he is.

Let the Muslim therefore strive to approach it to the best of his ability, then seek Allah’s forgiveness for any shortcoming or negligence, having recognized the perfection of the religion with which Allah Most High sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This concerns the words of Allah, Glorified and Exalted:

“Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due.”

And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 13888

Section

As for the words of Allah Most High:

“And when you judge between people, judge with justice.”

Judging between people concerns prescribed punishments and rights, which fall into two categories. The first comprises punishments and rights that do not belong to particular individuals, but benefit Muslims generally or a category of them. All are in need of them.

These are called Allah’s prescribed punishments and Allah’s rights. Examples include the punishments prescribed for highway robbers, thieves, those guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, and others of their kind, as well as adjudication concerning public funds, charitable endowments, and bequests not designated for particular individuals. These are among the most important responsibilities of governing authorities.

For this reason, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “People must have a government, whether righteous or wicked.”

He was asked: “Commander of the Faithful, we understand the righteous kind, but what of the wicked?”

He replied: “Through it, prescribed punishments are enforced, roads are made safe, the enemy is fought, and fay (public revenues) is distributed.”

Rulers must investigate and administer matters in this category without anyone bringing a claim. Likewise, testimony concerning them is given without anyone bringing a claim. The jurists have, however, differed over amputating a thief’s hand: does this require the victim of the theft to claim his property? There are two opinions on this in the school of Ahmad and other schools; but they agree that it does not

---

## Page 13889

require the victim of the theft to demand the prescribed punishment. Some of them have, however, stipulated that he must claim his property, to rule out any semblance of entitlement on the thief’s part.

These punishments must be enforced against the high-born, the lowly, and the weak. It is unlawful to suspend them because of intercession, a gift, or anything else, and interceding to prevent their enforcement is unlawful. Whoever suspends them for such reasons, despite being able to enforce them, incurs the curse of Allah, the angels, and all mankind. Allah will accept neither sarf nor ‘adl from him, and he is among those who have traded Allah’s revelations for a paltry price.

Abū Dāwūd narrated in his Sunan that ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever intercedes to prevent the enforcement of one of Allah’s prescribed punishments has opposed Allah in His command. Whoever knowingly argues in support of falsehood remains under Allah’s wrath until he desists. Whoever falsely attributes something to a devout Muslim will be confined in Radghat al-Khabāl until he clears himself of what he said.”

He was asked: “Messenger of Allah, what is Radghat al-Khabāl?”

He replied: “The discharge from the inhabitants of the Fire.”

Thus, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, mentioned adjudicators, witnesses, and litigants: these are the pillars of adjudication.

The two Sahīh collections relate from ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her:

“Quraysh were troubled by the case of the Makhzūmī woman who had stolen. They said, ‘Who will speak to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, on her behalf?’ They said, ‘Who would dare approach him except Usāmah ibn Zayd?’ He said, ‘Usāmah, do you intercede concerning one of Allah’s prescribed punishments? The Children of Israel were destroyed only because they

---

## Page 13890

would let a high-born person go when he stole among them, but would enforce the prescribed punishment when a weak person stole. By Him in Whose hand is Muhammad’s soul, if Fātimah, the daughter of Muhammad, were to steal, I would cut off her hand.’”

There is a lesson in this account. The two noblest clans in Quraysh were Banū Makhzūm and Banū ‘Abd Manāf. This woman’s theft warranted the amputation of her hand—her theft being, according to some scholars, her denial of having borrowed property, or, according to others, a separate act of theft. Although she belonged to one of the greatest tribes and noblest families, when Usāmah, the beloved of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, interceded for her, the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, became angry. He rebuked him for involving himself in something Allah had forbidden: interceding to prevent the enforcement of prescribed punishments. He then gave the example of the foremost of all women—whom Allah had declared innocent of such wrongdoing—saying:

“If Fātimah, the daughter of Muhammad, were to steal, I would cut off her hand.”

It is reported that this woman whose hand was cut off repented, and that she would subsequently visit the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who would attend to her needs.

It is also reported:

“If the thief repents, his hand precedes him into Paradise; if he does not repent, his hand precedes him into the Fire.”

Mālik related in al-Muwatta’ that a group of people seized a thief to bring him before ‘Uthmān, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Zubayr met them and interceded for him. They said, “When he is brought before ‘Uthmān, intercede for him with him.” He replied:

“If cases involving prescribed punishments reach the ruler, may Allah curse both the intercessor and the one who grants the intercession!”

He meant the person who accepts the intercession.

“Safwān ibn

---

## Page 13891

Umayyah was sleeping on a cloak of his in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, when a thief came and stole it. He seized the thief, who was brought before the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. The Prophet ordered that his hand be cut off. Safwān said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, would you cut off his hand over my cloak? I give it to him.’ He replied, ‘Why did you not do that before bringing him to me?’ Then he had his hand cut off.” Reported by the compilers of the Sunan.

He, peace and blessings be upon him, meant that pardoning the thief before bringing him would have been permissible, but not after the matter had been brought before him. Thus, a prescribed punishment may not be set aside through pardon, intercession, a gift, or any other means. For this reason, the scholars agree—as far as I know—that when highway robbers, thieves, and others like them are brought before the ruler and subsequently repent, the prescribed punishment is not waived. Rather, it must be carried out even if they repent. If their repentance is sincere, the punishment serves as an expiation for them, and their submitting to it completes their repentance—just as one must restore people’s rights and submit to legal retribution for violations of human rights.

The basis for this is Allah’s saying:

“Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in it, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will bear a share of it. Allah is ever a Keeper over all things.”

Intercession means assisting a petitioner, joining him so that they become a pair where previously he stood alone. If someone assists him in righteousness and piety, that is good intercession; if he assists him in sin and aggression, that is evil intercession. Righteousness is what one is commanded to do, and sin is what one is forbidden to do. If, however, they are lying about their repentance, Allah does not bring the schemes of the treacherous to success.

---

## Page 13892

Allah Most High has also said:

“The punishment of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption in the land is that they be killed, crucified, have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land. That is their disgrace in this world, and in the Hereafter they will suffer a tremendous punishment.”

“Except those who repent before you apprehend them. Know, then, that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

He thus excepted only those who repent before being apprehended. Anyone who repents after being apprehended remains among those subject to the prescribed punishment, as indicated by the general wording, its implied meaning, and the underlying rationale. This applies when the offence has been established by evidence.

If, however, it is established through a confession, and the person comes forward confessing the sin in repentance, there is a disagreement concerning this, discussed elsewhere. The apparent position of Ahmad’s school is that carrying out the prescribed punishment is not obligatory in such a case. Rather, if the person requests that it be carried out on him, it is carried out; but if he leaves, no prescribed punishment is inflicted on him. This is how the report concerning Mā‘iz ibn Mālik—in which the Prophet said, “Why did you not let him go?”—has been understood, as has the report of the man who said, “I have committed an offence requiring a prescribed punishment, so carry it out on me,” along with other reports.

In the Sunan collections of Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Amr reports that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Pardon one another for offences requiring prescribed punishments before bringing them to me. Once such a case reaches me, its punishment becomes obligatory.”

In the Sunan collections of al-Nasā’ī and Ibn Mājah, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reports that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“A prescribed punishment carried out on earth is better for its inhabitants than forty mornings of rain.”

This is because sins cause a reduction in provision and fear of the enemy, as the Quran and Sunnah indicate. Thus, when

---

## Page 13893

the prescribed punishments are carried out, obedience to Allah becomes manifest and disobedience to Allah Most High diminishes, bringing provision and victory.

It is not permissible to take money from someone guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, drinking intoxicants, highway robbery, or similar offences in exchange for suspending the prescribed punishments—whether for the public treasury or anyone else.

Money taken to suspend a prescribed punishment is vile, unlawful gain. If the ruler does this, he combines two grave evils: suspending the prescribed punishment and consuming unlawful gain. He thus neglects an obligation and commits a forbidden act. Allah Most High says:

“Why do the rabbis and religious scholars not forbid them from saying what is sinful and devouring what is unlawful? How wretched is what they have been practicing.”

Allah Most High also says concerning the Jews:

“Avid listeners to falsehood, devourers of unlawful gain.”

This is because they consumed unlawful gains from bribes, known as birtīl and sometimes called gifts or other names. Whenever the ruler consumes unlawful gain, he finds himself needing to listen to lies in the form of false testimony and the like. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, “cursed the giver of a bribe, its recipient, and the go-between—the intermediary between them.” This is reported by the compilers of the Sunan collections.

The two Sahīh collections relate:

“Two men brought a dispute before the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. One of them said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, judge between us according to the Book of Allah.’ The other, who had greater understanding, said, ‘Yes, O Messenger of Allah, judge between us according to the Book of Allah, and allow me to speak.’

“He said, ‘Speak.’

“The man said, ‘My son was a hired labourer in the household of

---

## Page 13894

this man—meaning a hired worker—and he had unlawful intercourse with his wife. I ransomed him with a hundred sheep and a servant. I asked some men of learning, and they told me that my son was liable to a hundred lashes and banishment for a year, and that this man’s wife was liable to stoning.’

He said, ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, I shall certainly judge between you according to the Book of Allah. The hundred sheep and the servant must be returned to you. Your son shall receive a hundred lashes and be banished for a year. Go in the morning, O Unays, to this man’s wife and question her. If she confesses, stone her.’ He questioned her, and she confessed, so he stoned her.”

This hadith shows that when this money was paid on the offender’s behalf to spare him the prescribed punishment, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, ordered that the money be returned to its owner and that the prescribed punishment be carried out. He did not take the money for the Muslims, whether those fighting in Allah’s cause, the poor, or others. The Muslims unanimously agree that suspending a prescribed punishment in exchange for money or otherwise is impermissible. They also unanimously agree that money taken from those guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, drinking intoxicants, armed aggression, highway robbery, or similar offences in exchange for suspending the prescribed punishment is vile, unlawful gain.

Much of the corruption in people’s affairs arises from suspending prescribed punishments in exchange for money or through influence. This is one of the chief causes of corruption among the inhabitants of the deserts, villages, and cities: the Bedouins, Turkomans, Kurds, peasants, and partisans such as Qays and Yaman; and among urban people, including their leaders, rich and poor, rulers, commanders, and soldiers. It causes the official in authority to lose people’s respect, diminishes his standing in their hearts, and undermines his authority. When he accepts bribes and payments to suspend one prescribed punishment, his resolve to enforce another is weakened

---

## Page 13895

and he becomes like the accursed Jews.

The word birtīl originally means an elongated stone. A bribe was given this name because it stops the recipient’s mouth from speaking the truth, just as a long stone would. As a report states:

“When bribery enters through the door, trustworthiness leaves through the window.”

The same applies when money is taken for the state in exchange for suspending a prescribed punishment, such as these unlawful payments called “disciplinary fines.” Do you not see how, when troublemaking Bedouins take people’s property and then come to the ruler, leading horses to present to him, or bringing other gifts, their eagerness to spread corruption grows, respect for the governing authority and its power is undermined, and the subjects become corrupt?

The same applies to peasants and others. Likewise, when someone who drinks intoxicants is caught and pays some of his money, see how emboldened the wine dealers become! They hope that, if caught, they too can buy their release with some of their wealth. That governor then takes it as unlawful gain, devoid of blessing, while the corruption continues.

The same applies to influential people who protect someone from having a prescribed punishment carried out against him. For example, a peasant may commit an offence and then seek refuge in a village belonging to the sultan’s deputy or one of his commanders, where he is protected in defiance of Allah and His Messenger. The person who protects him is then among those whom Allah and His Messenger have cursed. Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“May Allah curse whoever commits an offence or shelters an offender.”

Thus, whoever shelters any of these offenders

---

## Page 13896

has been cursed by Allah and His Messenger.

If the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever intercedes to prevent one of Allah’s prescribed punishments from being carried out has opposed Allah’s command,”

then what of someone who prevents these punishments through his power and direct intervention, accepting unlawful money in exchange for shielding criminals? This applies especially to prescribed punishments against desert dwellers. Among the greatest causes of corruption among them is protecting their transgressors through influence or money. Whether the money is taken for the public treasury or for the governor, secretly or openly, all of this is forbidden by Muslim consensus. It is akin to tadmīn (financial arrangements) involving taverns and wine. Anyone who is enabled to do this, or who helps another do it in return for money he receives, falls into the same category.

Money taken in this way resembles a prostitute’s earnings, a soothsayer’s fee, the price paid for a dog, and the payment received by someone who facilitates unlawful sexual relations—the person called a procurer. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The price paid for a dog is foul, a prostitute’s earnings are foul, and a soothsayer’s fee is foul.”

Narrated by al-Bukhārī. A prostitute’s earnings are what is called hudūr al-qihāb. The same applies to money given to effeminate boys, whether enslaved or free, in return for committing sexual immorality with them. A soothsayer’s fee includes such things as the gratuity given to an astrologer or someone similar for what he claims to be good news, and other such reports.

When a ruler refrains from opposing wrongdoing and enforcing the prescribed punishments for it in return for money he receives, he becomes like a bandit chief who shares the plunder with highway robbers, or a procurer who takes his payment to bring two people together for an act of sexual immorality,

---

## Page 13897

and his conduct resembles that of the wicked old woman, Lot’s wife, who directed evildoers to his guests. Concerning her, Allah Most High said:

“So We saved him and his family, except his wife; she was among those who remained behind.”

And He said:

“So set out with your family during a portion of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife; she will indeed suffer what they suffer.”

Thus Allah punished that wicked old woman, who acted as a procuress, with the same punishment He inflicted upon the wicked people who perpetrated vile deeds. This is because all such conduct amounts to taking money to assist in sin and transgression. A ruler is appointed only to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong: this is the purpose of authority. If a governor enables wrongdoing in return for money he receives, he acts in direct opposition to that purpose. He is like someone you appoint to help you against your enemy, only for him to help your enemy against you, or someone who takes money to wage jihad in Allah’s cause, then uses it to fight the Muslims.

This becomes clear when we consider that people’s well-being depends on enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. For the well-being of people and their livelihoods lies in obedience to Allah and His Messenger, and this cannot be fully achieved without enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. It is through this that this community became the best community brought forth for humanity. Allah Most High said:

“You are the best community brought forth for humanity: you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.”

And He said:

“Let there be among you a group who call to goodness, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong.”

And He said:

“The believing men and believing women are allies of one another: they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.”

And He said concerning the Children of Israel:

“They would not forbid one another

---

## Page 13898

from the wrongdoing they committed. Evil indeed was what they used to do.”

And Allah Most High said:

“When they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized the wrongdoers with a terrible punishment for their defiance.”

Allah Most High thus tells us that when the punishment descended, He saved those who forbade evil and subjected the wrongdoers to severe punishment.

An authentic hadith relates that Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, addressed the people from the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, saying:

“O people, you recite this verse but apply it incorrectly: ‘O you who believe, take care of yourselves. Those who go astray will not harm you if you are rightly guided.’ Yet I heard the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, say: ‘When people see wrongdoing and do not change it, Allah may soon encompass them all with a punishment from Him.’”

Another hadith states:

“When a sin is committed secretly, it harms only the one who commits it. But when it becomes public and is not condemned, it harms the community at large.”

The foremost purpose of this category of adjudication concerning Allah’s prescribed limits and His rights, which we have discussed, is to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

Enjoining what is right includes enjoining prayer, zakāh, fasting, pilgrimage, truthfulness, trustworthiness, dutifulness to parents, maintaining ties of kinship, treating one’s family and neighbours well, and similar matters. The ruler must therefore command everyone under his authority to perform the obligatory prayers and punish anyone who neglects them, according to the consensus of the Muslims.

---

## Page 13899

If those who neglect the prayers form a group that resists enforcement, they are to be fought for abandoning them, by the consensus of the Muslims. Likewise, they are to be fought for abandoning zakāh, fasting and other obligations, and for declaring lawful manifest prohibitions agreed upon by consensus, such as marrying women within the prohibited degrees of kinship, spreading corruption in the land, and similar acts. Every group that collectively resists compliance with any of Islam’s manifest ordinances established by mass transmission must be fought until religion is wholly for Allah, according to the agreement of the scholars.

If the person who neglects prayer is an individual, one view holds that he is to be punished by beating and imprisonment until he prays. The majority of scholars, however, hold that he must be executed if he refuses to pray after being called upon to repent. If he repents and prays, he is spared; otherwise, he is executed. Is he executed as a disbeliever or as a sinful Muslim? There are two views on this. Most of the early Muslim generations held that he is executed as a disbeliever. All of this concerns someone who acknowledges that prayer is obligatory. If, however, he denies its obligation, he is a disbeliever by the consensus of the Muslims. The same applies to anyone who denies the other obligations mentioned above or denies the prohibitions over which fighting is required.

Punishment for abandoning obligations and committing prohibited acts is thus the purpose of jihad in Allah’s cause. Jihad is obligatory upon the Muslim community by agreement, as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah, and it is among the best deeds.

A man said:

“O Messenger of Allah, direct me to a deed equal to jihad in Allah’s cause.”

He replied:

“You cannot do it,” or, “You would not be able to bear it.”

The man said:

“Tell me what it is.”

He replied:

“Can you, when the fighter sets out, fast without breaking your fast

---

## Page 13900

and pray without flagging?”

The man said:

“Who could do that?”

He replied:

“That, then, is what equals jihad in Allah’s cause.”

He also said:

“In Paradise there are indeed a hundred ranks, with a distance like that between heaven and earth between each rank and the next. Allah has prepared them for those who wage jihad for His cause.”

Both hadiths are recorded in the two Sahīh collections. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The foundation of the matter is Islam, its pillar is prayer, and its pinnacle is jihad in Allah’s cause.”

Allah Most High said:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

He Most High also said:

“Do you consider providing water to pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque equal to believing in Allah and the Last Day and striving in Allah’s cause? They are not equal in Allah’s sight, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.”

“Those who believe, emigrate, and strive in Allah’s cause with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank with Allah. It is they who are successful.”

“Their Lord gives them good news of mercy from Him, His pleasure, and gardens in which they will have lasting bliss.”

“They will remain there forever. Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.”

Section

Among such punishments is the punishment of armed aggressors and highway robbers: those who confront people with weapons on roads and elsewhere to seize their property openly, whether Bedouins, Turkomans, Kurds, peasants, wicked soldiers, or hardened evildoers among the townspeople

---

## Page 13901

or others. Allah Most High said concerning them:

“The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption in the land is that they be executed or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land. That is their disgrace in this world, and in the Hereafter they will suffer a tremendous punishment.”

Al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated in his Musnad that Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said concerning highway robbers:

“If they kill and seize property, they are executed and crucified. If they kill without seizing property, they are executed but not crucified. If they seize property without killing, their hands and feet are cut off on opposite sides. If they terrorize travelers without taking any property, they are banished from the land.”

This is the view of many scholars, including al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and it is close to the view of Abū Hanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him.

Some scholars hold that the ruler may exercise his judgment concerning them: he may execute anyone whose execution he considers beneficial, even if that person has not killed anyone—for example, a leader whose orders are obeyed in such activities. He may likewise order amputation for anyone whose amputation he considers beneficial, even if that person has not taken any property—for example, someone with the stamina and strength to seize property. Some scholars also hold that when they seize property, they are executed, subjected to amputation, and crucified. The first view is that of the majority.

If an armed aggressor has killed someone, the ruler must execute him as a prescribed punishment. By scholarly consensus, he may under no circumstances be pardoned. Ibn al-Mundhir reported this consensus. Nor is the decision in his case left to the heirs of the person killed. This differs from the case of a man who kills another because of enmity between them, a dispute, or some other

---

## Page 13902

personal motive. In that case, the decision concerning the killer’s life rests with the victim’s legal heirs: they may have him executed, pardon him, or accept blood money, because he killed for a personal purpose. Armed robbers, however, kill in order to seize people’s property, so their harm affects the public, like that of thieves. Their execution is therefore a prescribed punishment owed to Allah. This is agreed upon among the jurists. They have differed, however, over whether a person is to be executed for armed robbery even when the victim is not of equivalent legal status to the killer—for example, when the killer is free and the victim enslaved, or the killer is Muslim and the victim a non-Muslim under a covenant of protection or someone granted safe-conduct. The stronger view is that he is to be executed as a prescribed punishment because his killing spreads harm throughout society, just as he is subject to amputation for taking their property and imprisonment to enforce their rights.

When armed robbers form a group, and one of them personally commits the killing while the others assist and support him, one view holds that only the actual killer is executed. The majority, however, hold that all of them are executed, even if they number a hundred, and that those providing support and the actual killer are treated alike. This is what has been transmitted from the Rightly Guided Caliphs: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, executed the lookout of a band of armed robbers. The lookout is the observer who sits in an elevated position to watch for anyone approaching them. Moreover, the actual killer was only able to commit the killing through the strength and assistance of those supporting him. When members of a group reinforce one another until they can resist being subdued, they share in both reward and punishment, as do those who fight in Allah’s cause. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

---

## Page 13903

said:

“Muslims’ lives are equally inviolable; protection granted by the lowest in status among them is binding upon them all; they stand united against others; and their raiding detachments share their spoils with those who remain behind.”

This means that when a detachment goes out from the Muslim army and captures spoils, the army shares in those spoils, because the detachment succeeded through its backing and strength. The detachment, however, receives an additional allotment beyond that of the rest of the army. When a detachment went out at the beginning of a campaign, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would award it an additional quarter after the fifth had been set aside. On their return to their homelands, if a detachment went out, he would award it an additional third after the fifth had been set aside.

Likewise, if the army captured spoils, the detachment would share in them, because it was serving the army’s interests. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, allotted shares to Talha and al-Zubayr at Badr because he had sent them on a mission serving the army’s interests. The helpers and supporters of a group able to resist being subdued therefore belong to it, sharing its rights and liabilities.

The same applies to those who fight on wrongful grounds without any interpretive justification, such as those fighting out of tribal partisanship and rallying to the calls of pre-Islamic ignorance—Qays and Yaman, for example, and similar groups: both sides are wrongdoers. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When two Muslims confront one another with their swords, both the killer and the one killed are in the Fire.”

He was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, that is the killer, but why the one killed?”

He replied, “He intended to kill his companion.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded it in their Sahīh collections. Each faction is liable for the lives and property it has destroyed belonging to the other, even if the individual killer is not identified, because a faction whose members strengthen one another to resist being subdued is like a single person. Concerning this, Allah Most High says:

“Prescribed for you is legal retribution for those murdered.”

---

## Page 13904

If, however, they take property without killing anyone—as Bedouins often do—then, according to most scholars, including Abū Hanīfa, Ahmad and others, each offender’s right hand and left foot are to be amputated. This is the meaning of Allah Most High’s words:

“Or that their hands and feet be cut off on opposite sides.”

The hand with which he strikes and the foot on which he walks are amputated. The wounds are cauterized with boiling oil or the like to stop the bleeding, lest continued blood loss cause his death. Likewise, a thief’s amputated hand is cauterized with oil.

This punishment may be a stronger deterrent than execution. When Bedouins, lawless soldiers and others continually see someone among them whose hand and foot have been amputated, they are reminded of his crime and are deterred. An execution, by contrast, may be forgotten. Some proud individuals may prefer being killed to having their hand and foot amputated on opposite sides; thus, this punishment is more severe as an exemplary punishment for them and others like them.

If, however, they brandish weapons without killing anyone or taking any property, then sheathe them or flee and abandon armed aggression, they are to be banished. One view is that banishment means driving them from place to place, without allowing them to settle in any locality. Another is that it means imprisoning them. A third is that the ruler should adopt whichever measure he considers most beneficial, whether banishment, imprisonment or something similar.

The prescribed method of execution is to strike the neck with a sword or a similar implement, because this is the least painful manner of killing. Likewise, Allah has prescribed the killing of those humans and animals that may lawfully be killed

---

## Page 13905

in this manner when one has power over them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has prescribed excellence in all things. So when you kill, kill well; and when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade and spare his animal suffering.”

Narrated by Muslim. He also said:

“The believers are the most restrained of all people in killing.”

As for the crucifixion mentioned, it means raising them up in an elevated place so that people may see them and their case become widely known. According to the majority of scholars, this takes place after execution. Some scholars, however, say that they are crucified and then killed while crucified. Some scholars have permitted killing them by means other than the sword, even saying that they may be left in that elevated place until they die of their own accord, without being killed.

Mutilation in killing, however, is not permissible except as retaliation in kind. ‘Imrān ibn Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never delivered a sermon to us without commanding us to give charity and forbidding us to mutilate. Even when we kill disbelievers, we do not mutilate them after death, cut off their ears and noses, or slit open their bellies—unless they have done that to us, in which case we may do to them as they did to us.”

Yet refraining is better, as Allah Most High says:

“If you retaliate, then retaliate only to the extent that you have suffered. But if you are patient, that is certainly better for those who are patient.”

“And be patient; your patience is only through Allah.”

It is said that this was revealed when the polytheists mutilated Hamza and other martyrs of Uhud, may Allah be pleased with them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If Allah grants me victory over them, I will surely inflict twice as much mutilation as they inflicted on us.”

Allah then revealed this verse—although it had already been revealed earlier in Mecca

---

## Page 13906

as with His words:

“And they ask you about the spirit. Say, ‘The spirit is of my Lord’s command.’”

And His words:

“And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with misdeeds.”

The same applies to other verses revealed in Mecca: an occasion subsequently arose in Medina that called for the same address, so they were revealed a second time—the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then said:

“Rather, we shall be patient.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Burayda ibn al-Husayb, may Allah be pleased with him, reported:

“Whenever the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent a commander at the head of a detachment or an army, or on an errand of his own, he would instruct him personally to fear Allah Most High and to treat the Muslims accompanying him well. Then he would say: ‘Go forth in Allah’s name, in Allah’s cause. Fight those who disbelieve in Allah. Do not misappropriate the spoils, act treacherously, mutilate, or kill a child.’”

If they brandish weapons to seize property in a built-up area rather than in the open country, some scholars have said that they are not classed as brigands, but rather as snatch-thieves and plunderers, because help can reach the victim if he calls upon people for assistance.

Most scholars, however, hold that the same ruling applies to them in built-up areas and in the open country. This is the well-known position reported from Mālik, and the position of al-Shāfi‘ī, most of Ahmad’s followers, and some of Abū Hanīfa’s followers. Indeed, they deserve punishment even more in built-up areas than in the open country, because built-up areas are places of safety and tranquillity, where people support and help one another. Their daring to commit such acts there indicates the severity of their armed aggression and use of force. Moreover, they rob a man of all his property in his own home, whereas a traveller

---

## Page 13907

usually carries only part of his wealth. This is the correct view, particularly in the case of these organized gangs whom ordinary people in Syria and Egypt call al-minsar and who were known in Baghdad as al-ayyārīn. Even if they fight with sticks or stones thrown by hand or with slings and the like, they are still brigands.

Some jurists are reported to have held that brigandage can only be committed with edged weapons. Others have reported a consensus that it can be committed with either edged or blunt weapons. Whether or not there is disagreement on this, the correct view, held by the overwhelming majority of Muslims, is that anyone who fights to seize property, by whatever means of fighting, is a brigand and highway robber. Likewise, any disbeliever who fights Muslims, by whatever means of fighting, is a belligerent; and any Muslim who fights the disbelievers with a sword, spear, arrow, stones, or a stick is fighting in Allah’s cause.

As for someone who kills people secretly to seize their property—for example, someone who rents out an inn to travellers, then kills some of them and takes their property when he is alone with them; or someone who invites into his home a person he has hired for tailoring, medical treatment, or the like, then kills him and takes his property—this is called murder by treachery. Some ordinary people call such killers al-mu‘arrijīn. If their purpose is to seize property, are they treated as brigands, or are they subject to the law of retribution? The jurists hold two views on this.

The first is that they are treated as brigands, because killing through deception is like killing by force: neither can be guarded against. Indeed, the harm of the former may be greater, because one does not

---

## Page 13908

see it coming.

The second view is that a brigand is someone who fights openly, whereas the fate of someone who murders by stealth is left to the victim’s next of kin. The first view is more consistent with the principles of Islamic law. Indeed, the harm of such murder may be greater, because one does not see it coming.

The jurists also differed concerning those who kill the ruler, such as the murderers of ʿUthmān and the murderer of ʿAlī—may Allah be pleased with them both. Are they treated like brigands and executed as a prescribed punishment, or is their fate left to the victims’ next of kin? There are two views within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere, for killing the ruler causes harm to society at large.

Section

All of this applies when they have been brought under control. But if the ruler or his deputies seek to apprehend them to carry out the prescribed punishment without committing any injustice, and they resist him, then the Muslims must fight them, by scholarly consensus, until all of them have been brought under control. If they will submit only through fighting that leads to all of them being killed, they must be fought even if it leads to that outcome, whether or not they have killed anyone.

During the fighting, they may be killed by whatever means are possible, whether by striking the neck or elsewhere. Those who fight alongside them, protecting and assisting them, must also be fought. This is combat, whereas the former is the enforcement of a prescribed punishment. Fighting these people is even more imperative than killing groups that refuse to submit to the laws of Islam.

---

## Page 13909

For these people have banded together to destroy lives and property and ruin crops and offspring; their aim is neither to uphold a religion nor to establish a kingdom.

They are like brigands who take refuge in a fortress, a cave, a mountaintop, a valley bottom, or somewhere similar, robbing those who pass their way. When the ruler’s troops come to bring them into obedience to the Muslims and their collective authority so that the prescribed punishments may be enforced, they fight and repel them. Such are the Bedouins who rob pilgrims or other travellers along the roads, or the mountain dwellers who shelter on mountaintops or in caves to engage in highway robbery. Likewise are the confederates who have allied themselves to rob travellers between Syria and Iraq, calling this “al-nahīda.”

They are to be fought as we have explained. However, fighting them is not equivalent to fighting disbelievers if they are not themselves disbelievers. Nor may their property be seized unless they have wrongfully taken other people’s property. In that case, they are liable to compensate for it, and an amount equal to what they took is recovered from them, even if we do not know the identity of the actual taker. The same applies if his identity is known, for the supporting accomplice and the direct perpetrator are treated alike, as we have stated. When the actual taker is identified, however, ultimate liability rests with him.

Whatever is recovered from them is returned to its rightful owners. If returning it to them proves impossible, it is used for the public interests of the Muslims, including providing for the force fighting them and other such purposes.

Rather, the purpose of fighting them is to bring them under control so that the prescribed punishments may be enforced and they may be prevented from spreading corruption. Thus, if one of them is severely wounded, he must not be finished off and killed

---

## Page 13910

unless he has already incurred the death penalty. If he flees and no longer poses a threat to us, we do not pursue him unless he is liable to a prescribed punishment or we fear the consequences of letting him go. Anyone taken captive among them is subject to the same prescribed punishment as anyone else. Some jurists take a stricter position regarding them, even permitting their property to be taken as spoils of war, with one-fifth set aside; most, however, reject this. But if they join the realm of a group that has departed from the law of Islam and assist that group against the Muslims, they are fought in the same manner as that group.

As for someone who does not commit highway robbery but exacts a protection fee or levy from travellers for each person, animal, load, or the like, he is an unlawful toll collector and is subject to the punishment applicable to such collectors. The jurists have differed over whether he may be put to death. He is not a highway robber, since his activity does not cut off passage along the road, even though he will be among those most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning the woman from Ghāmid:

“She has repented so sincerely that, had an unlawful toll collector repented in this way, he would have been forgiven.”

By the consensus of the Muslims, those subjected to aggression—whose property is being sought—may fight their attackers. They are not obliged to surrender any property to them, whether little or much, if they are able to fight them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr; whoever is killed defending his life is a martyr; whoever is killed defending his religion is a martyr; and whoever is killed defending his honour is a martyr.”

This is the person whom the jurists call an “assailant”: one who commits aggression without any interpretive justification

---

## Page 13911

or lawful authority. If the assailant seeks property, he may be repelled by whatever means are possible. If he can only be repelled by fighting, he is to be fought. If, instead, the person refrains from fighting and gives the attackers some property, that is permissible.

If, however, the assailant seeks to violate someone’s honour—for example, by seeking illicit intercourse with a person’s female relatives, or seeking to commit a sexual act with a woman, an enslaved boy, or anyone else—the person targeted must defend himself by whatever means possible, even by fighting. Under no circumstances is it permissible to submit to this. Property is different: one may allow it to be taken, because giving up property is permissible, whereas submitting oneself or those under one’s protection to sexual immorality is not.

If the assailant intends to kill someone, the intended victim may defend himself. But is he obliged to do so? Scholars within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere hold two views on this. This applies when the people have an established ruler. But if there is civil strife—Allah forbid—such as when two Muslim rulers dispute sovereignty and fight over it, may a person defend himself during that strife when one ruler enters the other’s territory and bloodshed ensues? Or should he surrender and refrain from fighting in it? Scholars within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere hold two views on this.

When the ruler captures highway robbers who have taken people’s property, he must recover that property from them and restore it to its owners, while also carrying out the prescribed punishment upon them. The same applies to a thief. If they refuse to produce the property after their liability for it has been established, he must punish them with imprisonment and beating until they make its recovery possible, whether by producing it, appointing someone to bring it, or disclosing its whereabouts, just as punishment is imposed on anyone who refuses

---

## Page 13912

to discharge an obligation incumbent upon him. For Allah has permitted a man in His Book to strike his wife if she is defiant and refuses to fulfil the duty incumbent upon her, until she fulfils it. These offenders are all the more deserving of such treatment. The right to demand restitution and to have this punishment imposed belongs to the owner of the property. If he wishes to give them the property, reach a settlement over it, or waive their punishment, he may do so. This differs from carrying out the prescribed punishment upon them, which cannot be waived under any circumstances. Nor may the ruler compel the owner to relinquish any part of his right.

If the property has been consumed or otherwise destroyed while in their possession, or in the thief’s possession, one view is that they must compensate its owners, just as other debtors are liable. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with them both. If they are insolvent, the debt remains their liability until they have the means to pay.

Another view is that compensation and amputation cannot both be imposed. This is the view of Abū Hanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him.

A third view is that they are liable for compensation only if they have the means, not if they are insolvent. This is the view of Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him.

It is not permissible for the ruler to charge property owners a fee for pursuing highway robbers, carrying out the prescribed punishment, and recovering people’s property from them, or for pursuing thieves—whether for himself or for the soldiers he sends after them. Rather, pursuing these offenders is a form of jihad in Allah’s cause. The Muslim troops therefore go forth for this purpose just as they do on other military campaigns, known as baykār. Those fighting in this undertaking are to be supported from the same funds used to support other military expeditions. If their assigned revenue or stipend suffices, that is enough; otherwise, they are to be given whatever additional amount is needed for their campaign from charitable funds devoted to public interests;

---

## Page 13913

for this is in Allah’s cause. If the wayfarers who have been robbed—such as merchants who may fall victim to robbery—owe zakat, the ruler may collect the zakat on their wealth and spend it in Allah’s cause, such as on supporting those who pursue highway robbers. If the robbers possess considerable strength that makes it necessary to win them over, the ruler may give some of their chiefs payments from fay’ (revenues acquired without fighting), public-interest funds, and zakat, to help bring in the others, or to induce a chief to cease his wrongdoing, thereby weakening the rest, or for similar purposes. These recipients would fall among those whose hearts are to be won over. More than one imam, including Ahmad and others, has stated this, and it accords with the apparent meaning of the Book and the Sunnah and the fundamental principles of Islamic law.

The ruler must not send anyone too weak to confront the robbers, nor anyone who takes money from their victims—merchants and other wayfarers. Rather, he must send strong, trustworthy soldiers. If that is impossible, he must send the most suitable available, then the next most suitable.

If any of the ruler’s deputies, village chiefs, or others secretly or openly direct the robbers to plunder, then take a share of whatever they seize, shield them, and either appease the victims by returning some of their wealth or leave them unappeased, such an official’s crime is graver than that of the robbers’ chief. For the latter can be checked by lesser means than are needed to check the former. Such an official must be subject to the same ruling as those who provide the robbers with backing and assistance. If they kill, he too is to be put to death, according to the view of the Commander of the Faithful, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, and most of the people of

---

## Page 13914

knowledge. If they seize property, his hand and foot are to be cut off. If they kill and seize property, he is to be put to death and crucified. According to a group of scholars, he is to undergo amputation, be put to death, and be crucified. It has also been said that a choice may be made between these two penalties. This applies even if he had not authorized them, but, upon gaining power over them, shared in the wealth they had taken and left some claims and prescribed punishments unenforced.

Anyone who shelters a highway robber, thief, murderer, or someone else liable to a prescribed punishment or an obligation owed to Allah Most High or to another person, and prevents its lawful enforcement against him without transgression, is his accomplice in the crime. Allah and His Messenger have cursed him.

Muslim narrated in his Sahīh that ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah has cursed anyone who commits an offense or shelters an offender.”

Once the person sheltering the offender is apprehended, he is to be required to produce him or disclose his whereabouts. If he refuses, he is to be punished with imprisonment and repeated beatings until the offender can be apprehended, just as we have explained that someone who refuses to pay money he owes is to be punished. Whoever prevents a person or property from being brought forward when this is required is to be punished. Even if a man knows the whereabouts of property rightfully sought, or of a person rightfully sought, and is himself preventing access to it or him, he must disclose that information and indicate the location. He may not conceal it. This constitutes cooperation in righteousness and piety, which is obligatory.

By contrast, if the person or property is being sought unjustly, it is not permissible to disclose the whereabouts, for that constitutes cooperation in sin and aggression. Rather, one must protect that person or property, because

---

## Page 13915

supporting the oppressed is obligatory.

In the two Sahīhs, Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or is oppressed.”

I said, “O Messenger of Allah, I would help him if he were oppressed, but how should I help him if he is an oppressor?”

He said, “By preventing him from committing oppression; that is how you help him.”

Muslim narrated a similar report from Jābir. In the two Sahīhs, al-Barā’ ibn ‘Āzib, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded us to do seven things and forbade us seven things. He commanded us to visit the sick, follow funeral processions, invoke Allah’s mercy upon one who sneezes, help someone fulfill his oath, accept invitations, support the oppressed, and spread greetings of peace. He forbade us gold rings, drinking from silver vessels, saddle cushions, and wearing silk, qassī cloth, brocade, and heavy brocade.”

If someone who knows his whereabouts refuses to disclose them, he may be punished with imprisonment or otherwise until he provides that information. This is because he has refused to fulfill an obligation incumbent upon him that cannot be discharged by a proxy, and so he is punished as explained above. He may not, however, be punished for this unless it is known that he possesses the information. This principle applies consistently to matters handled by governors, judges, and others, whenever someone refuses to fulfill an obligation, whether in word or deed.

This does not amount to demanding that a man fulfill an obligation incumbent upon someone else, nor to punishing him for another person’s offense, such that it would fall under the words of Allah Most High:

“No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another,”

or the words of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Take heed! An offender’s guilt falls only upon himself.”

Rather, that would be the case, for example, if a man were required to pay money that

---

## Page 13916

was owed by someone else, although he is neither that person’s agent nor his guarantor and holds none of his property; or if a man were punished for an offense committed by his relative or neighbor, without himself having sinned by neglecting an obligation or committing a prohibited act. That is what is unlawful.

In the case under discussion, however, he is punished only for his own offense: he knows the whereabouts of the wrongdoer whose presence is required to secure the fulfillment of a rightful claim, or he knows the whereabouts of property to which others have rightful claims, yet refuses to provide the assistance and support incumbent upon him according to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus. He may do so out of favoritism or partisan zeal for that wrongdoer, as people bound by partisan loyalties sometimes do for one another, or out of hostility or hatred toward the oppressed.

Allah Most High has said:

“Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”

Or he may do so out of an unwillingness to stand up for Allah and uphold the justice Allah has enjoined, and out of cowardice, weakness, and failure to support His religion—like those who fail to support Allah, His Messenger, His religion, and His Book, and who, when told to go forth in Allah’s cause, cling heavily to the earth. Whatever the motive, a person of this kind deserves punishment by agreement of the scholars. Whoever does not adopt these measures leaves the prescribed punishments unenforced and rights unprotected, allowing the strong to prey upon the weak.

He is like someone who holds property belonging to an unjust debtor who delays repayment—whether tangible property or a debt owed to him—and has

---

## Page 13917

refused to surrender it to a just judge who would use it to repay his debt or provide the maintenance he owes his family, relatives, slaves, or animals. An obligation often falls upon a man on account of someone else, just as he must provide maintenance because of a relative’s need, and just as blood money is payable by the killer’s ʿāqilah (the group collectively liable for his blood money).

This form of discretionary punishment applies to someone known to have in his keeping property or a person that must be produced, yet who fails to produce it or him—such as highway robbers, thieves, and those who shelter them—or someone known to have information about their whereabouts, yet who refuses to disclose it. If, however, he refuses to disclose their whereabouts or produce them to prevent the person seeking them from committing aggression or injustice against them, then he is doing good. These two situations are often confused, and uncertainty becomes entangled with personal desire. What is required is to distinguish right from wrong.

This frequently occurs among chiefs in both nomadic and settled communities when someone seeks their protection or is related to them by kinship or friendship. With the partisan zeal of pre-Islamic ignorance, pride in sin, and concern for their reputation among the rabble, they consider it a point of honor to support him—even when he is an unjust wrongdoer—against the wronged party who is in the right. This is especially so if the wronged party is a chief who vies with them and opposes them: they regard surrendering someone under their protection to an opponent as humiliation or weakness. Such an unqualified stance is pure pre-Islamic ignorance. It is among the greatest causes of corruption in both religious and worldly affairs.

It has been related that many wars among the Bedouin, such as the War of al-Basūs between Banū Bakr and Taghlib, arose from things of this kind. Likewise, the reason for the Turks and Mongols entering the lands of Islam

---

## Page 13918

and their subjugation of the rulers of Transoxiana and Khurāsān lay in something of this kind.

Whoever humbles himself before Allah has truly honored himself, and whoever willingly renders what is due from him has ennobled himself. For the noblest of people in Allah’s sight are those most mindful of Him. Whoever seeks honor through wrongdoing—by withholding others’ rights and committing sins—has degraded and debased himself. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever desires honor—all honor belongs to Allah.”

He also says of the hypocrites:

“They say, ‘If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the lowlier from it.’ Yet honor belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers, but the hypocrites do not know.”

Describing people of this kind, Allah Most High says:

“Among people is one whose words about worldly life please you, and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of adversaries.”

“When he turns away, he strives throughout the land to spread corruption in it and destroy crops and livestock. And Allah does not love corruption.”

“When he is told, ‘Fear Allah,’ pride drives him to sin. Hell is enough for him—what an evil resting place!”

Rather, anyone whose protection is sought must support the person seeking it if he has been wronged. His having been wronged is not established merely by his own claim: many a man complains when he himself is the wrongdoer. Instead, the person offering protection must investigate his case by hearing from his adversary and others. If he is the wrongdoer, he must restrain him from wrongdoing gently if possible, whether through reconciliation or a just judgment; otherwise, by force. If each of them is both a wrongdoer and a victim of wrongdoing, as with those driven by partisan passions among Qays and Yaman

---

## Page 13919

and others like them, and most litigants in towns and the countryside—or if neither party is a wrongdoer, their dispute having arisen from some ambiguity, interpretation, or mistake—he must seek to reconcile them or adjudicate between them, as Allah Most High says:

“If two groups of believers fight, make peace between them. But if one transgresses against the other, fight the transgressing group until it returns to Allah’s command. If it returns, reconcile them justly and act equitably. Surely Allah loves those who act equitably.”

“The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your brothers, and fear Allah so that you may receive mercy.”

Allah Most High also says:

“There is no good in much of their private conversation, except in that of someone who urges charity, kindness, or reconciliation between people. Whoever does this seeking Allah’s pleasure, We shall grant him a great reward.”

Abū Dāwūd reported in al-Sunan that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked, “Is it tribal partisanship for a man to support his people when they are in the right?” He replied, “No.” He said, “Rather, tribal partisanship is for a man to support his people when they are in the wrong.”

He also said:

“The best of you is the one who defends his people, so long as he commits no sin.”

And he said:

“The one who supports his people in falsehood is like a camel that has fallen into a well and is being dragged by its tail.”

And he said:

“If you hear someone invoking the rallying cries of pre-Islamic ignorance, tell him to bite his father’s penis, and do not use euphemisms.”

Any allegiance that falls outside the call of Islam and the Quran—whether based on lineage, homeland, ethnicity, a school of thought, or a path—is among the rallying cries of pre-Islamic ignorance. Indeed, “When two men—one from the Emigrants and one from the Helpers—quarreled, the Emigrant called out, ‘Emigrants, rally to me!’

---

## Page 13920

and the Helper called out, ‘Helpers, rally to me!’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Do you invoke the rallying cries of pre-Islamic ignorance while I am among you?’” He became intensely angry at this.

Section

As for the thief, his right hand must be cut off, according to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus. Allah Most High says:

“As for male and female thieves, cut off their hands as punishment for what they have done—a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

“But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, Allah will surely turn to him in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Once liability for the prescribed punishment has been established against him through evidence or confession, its execution may not be deferred—whether by imprisonment, a payment to ransom himself, or any other means. Rather, his hand is to be cut off during sacred times as well as at other times, for enforcing the prescribed punishment is an act of worship, like fighting in Allah’s cause.

It should be understood that enforcing the prescribed punishments is a mercy from Allah toward His servants. The ruler should therefore be firm in enforcing the punishment, not allowing pity to lead him to suspend what Allah’s religion requires. His aim should be mercy toward people by restraining them from wrongdoing, not to vent his anger or seek supremacy over them. He is like a father disciplining his child: if he refrained from disciplining him—as the mother urges out of tenderness and compassion—the child would become corrupt. He disciplines him only out of mercy and to reform him, although he would much prefer that the child never made discipline necessary. He is also like a physician who gives a patient bitter medicine, or like amputating a decaying limb, cupping, and cutting

---

## Page 13921

the veins in bloodletting and similar procedures. Indeed, it is like a person taking bitter medicine or subjecting himself to hardship in order to obtain relief.

This is why the prescribed punishments were instituted, and this should be the ruler’s intention when enforcing them. Whenever his aim is to reform his subjects and prevent wrongdoing by securing benefits for them and warding off harm, seeking thereby the Face of Allah Most High and obedience to His command, Allah will soften people’s hearts toward him, facilitate the means of goodness for him, and spare him human punishment. Even the person receiving the prescribed punishment may be content when the ruler enforces it upon him. But if his aim is to exalt himself over them and establish his authority so that they will revere him or give him whatever wealth he wants, his efforts will produce the opposite of what he intended.

It is related that before becoming caliph, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—may Allah be pleased with him—served as al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik’s governor over the city of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He governed its people well. Al-Hajjāj came from Iraq, whose people he had subjected to terrible torment, and asked the people of Medina about ʿUmar:

“How much awe does he inspire among you?”

They replied, “We cannot bring ourselves to look at him.”

He asked, “How much do you love him?”

They replied, “He is dearer to us than our own families.”

He asked, “How does he discipline you?”

They replied, “With between three and ten lashes.”

He said, “Such awe, such love, and such discipline—this is something from heaven.”

When the thief’s hand is cut off, the wound is cauterized, and it is recommended that the hand be hung around his neck. If he

---

## Page 13922

steals a second time, his left foot is cut off. If he steals a third and a fourth time, there are two views among the Companions and subsequent scholars. The first is that the amputations continue for the third and fourth offences until both hands and both feet have been amputated. This is the view of Abū Bakr—may Allah be pleased with him—and the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, according to one of the two reports from him. The second is that he is imprisoned. This is the view of ʿAlī—may Allah be pleased with him—the scholars of Kufa, and Ahmad according to the other report from him.

His hand is cut off only if the stolen property reaches the prescribed minimum value: a quarter of a dinar or three dirhams, according to the majority of scholars among the people of the Hijaz, the hadith scholars, and others, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad. Some scholars hold that it is one dinar or ten dirhams. Whoever steals that amount is subject to amputation by scholarly agreement.

In the two Sahih collections, Ibn ʿUmar—may Allah be pleased with them both—reported:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cut off a hand for the theft of a shield whose price was three dirhams.”

In Muslim’s wording:

“He cut off a thief’s hand for stealing a shield worth three dirhams.”

A mijann is a shield.

In the two Sahih collections, ʿĀ’ishah—may Allah be pleased with her—reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The hand is to be cut off for stealing a quarter of a dinar or more.”

In a version recorded by Muslim:

“A thief’s hand is not to be cut off except for stealing a quarter of a dinar or more.”

In a version recorded by al-Bukhārī, he said:

“Cut off the hand for stealing a quarter of a dinar, but do not cut it off for anything less than that.”

At that time, a quarter of a dinar was equivalent to three dirhams, and a dinar to twelve dirhams. A person is not deemed a thief in the legal sense unless he takes property from a place of safekeeping. As for property

---

## Page 13923

lost by its owner, fruit growing on trees in open country without an enclosing wall, livestock with no herdsman present, and the like, no amputation is prescribed for taking them. The person who takes them is, however, subject to discretionary punishment and must pay double compensation, as stated in the hadith.

Scholars have differed over doubling the compensation. Ahmad and others are among those who hold this view. Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj said:

“I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: ‘No amputation is prescribed for stealing fruit or palm hearts.’”

Kathar means the tender core of a date palm. This was reported by the compilers of the Sunan.

ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb narrated from his father, from his grandfather—may Allah be pleased with him—who said:

“I heard a man from Muzaynah questioning the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, I have come to ask you about stray camels.’

“He replied, ‘A camel has its footwear and water supply with it. It feeds on trees and goes to water, so leave it until its owner comes looking for it.’

“The man asked, ‘What about stray sheep?’

“He replied, ‘It is for you, your brother, or the wolf. Take it in until its owner comes looking for it.’

“The man asked, ‘What about livestock stolen from their grazing grounds?’

“He replied, ‘The penalty is twice their value and a deterrent beating. For livestock taken from their enclosure, amputation is prescribed if the value of what is taken reaches the price of a shield.’

“The man asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, what about fruit and what is taken from its sheaths?’

“He replied, ‘Whoever eats some directly, without gathering any in the fold of his garment, bears no liability. Whoever carries any away must pay twice its value and receive a deterrent beating. For fruit taken from its drying floors, amputation is prescribed if the value of what is taken reaches the price of a shield. If it does not reach the price of a shield, the penalty is compensation of twice its value and deterrent lashes.’”

Reported by the compilers of the

---

## Page 13924

Sunan. This wording, however, is al-Nasā’ī’s. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No amputation is prescribed for a plunderer, a snatcher, or one who betrays a trust.”

A plunderer takes property openly while people are watching. A snatcher grabs an object and is noticed before taking it. As for the cutpurse—the thief who slits open pockets, kerchiefs, sleeves, and the like—amputation is prescribed according to the correct view.

Section

As for one who commits unlawful sexual intercourse, if he is muhsan (has the legal status conferred by consummating a valid marriage), he is stoned until he dies. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stoned Māʿiz ibn Mālik al-Aslamī, the woman of Ghāmid, the two Jews, and others. The Muslims continued to carry out stoning after him.

Scholars have differed over whether he should receive one hundred lashes before being stoned. There are two views on this within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. If he is not muhsan, he receives one hundred lashes in accordance with the Book of Allah and is banished for a year in accordance with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, although some scholars consider banishment obligatory.

According to many or most scholars, the prescribed punishment is not carried out unless four witnesses testify against him or he testifies against himself four times. Some scholars consider a single confession sufficient. If he confesses and then retracts his confession,

---

## Page 13925

some scholars hold that the prescribed punishment is waived, while others hold that it is not.

A muhsan is a man who, while free and legally accountable, has had vaginal intercourse, even once, with a woman whom he married under a valid marriage contract. Must the woman share these qualifications with the man? Scholars hold two views on this. Does a girl approaching puberty confer this status upon an adult man, and vice versa?

Non-Muslims living under Muslim protection may also have muhsan status according to most scholars, including al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stoned two Jews at the entrance to his mosque. This was the first stoning in Islam.

Scholars differ concerning a woman who is found to be pregnant, has neither husband nor master, and alleges no legally excusing circumstance surrounding her pregnancy. There are two views within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. One holds that she is not subject to the prescribed punishment, since she may have conceived through forced intercourse, the introduction of semen without intercourse, or intercourse involving a legal uncertainty. The other holds that she is subject to the prescribed punishment. This is the position transmitted from the Rightly Guided Caliphs, accords more closely with the principles of Islamic law, and is the position of the scholars of Medina. Rare possibilities are disregarded, just as the possibility that she or the witnesses may be lying is disregarded.

As for anal intercourse between men, some scholars hold that its prescribed punishment is the same as that for unlawful sexual intercourse. It has also been said that its punishment is less severe. The correct view, upon which the Companions agreed, is that both men—the active and the passive partner—are to be put to death, whether they are muhsan or not. For the compilers of the Sunan narrated from Ibn

---

## Page 13926

Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever you find committing the act of the people of Lot, put to death both the active and the passive partner.”

Abū Dāwūd also narrated that Ibn Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said concerning a man who was not muhsan and was found engaging in anal intercourse with another man: “He is to be stoned.” Something similar is related from Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him. The Companions did not differ over putting him to death, but they differed over the manner of execution.

It is related that al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, ordered that he be burned, while others prescribed killing him. Some held that a wall should be toppled onto him so that he dies beneath the rubble. It was also said that both men should be confined in the foulest place until they die. Others held that he should be taken to the top of the highest wall in the town, thrown from it, and have stones hurled after him, just as Allah did to the people of Lot. This is one report from Ibn Abbās. In the other report, he said: “He is to be stoned.”

This was the position of most of the early generations. They argued that Allah stoned the people of Lot and prescribed stoning for the adulterer as a punishment corresponding to His stoning of the people of Lot. Both men are therefore to be stoned, whether both are free, both are slaves, or one is a slave and the other free, provided that both have reached puberty. If one has not reached puberty, he is to receive a punishment short of death, and only the one who has reached puberty is to be stoned.
