## Page 13927

Section

As for the prescribed punishment for drinking intoxicants, it is established by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the consensus of the Muslims. The compilers of the Sunan collections narrated through several routes that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever drinks intoxicants, flog him. If he drinks again, flog him. If he drinks again, flog him. Then, if he drinks a fourth time, put him to death.”

It is established that he flogged those who drank on several occasions, as did his caliphs and the Muslims after him. Most scholars hold that the ruling prescribing execution was abrogated. Others hold that it remains in force. It is also said that it is a discretionary punishment which the ruler may impose when necessary.

The following is also established:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, administered forty strokes with palm stalks and sandals for drinking intoxicants. Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, administered forty strokes, while Umar administered eighty during his caliphate. Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, would sometimes administer forty strokes and sometimes eighty.”

Some scholars therefore hold that eighty strokes are obligatory. Others hold that forty are obligatory, and that the ruler may add more when necessary—for example, when people become addicted to intoxicants, when the drinker cannot be deterred by fewer strokes, or in similar circumstances.

---

## Page 13928

When drinkers are few and the drinker’s case is relatively mild, forty strokes suffice. This is the stronger of the two views. It is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and, according to one of the two reports from him, Ahmad—may Allah have mercy on them both.

When drinking became widespread, Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, added banishment and shaving the head as further deterrents. Thus, it would be appropriate to banish the drinker in addition to administering forty strokes, so that he is no longer heard of, or to remove him from his position of authority. Indeed, when Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, heard that one of his deputies had recited verses about intoxicating drink, he dismissed him.

The intoxicants which Allah and His Messenger prohibited, and for drinking which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed flogging, include every intoxicating beverage, whatever its source: fruits such as grapes, fresh dates and figs; grains such as wheat and barley; dews such as honey; or animal products such as mares’ milk.

Indeed, when Allah, glorified and exalted is He, revealed the prohibition of intoxicants to His Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the people of Medina had no grape wine. There were no grapevines in Medina; grape wine was brought in from Syria. Most of their drink was made from dates. Reports transmitted through numerous independent chains from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his rightly guided caliphs and his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, establish that he prohibited every intoxicating drink and made clear that every such drink is khamr.

They also used to drink sweet nabīdh, prepared by placing dates and raisins in water

---

## Page 13929

—that is, casting them into it, since nabdh means “casting in”—to sweeten the water, especially since much of the water in the Hijaz is salty. This nabīdh is permissible by the consensus of the Muslims because it does not intoxicate, just as grape juice is permissible to drink before it becomes intoxicating.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had forbidden them to prepare this nabīdh in wooden vessels, earthenware vessels made of clay, gourds, or pitch-coated containers. He instructed them instead to prepare it in containers whose mouths were tied shut with cords. This was because intoxicating strength develops gradually and imperceptibly in nabīdh, so a person might unknowingly drink something that had already acquired an intoxicating, exhilarating potency. If a waterskin was tied shut, it would split when the nabīdh fermented inside it, thus preventing a person from falling into what was forbidden. Those other vessels, however, would not split.

It is reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, subsequently permitted preparing nabīdh in those vessels, saying:

“I had forbidden you to prepare nabīdh in those vessels. Now prepare it, but do not drink anything intoxicating.”

The Companions and the scholars who came after them differed. Some had not learned of the abrogation or did not consider it established, and therefore prohibited preparing nabīdh in those vessels. Others accepted the later report as authentic and as abrogating the earlier prohibition, and therefore permitted preparing nabīdh in them.

Some jurists heard that certain Companions used to drink nabīdh and assumed that it was intoxicating. They consequently considered it permissible to drink certain kinds of beverages not made from grapes or dates. They also permitted boiled nabīdh made from dates and raisins, provided it did not intoxicate the drinker.

---

## Page 13930

The correct view, however, is that held by the great majority of Muslims: every intoxicant is khamr (wine), and whoever drinks it is to be flogged, even if he drinks only a single drop, whether for medicinal purposes or otherwise. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about using wine medicinally and replied:

“It is a disease, not a remedy. Allah has not placed the healing of my community in what has been forbidden to them.”

The prescribed punishment must be imposed when the offence is established by evidence or the drinker confesses. If, however, the smell of wine is detected on him, or he is seen vomiting it, or something similar occurs, one view holds that the prescribed punishment is not to be imposed, since he may have drunk something other than wine, or drunk wine without knowing what it was, or under compulsion, or in similar circumstances.

Another view holds that he is indeed to be flogged if he knew that it was intoxicating. This is what has been transmitted from the Rightly Guided Caliphs and other Companions, including 'Uthmān, 'Alī and Ibn Mas'ūd. It is supported by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and it is the position conducive to people's upright conduct. It is also the position of Mālik, of Ahmad in most of his recorded statements, and of others.

Hashish made from grape leaves is likewise forbidden, and whoever consumes it is to be flogged just as a wine drinker is flogged. It is more pernicious than wine in that it corrupts the mind and constitution, inducing effeminacy, indifference to sexual misconduct within one's family, and other forms of corruption. Wine is more pernicious in that it leads to quarrelling and fighting. Both turn people away from the remembrance of Allah Most High and from prayer.

Some later jurists hesitated over applying the prescribed punishment for it and held that whoever consumes it

---

## Page 13931

should receive a discretionary punishment less severe than the prescribed punishment, since they supposed that it altered the mind without producing euphoria, like the plant banj. We have found no discussion of it by the earlier scholars. Yet that supposition is incorrect: those who consume it experience euphoria and crave it just as wine drinkers crave wine, or even more. When they consume it excessively, it turns them away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer, besides its other harmful effects: indifference to sexual misconduct within one’s family, effeminacy, corruption of the constitution and mind, and so forth.

However, because it is a solid substance that is eaten rather than drunk, jurists within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere have differed over its ritual impurity, expressing three views. One holds that it is ritually impure, like wine that is drunk; this is the sound analogy. Another holds that it is not, because it is solid. A third distinguishes between its solid and liquid forms. In any event, both the wording and the meaning of Allah’s and His Messenger’s prohibition of wine and intoxicants encompass it.

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“O Messenger of Allah, give us a ruling on two drinks we used to make in Yemen: bitʿ, made from honey left to ferment until it becomes strong, and mizr, made from sorghum and barley left to ferment until it becomes strong.”

He continued: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had been endowed with comprehensive and conclusive speech. He said: ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden.’”

Reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim in their Sahīh collections.

Al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Wine can be made from wheat, from barley, from raisins, from dates, and from honey. I forbid every intoxicant.”

Reported by

---

## Page 13932

Abū Dāwūd and others; however, in the two Sahīh collections this is reported as a statement of ʿUmar himself. He delivered it in a sermon from the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying:

“Wine is whatever clouds the mind.”

Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every intoxicant is wine, and every intoxicant is forbidden.”

Another version reads:

“Every intoxicant is wine, and every wine is forbidden.”

Muslim reported both versions in his Sahīh.

ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden. Whatever causes intoxication when consumed in a faraq (a measure of volume) is forbidden even in a palmful.”

Al-Tirmidhī graded this hadith sound.

The compilers of the Sunan collections reported through several chains that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whatever intoxicates in large quantities is forbidden in small quantities.”

Leading hadith scholars graded it authentic.

Jābir, may Allah be pleased with him, reported:

“A man asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about a drink made from sorghum that they drank in their land, called mizr. He asked, ‘Does it intoxicate?’

“The man replied, ‘Yes.’

“He said, ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden. Allah has pledged that whoever drinks an intoxicant will be given tīnat al-khabāl to drink.’

“They asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, what is tīnat al-khabāl?’

“He replied, ‘The sweat of the people of Hell, or the discharge of the people of Hell.’”

Muslim reported it in his Sahīh.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Everything that clouds the mind is wine; every intoxicant is forbidden.”

Abū Dāwūd reported it. The hadiths on this subject are numerous and widely transmitted. The Messenger of Allah included

---

## Page 13933

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—everything that clouds the mind and intoxicates, using the concise, comprehensive speech he had been granted. He made no distinction between one kind and another. Whether a substance is eaten or drunk makes no difference. Indeed, wine is sometimes used as a condiment, while hashish may be dissolved in water and drunk. Thus every kind of wine can be drunk or eaten, and hashish can be eaten or drunk; all of this is forbidden. The earlier scholars did not discuss hashish specifically only because eating it became a practice relatively recently, towards the end of the sixth century AH or thereabouts. Likewise, intoxicating drinks were introduced after the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and all fall within the comprehensive statements of the Quran and Sunnah.

Section

Among the prescribed punishments established by the Quran and Sunnah, and unanimously agreed upon by the Muslims, is the punishment for accusations of unlawful sexual intercourse. If a man accuses a muhsan of unlawful sexual intercourse or sodomy, he incurs the prescribed punishment of eighty lashes. Here, muhsan means a free, chaste person; in the discussion of the prescribed punishment for unlawful sexual intercourse, it means someone who has had full sexual intercourse within a fully valid marriage.

---

## Page 13934

Section

As for sins for which there is neither a fixed prescribed punishment nor an expiation, examples include kissing a boy or a woman who is neither one’s wife nor unmarriageable kin; engaging in physical intimacy without intercourse; eating forbidden things, such as blood or carrion; making accusations against people other than accusations of unlawful sexual intercourse; stealing something not kept in a secure place, even something of little value; betraying a trust—as when administrators of public treasury funds, endowments, or orphans’ property and the like betray their trust, or when agents and partners do so; acting fraudulently in one’s dealings, as those who cheat in food, clothing, and similar goods do; giving short measure or weight; bearing false witness or coaching others to do so; accepting bribes when passing judgment; judging by other than what Allah has revealed; oppressing one’s subjects; raising the rallying cries of pre-Islamic ignorance or answering its call; and other kinds of forbidden acts.

Such offenders receive discretionary punishment to deter and discipline them, to the extent the ruler deems appropriate, taking into account how widespread or rare the particular sin is among the people. If it is widespread, he increases the punishment, unlike when it is rare. He also considers the offender’s circumstances: someone habitually engaged in wickedness receives a greater punishment than someone who seldom commits such acts. He likewise considers the gravity of the sin: someone who harasses other people’s women and children receives a greater punishment than someone who has harassed only a woman

---

## Page 13935

or a single boy. There is no fixed minimum for discretionary punishment. It may take any form that causes a person distress, whether through words, actions, withholding words, or withholding actions. A man may be disciplined by admonition, rebuke, or stern words. He may also be disciplined by shunning him and withholding greetings until he repents, when this serves the best interest, just as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and his Companions shunned “the three who were left behind.”

He may be disciplined by removal from office, as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and his Companions used to do. He may also be disciplined by no longer being employed in the Muslim army, as in the case of a soldier who flees the battlefield. Fleeing the battlefield is a major sin, and cutting off his pay is a form of discretionary punishment. Likewise, if a commander commits a grave offense, he may be removed from his command as a disciplinary punishment.

Discretionary punishment may also take the form of imprisonment, beating, blackening the offender’s face, or making him ride an animal backwards. It is reported that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb (may Allah be pleased with him) ordered such treatment for a false witness. For the liar has blackened his own reputation, so his face is blackened; he has turned the account upside down, so he is made to ride backwards.

As for its maximum, one view states: “No more than ten lashes may be administered.” Many scholars hold that discretionary punishment must fall short of a fixed prescribed punishment. They then differ between two views. Some say: “It must fall short of the least prescribed punishment.” Thus, for a free person, it must fall short of the least prescribed punishment applicable to a free person, which is forty or eighty lashes; and for a slave, it must fall short of the least prescribed punishment applicable to a slave, which is

---

## Page 13936

twenty or forty lashes. Another view holds that, for either, it must fall short of the prescribed punishment for a slave.

Some scholars say that the punishment for each offense must fall short of the prescribed punishment for its category, even if it exceeds the prescribed punishment for another category. Thus, someone who steals property not kept in a secure place must not have his hand amputated, even if he is given more lashes than the prescribed punishment for falsely accusing someone of unlawful sexual intercourse. Likewise, someone who commits acts short of unlawful sexual intercourse must not receive the prescribed punishment for that intercourse, even if his punishment exceeds that for a false accusation.

It is reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb (may Allah be pleased with him) that a man made an engraving on his seal ring and used it to obtain money from the public treasury. ʿUmar ordered that he be given a hundred strokes, then had him given a hundred strokes on the second day and a hundred on the third.

It is also reported from the Rightly Guided Caliphs concerning a man and woman found together under one blanket:

“They are each to be given a hundred lashes.”

It is reported from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), concerning a man who has intercourse with his wife’s slave woman, that if his wife had given him permission, he is to be given a hundred lashes; if she had not given him permission, he is to be stoned to death.

These views are found in the school of Ahmad and others. The first two views are found in the school of al-Shāfiʿī and others.

As for Mālik and others, it is reported that they held that certain crimes may warrant execution. Some scholars of Ahmad’s school agreed with him in cases such as that of a Muslim spy who spies on the Muslims for the enemy. Ahmad withheld judgment on whether such a person should be executed. Mālik and some Hanbalī scholars, such as Ibn ʿAqīl, permitted his execution, while Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and some Hanbalī scholars, such as Judge Abū Yaʿlā, prohibited it.

---

## Page 13937

A group of scholars from the schools of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad, and others, also permitted the execution of anyone who advocates religious innovations contrary to the Quran and Sunnah. Many scholars of Mālik’s school held the same view. They said that Mālik and others permitted the execution of the Qadariyya only for spreading corruption in the land, not for apostasy.

The same explanation has also been given for executing a sorcerer. Most scholars hold that he is to be executed. It has been narrated from Jundub (may Allah be pleased with him), both as his own statement and as a report traced back to the Prophet:

“The prescribed punishment for a sorcerer is a stroke of the sword.”

This was reported by al-Tirmidhī. The execution of sorcerers has also been reported from Umar, Uthmān, Hafsa, Abd Allāh ibn Umar, and other Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). Some scholars said that this is on account of disbelief, while others said that it is for spreading corruption in the land. Most of these scholars, however, regard his execution as a prescribed punishment.

Abū Hanīfa likewise allows execution as a discretionary punishment for repeated crimes when crimes of that kind warrant execution, as in the case of someone who repeatedly commits sodomy or treacherously murders people to seize their wealth, and similar offenses.

Evidence that someone who spreads corruption is to be executed if his evil cannot otherwise be stopped may be drawn from the report narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh, from Arfaja al-Ashja'ī (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: “I heard the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) say:

‘If someone comes to you while you are united under one man, seeking to break your unity or divide your community, kill him.’”

Another version states:

“There will be disturbances and more disturbances. Whoever seeks to divide this community while it is united, strike him with the sword, whoever he may be.”

---

## Page 13938

The same explanation may also be given for his command to execute a wine-drinker on the fourth occasion, as supported by what Ahmad narrated in his Musnad from Daylam al-Himyarī (may Allah be pleased with him), who said:

“I asked the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), saying: ‘O Messenger of Allah, we live in a land where we perform strenuous work, and we make a drink from wheat to strengthen us for our work and against the cold of our land.’

“He asked: ‘Does it intoxicate?’ I replied: ‘Yes.’ He said: ‘Then avoid it.’ I said: ‘The people will not give it up.’ He said: ‘If they do not give it up, kill them.’”

This is because someone who spreads corruption is like an aggressor: if the aggressor cannot be repelled except by killing him, he is killed.

In sum, punishment is of two kinds. The first is punishment for a past offense, as recompense for what the offender has done and an exemplary punishment from Allah, such as flogging a wine-drinker or someone who makes an accusation of unlawful sexual intercourse, and the amputation imposed on armed robbers and thieves.

The second is punishment intended to secure the fulfillment of an obligation and abstention from what is forbidden in the future. Thus, an apostate is called upon to repent and embrace Islam: if he repents, he is spared; otherwise, he is executed. Likewise, someone who neglects prayer, zakat, or the rights of others is punished until he fulfills them. Discretionary punishment in this second category is more severe than in the first. Hence, he may be beaten repeatedly until he performs the obligatory prayer or fulfills the duty incumbent upon him.

As for the hadith in the two Sahīh collections, in which the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“No one is to be flogged more than ten

---

## Page 13939

lashes, except where one of Allah’s limits has been violated.” Some scholars have explained that “Allah’s limits” here refers to prohibitions pertaining to Allah’s rights. In the Quran and Sunnah, “limits” denotes the boundary between the lawful and the unlawful: the furthest extent of what is lawful and the point at which the unlawful begins. Concerning the former, Allah says:

“These are Allah’s limits, so do not transgress them.”

Concerning the latter, He says:

“These are Allah’s limits, so do not approach them.”

Calling a prescribed punishment a hadd, however, is a later terminological convention. The hadith means that someone administering a beating to enforce a personal right—such as a man striking his wife for marital defiance—must not exceed ten lashes.

The flogging prescribed by Islamic law consists of moderate strokes with a whip, for the best course is the middle one. ‘Alī (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

“Moderation in the stroke, and moderation in the whip.”

Flogging is not to be administered with sticks or scourges, nor does a light whip suffice. Rather, a light whip is used for discretionary punishment, whereas prescribed punishments require flogging with a whip. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb (may Allah be pleased with him) used to administer discipline with a light whip, but when a prescribed punishment was to be carried out, he would call for a whip.

The person being flogged is not to be stripped of all his clothing. Only what prevents him from feeling the pain of the blows—such as padded garments, furs, and the like—is to be removed. He is not to be bound unless necessary, nor is his face to be struck, for the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“When one of you fights

---

## Page 13940

he must avoid the face and not strike his opponent’s vital parts.” The purpose is to discipline him, not to kill him. The blows should be distributed over the different parts of his body, such as his back, shoulders, thighs, and the like.

Section

The punishments prescribed by Islamic law for those who disobey Allah and His Messenger are of two kinds:

The first is punishment of those who are under control, whether one person or several, as discussed above.

The second is punishment of a group that resists enforcement, such as one that can only be brought under control through fighting. The foundation of this is jihad against the disbelievers, the enemies of Allah and His Messenger. Anyone whom the Messenger of Allah’s call to the religion with which Allah sent him reaches, but who does not respond to it, must be fought:

“Until there is no more persecution and worship is devoted entirely to Allah.”

For when Allah sent His Prophet and commanded him to call people to His religion, He did not permit him to kill or fight anyone on that account until he emigrated to Medina. Then He granted permission to him and the Muslims, saying:

“Permission to fight is granted to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged. And Allah is certainly able to grant them victory.”

“Those who have been driven from their homes unjustly, merely for saying, ‘Our Lord is Allah.’ Were it not for Allah restraining some people by means of others, destruction would surely have befallen monasteries and churches

---

## Page 13941

, synagogues, and mosques in which Allah’s name is often mentioned. Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is All-Powerful, Almighty.”

“Those who, if We establish them in the land, maintain prayer, give zakah, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters.”

Then, after that, He made fighting obligatory for them, saying, Most High:

“Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate something that is good for you, and perhaps you love something that is bad for you. Allah knows, while you do not know.”

He reaffirmed this obligation and emphasized the importance of jihad in most of the Medinan surahs. He censured those who abandoned it, describing them as having hypocrisy and sickness in their hearts. He, Most High, said:

“Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your relatives, the wealth you have acquired, the trade whose decline you fear, and the homes you cherish are dearer to you than Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His decree. Allah does not guide defiantly disobedient people.”

He, Most High, also said:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

He, Most High, also said:

“But when an unambiguous surah is revealed and fighting is mentioned in it, you see those in whose hearts is sickness looking at you like someone overcome by the throes of death. Yet better for them would be obedience and fitting words. Then, when the matter is resolved, if they were true to Allah, it would be better for them. If you turn away, would you then spread corruption on earth and sever your ties of kinship?”

There are many such passages

---

## Page 13942

in the Quran. Likewise, jihad and those who undertake it are exalted in Surah al-Saff, in which He says:

“O you who believe, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?

“Believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in Allah’s cause with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if only you knew.

“He will forgive your sins and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in Gardens of everlasting residence. That is the great triumph.

“And another blessing that you love: help from Allah and a victory near at hand. So give good tidings to the believers.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Do you regard providing water to the pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque as equal to the deeds of one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in Allah’s cause? They are not equal before Allah. Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.

“Those who believe, emigrate, and strive in Allah’s cause with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank before Allah. It is they who are successful.

“Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him, His pleasure, and gardens in which they will have lasting bliss,

“Remaining there forever. Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Whoever among you turns back from his religion, Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers and firm toward the disbelievers. They strive in Allah’s cause and do not fear the reproach of any critic. That is Allah’s bounty, which He grants to whom He wills. Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.”

He, Most High, also says:

“That is because no thirst, fatigue, or hunger afflicts them in Allah’s cause, nor do they tread any ground that enrages the disbelievers, nor inflict any loss on an enemy, without there being recorded for them

---

## Page 13943

a righteous deed on that account. Indeed, Allah does not allow the reward of those who do good to be lost.”

“Nor do they spend any amount, small or large, or cross any valley without it being recorded for them, so that Allah may reward them according to the best of what they used to do.”

Thus, He mentions both the effects of their deeds and the deeds they perform directly.

The commands to undertake jihad and the accounts of its virtues in the Quran and Sunnah are too numerous to enumerate. For this reason, it is the best voluntary deed a person can undertake. By scholarly agreement, it is superior to Hajj and ‘umrah, voluntary prayer, and voluntary fasting, as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah. Indeed, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The foundation of the matter is Islam, its pillar is prayer, and its highest peak is jihad.”

He also said:

“In Paradise there are a hundred degrees which Allah has prepared for those who strive in His cause. The distance between one degree and the next is like the distance between heaven and earth.”

Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

He also said:

“Whoever’s feet become dusty in Allah’s cause, Allah forbids the Fire from touching him.”

Reported by al-Bukhārī.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also said:

“Keeping guard for a day and a night in Allah’s cause is better than fasting for a month and spending its nights in prayer. If he dies, the reward for the deeds he used to perform continues, his provision continues, and he is spared the trial of the grave.”

Reported by Muslim. The Sunan collections also contain the following:

“Keeping guard for one day in Allah’s cause is better than a thousand days spent in any other station.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also said:

“Two eyes will not be touched by the Fire: an eye that wept out of fear of Allah, and an eye that spent the night intent on Allah’s cause.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is a sound hadith.” And in the Musnad of Imam

---

## Page 13944

Ahmad:

“Keeping guard for one night in Allah’s cause is better than a thousand nights spent in prayer with their days spent fasting.”

In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported that a man said: “O Messenger of Allah, tell me of something equal to jihad in Allah’s cause.”

He replied: “You would not be able to do it.”

The man said: “Tell me what it is.”

He replied: “When the one undertaking jihad sets out, can you fast without breaking your fast and stand in prayer without ceasing?”

The man said: “No.”

He replied: “That is what equals jihad.”

In the Sunan collections, it is reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Every community has its devotional journeying, and the devotional journeying of my community is jihad in Allah’s cause.”

This is a vast subject. Nothing comparable to what has been reported concerning its reward and virtue has been reported concerning other deeds.

This is also evident upon reflection, for the benefits of jihad extend both to those who undertake it and to others, in both religious and worldly affairs. It encompasses every kind of inward and outward worship. It includes love of Allah Most High, sincerity towards Him, reliance upon Him, surrendering one’s life and wealth to Him, patience, renunciation of worldly attachments, remembrance of Allah, and all other kinds of deeds to an extent unmatched by any other deed.

Whether an individual or a community undertakes it, they are always assured of one of two good outcomes: either victory and triumph, or martyrdom and Paradise. For people must live and die, and jihad puts their lives and deaths to use

---

## Page 13945

to attain their greatest happiness in this world and the Hereafter. Abandoning it means losing or diminishing happiness in both. Some people seek arduous undertakings in religious or worldly affairs despite their limited benefit; yet jihad is more beneficial in both respects than any other arduous undertaking. Others may wish to live in comfort until death overtakes them, yet the martyr’s death is easier than any other death, and it is the best way to die.

If the basis of lawfully prescribed fighting is jihad, and its purpose is that religion should be entirely for Allah and that Allah’s word should be supreme, then whoever refuses this is to be fought, by agreement of the Muslims. As for those who are not among those who offer resistance and engage in combat—such as women, children, monks, elderly men, the blind, those with disabilities, and others like them—the majority of scholars hold that they must not be killed unless they fight through their words or deeds. Some scholars, however, consider it permissible to kill everyone solely on account of unbelief, except women and children, because they constitute property for the Muslims. The first view is correct, because fighting is directed against those who fight us when we seek to make Allah’s religion prevail. As Allah Most High says:

“Fight in the cause of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”

The Sunan collections report that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, passed by a slain woman during one of his military expeditions. People had gathered around her, and he said:

“This woman would not have fought.”

He said to one of them: “Catch up with Khālid and tell him: ‘Do not kill children or hired laborers.’”

It is also reported in both that he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say:

“Do not kill a decrepit old man, nor

---

## Page 13946

a young child or a woman.”

This is because Allah Most High has permitted taking life to the extent necessary for the welfare of His creation. As He Most High says:

“Persecution is worse than killing.”

That is, although killing involves evil and corruption, the persecution perpetrated by the unbelievers involves greater evil and corruption. Whoever does not prevent Muslims from upholding religion for Allah harms only himself through his unbelief.

For this reason, the jurists have stated that someone who promotes innovations contrary to the Quran and Sunnah is subject to punishments not imposed on someone who remains silent.

It is related in a hadith:

“When a sin is concealed, it harms only its perpetrator; but when it becomes public and is not denounced, it harms the community at large.”

For this reason, Islamic law has made fighting the unbelievers obligatory, but has not made it obligatory to kill those of them who have been subdued. Rather, if one of their men is captured, whether in battle or otherwise—for example, if a ship casts him onto our shores, he loses his way, or he is captured through a ruse—the ruler is to choose whichever course best serves the public interest: killing him, enslaving him, releasing him without ransom, or ransoming him for money or in exchange for another person. This is the position of most jurists, as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah, although some jurists hold that the permission to release him without ransom or to ransom him has been abrogated.

As for the People of the Book and the Magians, they are to be fought until they embrace Islam or pay the jizya directly, in a state of submission.

---

## Page 13947

As for all others, the jurists have differed over accepting jizya from them, although most do not accept it from the Arabs.

Any group that professes Islam yet refuses to observe any of its manifest precepts established through mass transmission must be fought, by agreement of the Muslims, until religion is entirely for Allah. Thus Abū Bakr al-Siddīq—may Allah be pleased with him—and the other Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—fought those who withheld zakat. Some Companions had initially hesitated to fight them, but they subsequently reached agreement. Umar ibn al-Khattāb had asked Abū Bakr—may Allah be pleased with them both:

“How can you fight the people when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Once they say this, their lives and property are protected from me, except as required by the rights it entails; and their reckoning rests with Allah’?”

Abū Bakr replied:

“Zakat is among those rights. By Allah, if they withheld from me even a young she-goat that they used to give to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I would fight them for withholding it.”

Umar said:

“As soon as I saw that Allah had opened Abū Bakr’s heart to fighting, I knew that it was right.”

It is also established through numerous routes of transmission that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded fighting the Khawārij. In the two Sahīh collections, Alī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him—reported:

“I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say, ‘In the last days, a people will emerge who are young in age and foolish in judgment. They will speak the words of the best of creation, yet their faith will not go beyond their throats. They will pass out of the religion just as an arrow passes

---

## Page 13948

through the prey. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will receive a reward on the Day of Resurrection.’”

In a version recorded by Muslim, Alī—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say, ‘A people will emerge from my ummah whose recitation of the Quran will make yours seem insignificant, and whose prayer will make yours seem insignificant. They will recite the Quran, thinking that it supports them, whereas it is against them. Their recitation will not go beyond their collarbones. They will pass out of Islam just as an arrow passes through the prey. If the army that encounters them knew what had been decreed for them through their Prophet, they would cease performing good deeds.’”

Abū Saīd also reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in this hadith:

Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim. In another version recorded by Muslim:

“My ummah will split into two groups, and a group that departs from the religion will emerge between them. The group closer to the truth will undertake to kill them.”

These were the people whom the Commander of the Faithful, Alī—may Allah be pleased with him—killed when division arose between the people of Iraq and Syria. They were known as the Harūriyya. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made clear that both opposing groups belonged to his ummah and that Alī’s followers were the closer of the two to the truth. He urged fighting only against those who had passed out of Islam, separated themselves from the Muslim community, and deemed the blood and property of all other Muslims lawful.

Thus, it is established by the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the ummah that one is to fight anyone who departs from

---

## Page 13949

the law of Islam, even if he utters the two testimonies of faith.

The jurists have differed over whether it is permissible to fight a group that refuses compliance if it abandons a regular sunnah prayer, such as the two rakahs before the dawn prayer. There are two opinions on this.

As for manifest and widely known obligations and prohibitions, there is agreement that such people are to be fought until they commit themselves to performing the prescribed prayers, paying zakat, fasting the month of Ramadan, making pilgrimage to the House, and refraining from prohibited acts, such as marrying sisters, consuming impure things, attacking Muslims’ lives and property, and similar acts. It is obligatory to initiate fighting against such people once the call of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has reached them concerning the requirements over which they are fought. If, however, they attack the Muslims first, the obligation to fight them becomes more emphatic, as we explained when discussing fighting aggressors who resist enforcement, namely highway robbers.

The most far-reaching form of obligatory jihad—against unbelievers and those who refuse to observe certain religious laws, such as those who withhold zakat, the Khawārij, and others like them—is required both offensively and defensively.

When undertaken offensively, it is a communal obligation: if some fulfil it, the obligation is lifted from the rest, while the merit belongs to those who undertake it. As Allah Most High says:

“Not equal are those believers who remain behind, other than those with disabilities…”

And so the verse continues. But if the enemy intends to attack the Muslims, repelling them becomes obligatory upon all those targeted, and upon those not targeted as well, to assist them. As Allah Most High says:

---

## Page 13950

“And if they seek your help in matters of religion, you must help them, except against a people with whom you have a treaty.”

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded that a Muslim be supported, whether or not one is a salaried soldier. This is obligatory upon everyone according to their ability, through their person and wealth, whether their numbers are few or many, and whether on foot or mounted. Thus, when the enemy attacked the Muslims in the year of the Trench, Allah did not permit anyone to refrain from defending them, whereas He had permitted some to refrain from initiating jihad in pursuit of the enemy, distinguishing between those who remained behind and those who went forth. Rather, He censured those who sought the Prophet’s permission to leave, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Saying, ‘Our homes are exposed,’ though they were not exposed. They wanted nothing but to flee.”

This is the defence of religion, inviolable rights, and lives: fighting undertaken out of necessity. The other is fighting undertaken by choice to advance and exalt the religion and to deter the enemy, as in the expedition to Tabūk and similar campaigns. This form of punishment applies to groups that resist enforcement.

As for inhabitants of Muslim lands and others like them who do not resist enforcement, they must be compelled to fulfil their obligations: the five pillars of Islam and other duties, such as discharging trusts, honouring agreements in dealings, and so forth.

Anyone who does not pray, whether male or female, must be commanded to pray. If they refuse, they are to be punished until they pray, by scholarly consensus. Moreover, most scholars hold that such a person must be executed if they do not pray. They are first called upon to repent; if they repent, they are spared, but otherwise they are executed. Is such a person executed as an unbeliever or

---

## Page 13951

an apostate, or a sinner? There are two well-known positions on this in the school of Ahmad and among other scholars. What is transmitted from most of the early generations implies that he is an unbeliever. This concerns someone who acknowledges that prayer is obligatory. As for someone who denies its obligation, he is an unbeliever by consensus.

Indeed, guardians must instruct a child to pray upon reaching seven years of age and strike him for failing to pray at ten, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded when he said:

“Instruct them to pray at seven, strike them for failing to pray at ten, and give them separate sleeping places.”

The same applies to the obligatory purification and other requirements of prayer.

Completing this duty entails attending to the Muslims’ mosques and their imams, and instructing the imams to lead them in prayer as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed. He said:

“Pray as you have seen me pray.”

Narrated by al-Bukhārī.

“He once led his Companions in prayer on the edge of the pulpit and said: ‘I have done this only so that you may follow me and learn how I pray.’”

Whoever leads the people, in prayer or otherwise, must look to their welfare, ensuring that they do not miss out on anything that completes their religious practice and depends upon his actions. Indeed, every prayer leader must lead them in a complete prayer, rather than confining himself to the minimum sufficient for validity that someone praying alone may observe, unless there is a valid excuse. The same applies to their leader during Hajj and their commander in war.

Do you not see that an agent or guardian conducting sales and purchases must act in the best financial interests of his principal or ward? Yet, with his own wealth, he may forgo whatever benefit he wishes. Thus, the matter of

---

## Page 13952

religion is more important, and the jurists have discussed this point.

Whenever rulers attend to setting people’s religious affairs right, both rulers and subjects prosper in their religious and worldly affairs; otherwise, their affairs fall into disorder. The foundation of all this is sincere concern for the subjects, complete sincerity in devotion to Allah, and reliance upon Him.

Sincerity and reliance upon Allah together encompass what sets right the affairs of both the elite and the general populace, just as He commanded us to say in our prayers:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

It has been said that these two statements encompass the meanings of the Books revealed from heaven. It has also been reported:

“Once, during one of his military expeditions, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘O Master of the Day of Judgment, You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.’ Then heads began falling from shoulders.”

Allah has mentioned this in several places in His Book, as in His words:

“So worship Him and rely upon Him.”

And His words, Exalted is He:

“Upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn.”

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, slaughtered his sacrificial animal, he would say: ‘O Allah, this is from You and for You.’”

Three things provide the greatest assistance to those in authority in particular, and to everyone else in general:

First: sincerity towards Allah and reliance upon Him through supplication and other means. The foundation of this is diligently observing the prayers with both heart and body.

Second: doing good to people by benefiting them and giving wealth in zakah.

Third: patiently enduring the harm people cause and other adversities.

This is why Allah frequently joins prayer and patience together, as in His words, Exalted is He:

“And seek help through patience and prayer.”

And His words, Exalted is He:

“And establish prayer at the two ends of

---

## Page 13953

the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who are mindful.”

“And be patient, for Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

And His words, Exalted is He:

“So be patient with what they say, and glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.”

Likewise, in Surah Qāf:

“So be patient with what they say, and glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before sunset.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“We certainly know that your heart is distressed by what they say.”

“So glorify your Lord with praise and be among those who prostrate.”

As for His joining prayer and zakah together in the Quran, this occurs very frequently.

Thus, observing prayer, zakah, and patience sets right the affairs of rulers and subjects, provided one understands what these comprehensive terms encompass.

Prayer encompasses remembering Allah Most High, supplicating to Him, reciting His Book, devoting one’s religion sincerely to Him, and relying upon Him.

Zakah encompasses doing good to people through wealth and other benefits, such as supporting the oppressed, aiding those in distress, and meeting the needs of those in need.

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Every act of kindness is charity.”

This therefore includes every act of kindness, even a cheerful face or a kind word.

In the two Sahīh collections, ‘Adī ibn Hātim, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is not one of you but that his Lord will speak to him, with no doorkeeper or interpreter between them. He will look to his right and see only what he has sent ahead, and he will look to his left and see

only what he has sent ahead. Then he will look before him, and the Fire will confront him. Whoever among you can protect himself from the Fire, even with half a date, let him do so. If he has nothing to give, then let him do so with a kind word.”

In the Sunan collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not belittle any act of kindness, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face, or pouring water from your bucket into the vessel of someone drawing water.”

The Sunan collections also report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

It is also related that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Umm Salamah:

Patience encompasses enduring harm, restraining anger, pardoning people, resisting one’s desires, and abandoning arrogant exultation and insolence. As Allah Most High says:

“If We let man taste mercy from Us and then withdraw it from him, he becomes utterly despairing and ungrateful.”

“But if We let him taste prosperity after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, ‘My troubles have gone.’ Indeed, he is exultant and boastful.”

“Except for those who are patient and do righteous deeds: they will have forgiveness and a great reward.”

He said to His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Be forgiving, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous.”

“Those who spend in prosperity and adversity, restrain their anger, and pardon others—and Allah loves those who do good.”

And Allah Most High says:

is best, and then the one between you and whom there was enmity will become like a close friend.”

Al-Hasan al-Basrī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: “On the Day of Resurrection, a caller will proclaim from within the Throne: ‘Let those whose reward is due from Allah rise!’ None will rise except those who pardoned and made reconciliation.”

Having good intentions towards one’s subjects and treating them well does not mean doing what they desire and refraining from what they dislike. Allah Most High says:

Allah Most High said to the Companions:

Rather, treating them well means doing what benefits them in their religious and worldly affairs, even if some dislike it. Nevertheless, he should deal gently with them in matters they dislike.

It is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Gentleness never enters anything without adorning it, and harshness never enters anything without marring it.”

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: “By Allah, I do indeed wish

to set before them the bitter demands of what is right, but I fear that they will recoil from them. “On one occasion, some of his relatives asked him to appoint them to administer the alms and pay them from those funds. He said: ‘Alms are not lawful for Muhammad or the family of Muhammad.’” He therefore withheld those funds from them and compensated them from the fay’ revenues.

“ʿAlī, Zayd and Jaʿfar brought their dispute over Hamza’s daughter before him. He did not award custody to any of them, but awarded it to her maternal aunt. He then comforted each of them with kind words. He said to ʿAlī: ‘You are of me, and I am of you.’ He said to Jaʿfar: ‘You resemble me in appearance and character.’ And he said to Zayd: ‘You are our brother and our freedman.’”

This is how a ruler should act when distributing resources and passing judgment. People constantly ask the ruler for things that it would not be proper to grant: appointments, money, benefits, remuneration, intercession concerning prescribed punishments, and other things. He should therefore compensate them in some other way if possible, or turn them away with kindly words, unless sternness is needed. Refusing a petitioner causes him pain, especially someone whose goodwill needs to be won. Allah Most High says:

“So do not rebuff the petitioner.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Give close relatives their due, as well as the needy and the traveller, and do not squander wastefully,”

up to His words: “And if you turn away from them

seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope to receive, then speak to them kindly.”

When a ruler passes judgment against someone, that person may be distressed. If he then reassures him with appropriate words and deeds, this completes the exercise of sound governance. It is like a physician giving a patient something to make an unpleasant medicine easier to swallow. When Allah sent Moses, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh, He said:

“Speak to him gently, so that he may take heed or be moved to fear.”

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal and Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī, may Allah be pleased with them both, when he sent them to Yemen: ‘Make things easy, not difficult; give glad tidings, and do not drive people away. Cooperate with one another, and do not disagree.’”

“Once, a Bedouin urinated in the mosque, and the Prophet’s Companions rose to stop him. He said: ‘Do not interrupt him’—meaning, do not interrupt his urination. He then ordered that a bucket of water be poured over the spot. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘You have been sent to make things easy, not to make them difficult.’”

Both reports are found in the two Sahīh collections. A person needs this approach in governing himself, his household, and his subjects. People do not accept the truth without drawing strength from the share of life’s enjoyments that they need. With a righteous intention, those enjoyments thus become worship of Allah and obedience to Him. Do you not see that eating, drinking, and clothing oneself are obligatory? Indeed, if someone

## Page 13958

is compelled by necessity to eat carrion, he is obliged to eat it according to the majority of scholars. If he refuses to eat until he dies, he will enter the Fire, for acts of worship cannot be performed without these necessities, and whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation is itself obligatory. This is why a person’s spending on himself and his family takes precedence over other spending.

In the Sunan collections, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Give in charity.” A man said, “O Messenger of Allah, I have a dinar.” He replied, “Spend it on yourself.”
The man said, “I have another.” He replied, “Spend it on your wife.”
He said, “I have another.” He replied, “Spend it on your child.”
He said, “I have another.” He replied, “Spend it on your servant.”
He said, “I have another.” He replied, “You know best what to do with it.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Of a dinar you spend in Allah’s cause, a dinar you spend to free a slave, a dinar you give in charity to a needy person, and a dinar you spend on your family, the one that brings the greatest reward is the one you spend on your family.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Umāmah, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O son of Adam, giving away your surplus is good for you, and withholding it is bad for you. You are not to blame for keeping what you need. Begin with those you support. The upper hand is better than the lower hand.”

This explains the words of Allah Most High:

“They ask you what they should spend. Say, ‘Whatever is beyond your needs.’”

That is, the surplus. This is because a man’s spending on himself and his family is an individual obligation, unlike

---

## Page 13959

spending on military campaigns and the needy, which is, in principle, either a communal obligation or recommended, although it may become an individual obligation when no one else undertakes it. Feeding the hungry is obligatory. Hence the statement in the hadith:

“If the beggar were truthful, whoever turned him away would not prosper.”

Imam Ahmad cited this and stated that if one knows the beggar is truthful, one must feed him. Abū Hātim al-Bustī also narrated in his Sahīh the lengthy hadith reported by Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which contains various kinds of knowledge and wisdom. It includes the following saying from the wisdom of the house of David, peace be upon him:

“A person of sound judgment ought to set aside four periods: a period in which he communes privately with his Lord; a period in which he calls himself to account; a period in which he meets privately with companions who tell him his faults and speak to him about himself; and a period in which he enjoys lawful and becoming pleasures in private. This last period helps him with the others.”

This makes clear that lawful, becoming pleasures are indispensable, for they help one attend to those other matters. Hence the jurists stated that uprightness consists in religious rectitude and dignified conduct: doing what enhances and adorns a person, and avoiding what taints and disgraces him.

Abū al-Dardā’, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say:

“I refresh myself with a little idle diversion to help me uphold what is right.”

Allah, glorified is He, originally created pleasures and desires to serve the full welfare of His creation, for through them they obtain what benefits them, just as He created anger so that they might use it to ward off

---

## Page 13960

what harms them. He has forbidden those desires whose indulgence is harmful and condemned those who devote themselves solely to them.

As for someone who uses what is lawful and becoming to help him uphold what is right, this is a righteous deed. Hence the authentic hadith in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When one of you has sexual intercourse, that is an act of charity.” They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, can one of us satisfy his desire and be rewarded for it?” He replied, “Tell me: if he satisfied it unlawfully, would he not incur sin?” They said, “Yes.” He said, “Then why do you count sin for what is unlawful, but not reward for what is lawful?”

The two Sahīh collections also report from Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to him:

“Whatever you spend seeking Allah’s Face will increase you in rank and standing—even the morsel you place in your wife’s mouth.”

There are many reports on this subject. Thus, when a believer has a good intention, it extends to his actions in general, and his permissible activities become righteous deeds because of the soundness of his heart and intention. The hypocrite, however, because of the corruption of his heart and intention, is punished for the acts of worship he outwardly performs to show off. For it is related in an authentic hadith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, there is a piece of flesh in the body which, if sound, makes the rest of the body sound, and if corrupt, makes the rest of the body corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.”

Just as punishments have been prescribed to encourage the fulfilment of obligations and the avoidance of forbidden acts, so too has everything that helps achieve this. The path to goodness and obedience should therefore be made easy, and people should be helped and encouraged to follow it by every possible means—for example, by giving

---

## Page 13961

his children and family, or those under his authority, whatever encourages them to perform righteous deeds—whether money, praise, or anything else. This is why horse and camel racing, archery contests, and receiving prizes for them have been prescribed: they encourage the preparation of strength and the readiness of horses for jihad in Allah’s cause. Indeed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Rightly Guided Caliphs used to organize horse races and provide prizes from the public treasury. The same applies to giving to those whose hearts are to be won over, for it is related:

“A man would embrace Islam at the beginning of the day out of desire for worldly gain, yet before the day ended, Islam would be dearer to him than everything upon which the sun rises.”

Likewise, the sources of evil and disobedience should be cut off, the avenues leading to them blocked, and whatever leads to them prevented, unless it brings an overriding benefit. An example is the Prophet’s prohibition, expressed in his words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“No man should be alone with a woman, for Satan is the third of them.”

He also said:

“It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to undertake a journey of two days unless accompanied by her husband or a mahram—a relative whom she is permanently forbidden to marry.”

Thus, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade being alone with a woman who is neither one’s wife nor a mahram, and travelling with her, because this provides an avenue to evil. It is related from al-Sha‘bī:

“When the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, there was among them a strikingly handsome boy, whom he seated behind him. He said, ‘David’s sin lay only in looking.’”

And ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, while patrolling Medina at night, heard a woman singing verses in which she said:

## Page 13962

“Is there a way to wine, that I might drink it?
Is there a way to Nasr ibn Hajjāj?”

“Is there a way to wine, that I might drink it?
Is there a way to Nasr ibn Hajjāj?”

He summoned him and found him to be a handsome young man. He had his head shaved, but this only increased his beauty, so he banished him to Basra lest women be tempted by him.

It is also related of him that he learned of a man with whom boys would sit, and he forbade them to keep his company. Thus, if a boy’s appearance is feared to be a temptation to men or women, his guardian should be prevented from displaying him unnecessarily or enhancing his beauty, especially by pampering him in bathhouses and bringing him to gatherings of entertainment and singing. Such conduct warrants discretionary punishment. Likewise, anyone whose immoral conduct has become apparent should be prevented from owning handsome, beardless slave boys, and they should be separated from him.

The jurists agree that if someone gives testimony before a judge, but is widely known for some form of sinful conduct that disqualifies him as a witness, his testimony must not be accepted. A person may challenge his credibility on that basis even without having witnessed that conduct himself.

It is authentically reported that a funeral procession passed by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and those present spoke well of the deceased. He said:

“It is assured; it is assured.”

Then another funeral procession passed by him, and they spoke ill of the deceased. He said:

“It is assured; it is assured.”

They asked him about this, and he replied:
