## Page 14076

from this prohibition.

In His Book, He has declared Muslims’ lives, property, and honour inviolable, and forbidden backbiting, mockery, and disparagement; yet they are the foremost in deeming such violations lawful. In His Book, He has commanded unity and concord and forbidden division and discord, yet no one is further than they from these teachings. In His Book, He has enjoined obedience to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, love for him, and adherence to his judgments, yet they depart from these commands. In His Book, He has set forth the rights of the Prophet’s wives, yet they disavow them. In His Book, He has affirmed His oneness, declared that sovereignty belongs exclusively to Him, and commanded that He alone be worshipped, without any partner, yet they depart from these teachings. Indeed, they are polytheists, as stated in the hadith concerning them, for no one venerates more than they the graves that have been made into idols besides Allah. This subject would take a long time to describe. In His Book, He has revealed His names and attributes, yet they disbelieve in them. In His Book, He has related the accounts of the prophets and forbidden seeking forgiveness for polytheists, yet they disbelieve in these teachings.

In His Book, He has declared that He has power over all things, that He is the Creator of all things, that whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and that there is no power except through Allah; yet they disbelieve in these truths. There is room in this fatwa for only a brief outline. It is known with certainty that the Kharijites’ faith in what Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought was greater than theirs. Thus, if the Commander of the Faithful, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, killed them, and his troops plundered the mounts, weapons, and wealth in their camp, then these people are all the more deserving of being fought and having their property seized, just as the Commander of the Faithful, ‘Alī ibn

---

## Page 14077

Abī Tālib seized the Kharijites’ property.

Anyone claiming scholarly learning, or anyone else, who believes that fighting these people is equivalent to fighting rebels who rise against the ruler on the basis of an admissible interpretation—as when the Commander of the Faithful, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, fought the people of the Camel and Siffīn—is mistaken and ignorant of the true nature of Islamic law and its particular treatment of those who depart from it. Had these people governed the lands they conquered according to Islamic law, they would have been kings like other kings. Rather, they depart from the very law and Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, more grievously than the Harūrī Kharijites departed from them.

They have no admissible interpretation to justify their actions. An admissible interpretation is a permissible one whose proponent is allowed to maintain it when there is no rebuttal to it, such as the interpretations of scholars who disagree on matters open to independent scholarly judgment. According to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus, these people have no such interpretation. Rather, theirs is an interpretation of the same kind as those of the people who withheld zakat, the Kharijites, the Jews, and the Christians. Their interpretation is the worst of the interpretations advanced by the followers of deviant inclinations.

Yet these students of jurisprudence have found no thorough examination of these questions in their abridged manuals. Many leading scholars who have written on Islamic law have discussed fighting those who depart from its doctrinal and practical foundations—such as those who withheld zakat, the Kharijites, and others like them—only as a form of fighting those who rebel against the ruler, such as the people of

---

## Page 14078

the Camel and Siffīn. This is mistaken. Rather, the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Companions distinguish between the two categories, as most leading scholars of jurisprudence, Sunnah, hadith, Sufism, speculative theology, and other disciplines have explained. Furthermore, reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, encompass these people and others. Among them is what Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from Abū Hurayrah, who said:

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever abandons obedience and separates from the Muslim community, then dies, dies a death of pre-Islamic ignorance. Whoever is killed under a banner of blind allegiance, becoming angry out of partisan loyalty and fighting for partisan loyalty, is not of me. Whoever rises against my ummah, striking its righteous and wicked alike, neither sparing its believers nor keeping faith with those under its covenant, is not of me.”

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus mentioned the rebels who abandon obedience to the ruler and separate from the Muslim community, stating that whoever among them dies has died a death of pre-Islamic ignorance. For the people of the pre-Islamic age did not appoint rulers over themselves; rather, each group sought to overpower the others. He then mentioned fighting out of partisan loyalty, as with those who fight on grounds of lineage, such as Qays and Yaman, stating that whoever is killed under these banners is not part of his ummah. He then mentioned the fighting waged by violent aggressors, the Kharijites, and their like, stating that whoever does this is not of him. These people combine all three characteristics and go beyond them.

For they have abandoned obedience and the Muslim community. They kill believers and those protected by covenants, and they recognize none of the rulers of

---

## Page 14079

the Muslims as entitled to obedience, whether just or sinful, except for someone who does not exist.

They fight out of a partisan loyalty worse than loyalty based on lineage: loyalty to a corrupt religion. Their hearts harbour unparalleled rancour and rage against Muslims, great and small, righteous and otherwise. What they regard as their greatest act of worship is cursing Muslims who are allies of Allah, from earlier and later generations alike. The best among them, in their estimation, is the one who neither curses them nor seeks forgiveness for them.

As for rising up and killing believers and those protected by covenants, this too describes their conduct, despite their claim that they alone are believers and that the rest of the ummah are unbelievers.

Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from Muhammad ibn Shurayh, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There will be troubles upon troubles. Whoever seeks to divide this ummah while it is united, strike him with the sword, whoever he may be.” In another wording: “Kill him.”

Another wording reads:

“Whoever comes to you while you are united under one man, seeking to break your unity and divide your community, kill him.”

These people are the most eager of all to divide the Muslim community. They acknowledge no ruler’s right to obedience, whether he is just or sinful, and they do not obey him in matters of obedience to Allah or in anything else. Rather, what they regard as their greatest foundational principle is declaring the finest leaders of the Muslims to be unbelievers, cursing them and reviling them—such as the Rightly Guided Caliphs, Muslim scholars and their shaykhs. For they believe that anyone who does not believe in the infallible imam, who does not exist, has not believed

---

## Page 14080

in Allah and His Messenger. These people were worse than the Harūriyya Khawārij and other adherents of deviant doctrines because their doctrines contained greater evil than those of the Khawārij. The Harūriyya Khawārij were the first adherents of deviant doctrines to depart from the Sunnah and the Muslim community. This happened while the remaining Rightly Guided Caliphs and surviving Emigrants and Helpers were still present, while knowledge, faith and justice prevailed in the ummah, and while the light of prophethood shone and both proof and power held sway. Allah had made His religion prevail over all other religions through proof and power. Their rebellion was prompted by various actions involving interpretive judgment undertaken by the Commanders of the Faithful, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī, and those with them. They could not tolerate these things: they treated matters open to scholarly judgment—indeed, even good deeds—as sins, and treated sins as unbelief. This is why they did not rebel during the time of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar: those interpretive judgments were absent, and they themselves were weak.

It is well known that the more brightly the light of prophethood shines, the weaker the innovation that opposes it becomes. Thus, the first innovation was less grave than the second, while later innovations contain elements of the same kind as earlier ones, with further additions. Likewise, the closer a practice of the Sunnah is in origin to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the better it is. Practices of the Sunnah are therefore the opposite of innovations: whatever was closer to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—such as the conduct of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar—was better than that which

---

## Page 14081

came later, such as the conduct of ʿUthmān and ʿAlī. Innovations are the opposite: the further removed they were from him, the worse they were than those closer to him. The innovation closest to his time was that of the Khawārij. Their innovative teachings were already being voiced during his lifetime, but they did not organize themselves and acquire strength until the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him.

The doctrine of the Rāfida then began to be voiced during ʿAlī’s time, but its adherents did not organize themselves and acquire strength until after the killing of al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him. Indeed, the name Rāfida did not appear until the uprising of Zayd ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Husayn, after the first century AH. When he openly prayed for mercy upon Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, the Rāfida rejected him and were therefore called “Rāfida.” They believed that Abū Jaʿfar was the infallible imam. Others followed Zayd and were called “Zaydiyya” after him.

Then, towards the end of the era of the Companions, the innovative doctrines of the Qadariyya and the Murjiʾa began to emerge. The surviving Companions refuted them, including Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, Abū Saʿīd, Wāthila ibn al-Asqaʿ and others. Their adherents did not acquire authority or become an organized body until the Muʿtazila and the Murjiʾa subsequently grew in number.

Then, towards the end of the era of the Successors, the innovative doctrine of the Jahmiyya, who deny the divine attributes, began to be voiced. They did not become an organized body or acquire authority until after the second century AH, during the rule of Abū al-ʿAbbās, known as al-Maʾmūn. He openly espoused Jahmī doctrine, subjected people to an inquisition over it, and translated into Arabic the books of

---

## Page 14082

the non-Arabs: Romans, Greeks, and others. During his reign, the “Khurramiyya” emerged. They were heretics and hypocrites who outwardly professed Islam, and later branched into the Qarāmita, the Bātiniyya, and the Ismāʿīliyya. Most of these outwardly professed Rāfidī doctrine.

During the rule of the Banū Buwayh, after the third century AH, the Imāmī Rāfida came to embrace most of these misguided doctrines: rebellion, Rāfidī doctrine, Qadarī doctrine, and Jahmī doctrine. When a scholar considers the texts of the Quran and Sunnah that they have contradicted, he finds that none but Allah can enumerate them. All this shows that they possess what is found among the Harūrī Khawārij, and more besides.

Moreover, the Harūrī Khawārij professed to follow the Quran according to their own opinions, and claimed to follow traditions which they alleged contradicted the Quran. The Rāfida profess to follow the Prophet’s household and claim that among them is an infallible person from whom no knowledge is hidden and who never errs—neither deliberately nor inadvertently nor when exercising sound judgment.

Following the Quran is obligatory upon the Muslim community; indeed, it is the foundation of faith and the guidance of Allah with which He sent His Messenger. Likewise, it is obligatory to love the household of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to maintain allegiance to them, and to uphold their rights. These are the two weighty trusts concerning which the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave his instructions.

Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, addressed us at a pool called Khumm, between Mecca and Medina, saying: ‘O people, I am leaving among you the two weighty trusts’—and in another version, ‘one of them is greater than the other’—‘the Book of Allah, in which there is guidance

---

## Page 14083

and light.’ He then urged adherence to the Book of Allah.” Another version reads:

“It is the rope of Allah: whoever follows it is rightly guided, and whoever abandons it goes astray. And my kindred, the members of my household. I remind you of Allah concerning my household; I remind you of Allah concerning my household; I remind you of Allah concerning my household.”

Zayd ibn Arqam was asked, “Who are the members of his household?” He replied, “His household are those forbidden to receive charity: the family of al-ʿAbbās, the family of ʿAlī, the family of Jaʿfar, and the family of ʿAqīl.” The scriptural texts requiring adherence to the Quran are too numerous to recount here.

It has also been narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through several good chains of transmission, that he said concerning his household:

“By Him in Whose Hand is my soul, they will not enter Paradise until they love you for my sake.”

Allah has commanded us to invoke blessings upon the family of Muhammad, kept them pure from charity—which is the impurities people cast off—and assigned them a share in the fifth of war spoils and in property acquired without battle. As authentically recorded in the Sahīh, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah chose the descendants of Ishmael, chose Kināna from the descendants of Ishmael, chose Quraysh from Kināna, chose Banū Hāshim from Quraysh, and chose me from Banū Hāshim. Thus I am the best of you in person and the best of you in lineage.”

Were we to recount what has been narrated concerning the rights of the Prophet’s relatives and the rights of the Companions, the discussion would become lengthy, for the Quran and Sunnah contain abundant evidence on this subject. Hence, Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿa have agreed upon upholding the rights of the Companions and the Prophet’s relatives. They have disavowed the Nāsiba, who declare ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib an unbeliever and brand him a sinner

---

## Page 14084

and violate the sanctity of the Prophet’s household—such as those who opposed them over political rule, disregarded their obligatory rights, or went to unjustified extremes in venerating Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya. They have also disavowed the Rāfida, who malign the Companions and the vast majority of believers, and declare most righteous Muslims to be unbelievers. They know that the latter are greater in sin and misguidance than the former, as we have mentioned in explaining that these warring Rāfida are worse than the Khawārij. Each of the two groups has claimed adherence to one of the two weighty trusts; the Quran, however, is greater. Thus, the Khawārij are less misguided than the Rāfida, although both groups oppose the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, his Companions and relatives, the Sunnah of his rightly guided caliphs, and his kindred, the members of his household.

Scholars among the followers of Imam Ahmad and others have disagreed over whether the consensus of the caliphs and the consensus of the Prophet’s kindred constitute binding authority that must be followed. The correct view is that both do. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me. Hold fast to it and bite onto it with your molar teeth.”

This is an authentic hadith recorded in the Sunan collections. He also said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I am leaving among you the two weighty trusts: the Book of Allah and my kindred, and they will never part until they reach the Cistern.”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated it and graded it good, though this warrants scrutiny. Likewise, the consensus of the people of the Prophet’s city during the time of the rightly guided caliphs holds the same standing.

---

## Page 14085

The purpose here is to make clear that these groups—the Rāfida and others who wage war against the Muslim community—are worse than the Khawārij, whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explicitly commanded and encouraged fighting. This is agreed upon by the scholars of Islam who understand the matter’s true nature. Some hold that the Messenger’s wording, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, encompasses all these groups; others hold that they are included by implication and a fortiori inference, or because they are analogous to the Khawārij.

The hadith has been transmitted in various wordings. In the Sahīh collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim—the wording here is al-Bukhārī’s—Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“When I relate a hadith to you from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by Allah, I would rather fall from the sky than tell a lie about him. But when I speak to you about matters between you and me, war is deception. I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

‘Towards the end of time, people will emerge who are young in age and foolish in judgment. They will utter some of the finest words spoken by mankind, yet their faith will not pass beyond their throats. They will pass out of the religion as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will receive a reward on the Day of Resurrection.’”

In Sahīh Muslim:

“Zayd ibn Wahb reported that he was in the army accompanying Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, which marched against the Khawārij. Alī said:

‘O people, I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

“A people will emerge from my community who recite the Quran. Your recitation will be as nothing compared with theirs, your prayer as nothing compared with theirs, and your fasting as nothing compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, thinking that it counts in their favour, whereas it counts against them.

---

## Page 14086

Their prayer does not pass beyond their collarbones. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. If the army that encounters them knew what had been decreed for them through the words of their Prophet, they would cease doing good deeds. Their distinguishing sign is that among them is a man with an upper arm but no forearm; at the end of his upper arm is something like the nipple of a breast, bearing a few white hairs.”

By Allah, I certainly hope that these are those people, for they have shed blood that is forbidden to shed and raided people’s grazing livestock. So march forth in the name of Allah.’ He then related the hadith to its end.”

Also in Sahīh Muslim:

“Ubayd Allah ibn Abī Rāfiʿ, Alī’s scribe, reported that when the Harūriyya rebelled, he was with Alī, may Allah be pleased with him. They said, ‘Judgment belongs to Allah alone.’

Alī replied:

‘A true statement intended for a false purpose. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, described people whose characteristics I certainly recognize in these men. They speak the truth with their tongues, but it goes no further than here’—and he pointed to his throat—‘They are among the most hateful of Allah’s creatures to Him. Among them is a black man, one of whose hands resembles a ewe’s teat or the nipple of a breast.’

When Alī ibn Tālib killed them, he said, ‘Search.’ They searched but found nothing.

He said, ‘Go back! By Allah, I have not lied, nor have I been lied to’—repeating this twice or three times. Then they found him in a ruined place and brought him and laid him before Alī.”

This sign mentioned by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, identifies the first of them to emerge; they are not confined to those particular people. For he has stated

---

## Page 14087

in another hadith that they will continue to emerge until the time of the Dajjāl. The Muslims agree that the Khawārij are not confined to that particular army. Moreover, the characteristics he described also apply to others besides that army.

For this reason, the Companions narrated the hadith without restricting its application, as in the report in the two Sahīhs from Abū Salama and ʿAtāʾ ibn Yasār. They went to Abū Saʿīd and asked him about the Harūriyya: “Did you hear the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mention them?”

He replied: “I do not know. But the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

‘There will emerge within this community—he did not say “from it”—people whose prayer will make you regard your own prayer as insignificant. They recite the Quran, but it does not pass beyond their throats or gullets. They pass out of the religion as an arrow passes through its quarry. The archer examines his arrow, its head and its sinew bindings, and wonders whether any blood has clung to its nock.’”

This is Muslim’s wording.

Also in the two Sahīhs, Abū Saʿīd reported:

“While the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was distributing something, ʿAbd Allah Dhū al-Khuwaysira al-Tamīmī came—in another version, Dhū al-Khuwaysira, a man from Banū Tamīm, came to him—and said: ‘Be just, O Messenger of Allah!’

He replied: ‘Woe to you! Who would be just if I were not just? You would indeed have failed and lost if I were not just.’

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb said: ‘Allow me to strike off his head.’

He said: ‘Leave him alone. He has companions whose prayer will make any one of you regard his own prayer as insignificant, and whose fasting will make him regard his own fasting as insignificant. They pass out of the religion as an arrow passes through its quarry. The archer looks at its head, but nothing is found on it

---

## Page 14088

, then he looks at its sinew bindings, but nothing is found on them; then he looks at its shaft—that is, its wooden body—but nothing is found on it; then he looks at its feathers, but nothing is found on them. It has passed through too swiftly for dung or blood to cling to it.’” He then related the rest of the hadith.

The root of these people’s misguidance is their belief that the rightly guided leaders and the Muslim community have departed from justice and gone astray. This is the starting point of those who depart from the Sunnah, such as the Rāfida and others like them. They then regard what they consider injustice as unbelief, and attach to that unbelief rulings of their own invention. These, then, are three stages followed by those who pass out of the religion, such as the Harūriyya, the Rāfida and others like them.

At each stage, they abandon some of the foundations of Islam, until they pass out of it as an arrow passes through its quarry. In the two Sahīhs, the hadith of Abū Saʿīd states:

“They kill the Muslims and leave the idolaters alone. If I live to encounter them, I will kill them as ʿĀd were killed.”

This also describes all the others who depart from the Sunnah, such as the Rāfida and those like them. They regard the blood of those who face the qiblah as lawful to shed, believing them to be apostates, more readily than they regard the blood of unbelievers who are not apostates as lawful to shed, because an apostate is worse than other unbelievers.

In another hadith, Abū Saʿīd reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned people who would arise within his community:

“They will emerge amid division among the people. Their distinguishing mark will be shaved heads.”

He said:

“They are the worst of creation—or among the worst of creation. They will be killed by whichever of the two factions is closer to the truth.”

This mark characterized the earliest of them, as in the case of Dhū al-Thudayya, for this is a characteristic inseparable from them.

---

## Page 14089

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim also recorded in their two Sahīhs a hadith concerning them, narrated by Sahl ibn Hunayf, conveying the same meaning. Al-Bukhārī also related it from Abd Allāh ibn Umar, while Muslim related it from Abū Dharr, Rāfi‘ ibn Amr, Jābir ibn Abd Allāh and others. Al-Nasā’ī narrated:

“Abū Barza was asked, ‘Did you hear Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mention the Khawārij?’

“He replied, ‘Yes. I heard Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with my own ears and saw him with my own eyes. Some wealth was brought to Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he distributed it, giving to those on his right and those on his left, but giving nothing to those behind him. A man behind him stood up and said, “Muhammad, you have not been just in this distribution!” He was a black man with cropped hair, wearing two white garments.

“‘Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, became intensely angry and said to him, “By Allah, after me you will find no man more just than I am.” Then he said, “At the end of time, people will emerge, as though this man were one of them. They will recite the Quran, but it will not pass beyond their collarbones. They will pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Their distinguishing mark will be shaved heads. They will continue to emerge until the last of them emerge alongside the Dajjāl. When you encounter them, kill them. They are the very worst of creation.”’”

In Sahīh Muslim, Abd Allāh ibn al-Sāmit narrates from Abū Dharr, who said that Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“After me, there will be people from my community—or: there will arise after me people from my community—who recite the Quran, but it will not pass beyond their throats. They will pass out of the religion as an arrow passes through its quarry, then never return to it. They are the very worst of creation.”

Ibn al-Sāmit said: “Then I met

---

## Page 14090

Rāfi‘ ibn Amr al-Ghifārī, the brother of al-Hakam ibn Amr al-Ghifārī. I said, ‘What of the hadith I heard from Abū Dharr about such-and-such?’ I related the hadith to him, and he replied, ‘I too heard it from Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’”

These characteristics are found both among those whom Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, killed and among others. When we say that Alī fought the Khawārij at the command of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, this is like saying that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, fought the unbelievers: that is, he fought unbelievers as a category, even though unbelief takes different forms. Likewise, polytheism takes different forms. Although the gods worshipped by the Arabs were not those worshipped by the Indians, Chinese and Turks, the term polytheism and its meaning encompass them all.

Likewise, the descriptions of departing from the religion and passing out of it apply to everyone who resembles those people. Fighting them is obligatory by the Prophet’s command, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, just as fighting those people was obligatory, even though departure from the religion and Islam takes different forms. We have already explained that the Rāfidah’s departure from the religion and passing out of it are far greater.

As for killing an individual member of the Khawārij who is under one’s control—such as one of the Harūriyyah, the Rāfidah or similar groups—the jurists hold two opinions, both transmitted from Imam Ahmad. The correct view is that it is permissible to kill an individual among them, such as one who calls others to his doctrine, and others of that kind in whom there is

---

## Page 14091

corruption.

For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Wherever you encounter them, kill them.”

He also said:

“If I live to encounter them, I will surely kill them as ‘Ād were killed.”

Umar said to Subaygh ibn ‘Isl, “Had I found your head shaved, I would have struck the head that holds your eyes.” Moreover, Alī ibn Abī Tālib sought to kill Abd Allāh ibn Saba’, the first of the Rāfidah, until he fled from him. These people are also among the greatest spreaders of corruption on earth. If their corruption cannot be stopped except by killing them, they are to be killed. It is not, however, obligatory to kill every individual among them when this doctrine has not been openly expressed, or when killing him would cause greater harm.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, initially refrained from killing that Khārijī, lest people say, “Muhammad kills his companions.” At that time, he was not causing widespread corruption. Likewise, Alī refrained from killing them when they first appeared, because they were numerous and outwardly remained obedient and part of the Muslim community. They had not fought the members of the community, nor had it become clear to him that they were the ones intended.

As for declaring them unbelievers and holding that they will remain eternally in Hell, scholars likewise have two well-known opinions, both transmitted from Ahmad. These two opinions concern the Khawārij and those who pass out of the religion among the Harūriyyah, the Rāfidah and similar groups.

The correct view is that those statements of theirs which are known to contradict what the Messenger brought constitute unbelief. Likewise, their actions resembling those committed by unbelievers against Muslims also constitute unbelief. I have mentioned the evidence for this elsewhere. However, declaring a particular individual among them an unbeliever and judging that he will remain eternally in Hell depend upon establishing that the conditions for declaring him an unbeliever are fulfilled and that the impediments to doing so are absent. For we affirm in general terms

---

## Page 14092

what the scriptural texts state concerning promises of reward, threats of punishment, and judgments of unbelief and sinfulness. Yet we do not judge that a particular individual falls under such a general ruling until the grounds for applying it to him are established without any countervailing impediment. I have explained this principle at length in “The Principle Governing Declarations of Unbelief.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not declare an unbeliever the man who said:

“When I die, burn me, then scatter my ashes in the sea. By Allah, if Allah has power over me, He will punish me as He has never punished anyone in all the worlds.”

This was despite his doubt concerning Allah’s power and His ability to bring him back to life. Likewise, scholars do not declare someone an unbeliever for considering something forbidden to be lawful when this is due to his having only recently embraced Islam or having grown up in a remote desert region. A judgment of unbelief can only be made after the message has reached a person. Many of these people may not have received the scriptural texts that contradict their views, nor know that the Messenger was sent with those teachings. Thus, it is stated in general terms that a particular statement constitutes unbelief, while an individual is declared an unbeliever only when the proof whose rejection constitutes unbelief has been established against him—not otherwise. And Allah knows best.

What do the jurists, the imams of the religion, say concerning these Tatars who arrived in the year 699 AH and committed the widely known acts of killing Muslims, taking some of their offspring captive, and plundering the Muslims they encountered; who violated the sanctities of religion by humiliating Muslims and desecrating mosques—especially “the Holy House in Jerusalem”—and wreaked havoc there

---

## Page 14093

and seized vast sums from the property of the Muslims and the public treasury, took great numbers of Muslim men captive, and uprooted them from their homelands. Despite this, they claimed adherence to the two testimonies of faith and maintained that fighting their combatants was forbidden, on the grounds that they followed the foundations of Islam and had refrained from exterminating the Muslims. Is fighting them permissible or obligatory? In either case, on what grounds is it permissible or obligatory? Give us your ruling, and may you be rewarded.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah. Any group—whether these people or others—that refuses to abide by any of the manifest laws of Islam established through mass transmission must be fought until they abide by its laws, even if they profess the two testimonies of faith and observe some of its laws. Thus Abū Bakr al-Siddīq and the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, fought those who withheld zakah. The jurists after them agreed on this, following the earlier debate between ʿUmar and Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, thus agreed on fighting to uphold the rights of Islam, acting upon the Quran and the Sunnah.

Likewise, the hadith concerning the Khawārij is authentically transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through ten routes. He described them as the worst of all created beings, despite saying:

“You would consider your prayers insignificant beside theirs, and your fasting insignificant beside theirs.”

It is therefore clear that merely invoking the protection of Islam, while failing to abide by its laws, does not remove the obligation to fight. Fighting is obligatory until religion is entirely for Allah and there is no more strife. Thus, whenever religion is devoted to other than Allah

---

## Page 14094

then fighting is obligatory. Any group that refuses to observe some of the obligatory prayers, fasting, or Hajj; to uphold the inviolability of blood and property and the prohibitions against wine, unlawful sexual intercourse, gambling, or marrying women within the prohibited degrees; to undertake jihad against the disbelievers or levy the jizyah on the People of the Book; or to comply with other religious obligations and prohibitions—whose denial or neglect admits of no excuse, and whose binding character it is disbelief to deny—must be fought on that account, even if it acknowledges them. I know of no disagreement among the scholars concerning this.

The jurists have differed only concerning a group that persistently refuses to observe certain sunnah practices, such as the two units of prayer before the dawn prayer, the call to prayer, and the call announcing its commencement—according to those who do not consider these obligatory—and similar religious observances. Is a group that refuses to observe them to be fought for abandoning them or not? As for the obligations and prohibitions mentioned above and others like them, there is no disagreement that fighting is required to enforce them.

According to the scholars of discerning judgment, these people do not have the same status as rebels who rise against the ruler or withdraw from obedience to him, such as the people of Syria in relation to the Commander of the Faithful, Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him. Those people withdrew from obedience to a particular ruler or rose against him to remove him from office. But those under discussion have departed from

---

## Page 14095

Islam; they are comparable to those who withheld zakat and to the Kharijites whom Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, fought.

For this reason, Alī’s conduct, may Allah be pleased with him, differed between his fighting against the people of Basra and Syria and his fighting against the people of Nahrawān. He treated the people of Basra and Syria as a brother treats his brother, whereas his treatment of the Kharijites was different. Authentic reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, support the consensus ultimately reached by the Companions concerning the fighting undertaken by Abu Bakr al-Siddīq and the fighting against the Kharijites. This differs from the internal conflict involving the people of Syria and Basra: the scriptural texts convey what they convey concerning it, and the Companions and Successors differed over it.

Moreover, some leading jurists hold that the rebels who must be fought are those who rise against the ruler on the basis of a tenable interpretation, not those who withdraw from obedience to him. Others regard both categories as rebels. There is, however, a clear distinction between rebels and the Tatars. As for those who do not adhere to the manifest laws of Islam established through mass transmission, I know of no disagreement concerning the obligation to fight them.

With this principle established, the army of the people asked about comprises disbelievers—Christians and polytheists—as well as people who profess Islam, who constitute the majority of the army. They pronounce the two testimonies of faith when asked to do so and revere the Messenger. Yet very few of them pray, although fasting Ramadan is more common among them than prayer. They hold Muslims in higher esteem than others

---

## Page 14096

and they esteem the righteous among the Muslims. They possess some measure of Islam, though they differ in this regard. Yet the way followed by most of them, on account of which they are fought, entails abandoning many, or most, of the laws of Islam. First, they make Islam obligatory, but do not fight those who abandon it. Rather, they honour and leave alone anyone who fights for the Mongol state, even if he is a disbeliever and an enemy of Allah and His Messenger. Conversely, they deem it lawful to fight anyone who withdraws from the Mongol state’s authority or rises against it, even if he is among the finest Muslims.

They neither wage jihad against the disbelievers nor require the People of the Book to pay jizya (poll tax) and submit to subjection. Nor do they forbid anyone in their army from worshipping whatever he wishes—the sun, the moon, or anything else. Rather, their conduct indicates that a Muslim holds, in their eyes, a position comparable to that of an upright person, a righteous man, or someone who performs voluntary acts of worship among the Muslims. A disbeliever, in their eyes, is comparable to a sinful Muslim or someone who neglects voluntary acts of worship.

Likewise, most of them do not consider it forbidden to shed Muslims’ blood or seize their property unless their ruler forbids them to do so. That is, they do not undertake to refrain from these things. When he forbids them from these or other acts, they obey him because he is their ruler, not simply out of religious obligation. Most of them do not undertake to fulfil their religious duties, whether prayer, zakat, Hajj, or anything else.

Nor do they undertake to adjudicate their disputes according to Allah’s law. Rather, they judge according to regulations of their own, which sometimes agree with Islam and sometimes contradict it. It was only al-Shīzbarūn who adhered to the laws of Islam; he was the one who publicly established those Islamic observances that became widely known among the people. These people, however, entered Islam without committing themselves to its laws.

---

## Page 14097

Fighting people of this kind is obligatory by the consensus of the Muslims. No one who knows the religion of Islam and understands their true circumstances doubts this, for the peace they maintain and the religion of Islam can never coexist. If those Kurds, Bedouin Arabs, and other desert dwellers who do not abide by Islamic law must be fought even when their harm does not extend to the townspeople, then how much more so these people. Nevertheless, fighting them must follow the course prescribed by Islamic law: they must be called upon to abide by the laws of Islam if that call has not already reached them, just as a belligerent disbeliever is first called to affirm the two testimonies of faith if the call has not already reached him.

If there are those who fight them in the fully proper manner, that is the highest attainment in gaining Allah’s pleasure, exalting His word, establishing His religion, and obeying His Messenger. But if some of those fighting them are immoral and have corrupt intentions—fighting for leadership, for example, or transgressing against them in certain matters—and the harm to religion from refraining from fighting them is greater than the harm of fighting them in this manner, then fighting them remains obligatory, to avert the greater of two harms by accepting the lesser. This is one of the fundamental principles of Islam that must be observed.

For this reason, one of the principles of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah is to undertake military campaigns under every ruler, whether righteous or immoral. For Allah supports this religion through an immoral man and through people who have no share in the Hereafter, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, foretold. For if military campaigns are possible only under immoral rulers or with an army rife with immorality, then there is no alternative but one of

---

## Page 14098

two courses:
either to refrain from campaigning with them, thereby allowing others who pose a greater threat to religious and worldly life to gain the upper hand; or to campaign under the immoral ruler, thereby repelling those who are even more immoral and upholding most of the laws of Islam, even if it is impossible to uphold them all. This is what is obligatory in this situation and all comparable situations. Indeed, many military campaigns after the Rightly Guided Caliphs took place only in this manner.

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Goodness is bound to the forelocks of horses until the Day of Resurrection: reward and spoils of war.”

This authentic hadith supports the meaning of what Abū Dāwūd narrated in his Sunan from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Military campaigns will continue from the time Allah sent me until the last of my community fight the Dajjāl. Neither the injustice of an unjust ruler nor the justice of a just ruler will bring them to an end.”

It also supports what has been widely reported from him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“A group of my community will continue to prevail upon the truth, unharmed by those who oppose them, until the Day of Resurrection.”

There are other such texts which Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, across all their groups, have agreed to act upon by waging jihad against those against whom it is warranted, under rulers both righteous and immoral. This is contrary to the Rāfidah and the Khawārij, who have departed from the Sunnah and the community.

This is despite his foretelling, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Unjust, treacherous, immoral rulers will come to power. Whoever believes their lies and assists them is not of me, nor am I of him

---

## Page 14099

nor will he come to me at the Cistern. Whoever does not believe their lies or assist them in their injustice is of me, and I am of him, and he will come to me at the Cistern.”

When a person fully understands both the jihad commanded by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which rulers will conduct until the Day of Resurrection, and his prohibition against assisting oppressors in their injustice, he will recognize the middle course that constitutes the religion of pure Islam: to wage jihad against those against whom it is warranted, such as the people asked about here, alongside any ruler and any group closer to Islam than they are, if fighting them is possible only in this way, while avoiding assistance to the group alongside whom he campaigns in any act of disobedience to Allah. Rather, he obeys them in obedience to Allah but does not obey them in disobedience to Allah, for no created being may be obeyed in disobedience to the Creator.

This is the way of the best members of this community, past and present, and it is obligatory upon every legally accountable person. It is the middle course between the way of the Harūriyyah and those like them, who follow a path of misguided scrupulousness arising from insufficient knowledge, and the way of the Murji’ah and those like them, who follow a path of unconditional obedience to rulers, even when they are not righteous.

We ask Allah to guide us and our fellow Muslims to the words and deeds that He loves and is pleased with. Allah knows best. May Allah bless our Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions, and grant them peace.

---

## Page 14100

What do the esteemed jurists, the imams of religion—may Allah be pleased with them all and help them clarify the manifest truth and dispel the confusion engulfing the ignorant and those who stray—say concerning these Tatars who repeatedly advance into Syria, who have uttered the two testimonies of faith and professed Islam, and who have not remained in their original state of unbelief? Is fighting them obligatory or not? What is the evidence for fighting them, and what are the scholarly positions on this matter?

What is the ruling concerning those who join them by deserting the Muslim army, whether commanders or others? What is the ruling concerning those whom they have forcibly brought out with them? What is the ruling concerning those accompanying their army who identify with religious learning, jurisprudence, spiritual poverty, Sufism, and the like?

What should be said about someone who claims that they are Muslims, that those fighting them are also Muslims, and that both sides are unjust, so one should fight alongside neither? And what of the assertion that they should be fought in the same manner as rebels acting on an interpretation of religion?

What duties concerning them fall upon the Muslim community: its people of learning and religion, its fighting men, and its people of wealth? Give us detailed, satisfactory legal answers on these matters, for their case has become unclear to many Muslims—indeed, to most of them—sometimes because they lack knowledge of their circumstances, and sometimes because they lack knowledge of Allah’s ruling

---

## Page 14101

—exalted is He—and that of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning people such as these. Allah facilitates all good through His power and mercy. He has power over all things; He is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. Yes, fighting these people is obligatory according to the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, and the agreement of the imams of the Muslims.

This rests upon two foundations: first, knowledge of their circumstances; and second, knowledge of Allah’s ruling concerning people such as these. As for the first, everyone who has dealt with these people directly knows their circumstances. Those who have not dealt with them directly know this through the mass-transmitted reports and the accounts of truthful people that have reached them.

We shall describe the main aspects of their conduct after explaining the other foundation, knowledge of which belongs specifically to scholars of Islamic law. We therefore say:

Any group that departs from any of Islam’s manifest ordinances established through mass transmission must be fought, by agreement of the imams of the Muslims, even if it pronounces the two testimonies of faith. Thus, if they affirm the two testimonies but refuse to perform the five daily prayers, they must be fought until they pray. If they refuse to pay zakat, they must be fought until they pay it. The same applies if they refuse to fast the month of Ramadan or perform pilgrimage to the Ancient House.

The same applies if they refuse to abide by the prohibition of indecencies, unlawful sexual intercourse, gambling, intoxicants, or other things forbidden by Islamic law. Likewise, if they refuse to adjudicate matters involving bloodshed, property, honour, sexual relations, and the like according to the rulings of the Quran and Sunnah. Likewise,

---

## Page 14102

if they refuse to enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and wage jihad against the unbelievers until they embrace Islam and pay the jizya in submission, humbled. The same applies if they openly propagate religious innovations contrary to the Book, the Sunnah, and adherence to the early generations of the Muslim community and its imams. Examples include deviating concerning Allah’s names and signs; denying His names and attributes; denying His predestination and decree; rejecting what the Muslim community adhered to during the time of the rightly guided caliphs; disparaging the earliest and foremost of the Emigrants and Helpers and those who followed them in righteousness; or fighting Muslims until they submit to them in an obedience that entails departing from Islamic law; and similar matters.

Allah Most High says:

“Fight them until there is no more religious strife and religion is entirely for Allah.”

Thus, if part of religion is for Allah and part is for others, fighting becomes obligatory until religion is entirely for Allah.

He Most High also says:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of usury, if you are believers.”

“If you do not, then be informed of war from Allah and His Messenger.”

This verse was revealed concerning the people of Tā’if. They had embraced Islam, prayed, and fasted, but they continued to engage in usurious transactions. Allah therefore revealed this verse, commanding the believers to give up what remained of usury.

He said:

“If you do not, then be informed of war from Allah and His Messenger.”

The word has been read as both fa’dhanū (“be informed”) and ādhinū (“give notice”), and both meanings are valid. And usury

---

## Page 14103

was the last thing to be prohibited in the Quran, and it is money taken with the mutual consent of the parties to a transaction. If someone who does not desist from it is at war with Allah and His Messenger, what, then, of someone who does not desist from other forbidden matters whose prohibition came earlier and is more severe? Hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning fighting the Khawārij have been widely transmitted; hadith scholars regard them as mass-transmitted.

Imam Ahmad said, “The hadith concerning the Khawārij has been authentically transmitted through ten routes.” Muslim recorded them in his Sahīh, while al-Bukhārī recorded three of them: the reports of ‘Alī, Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, and Sahl ibn Hunayf. The Sunan and Musnad collections contain numerous additional routes of transmission. Describing them, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Any one of you would consider his prayer insignificant beside theirs, his fasting beside theirs, and his recitation beside theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not pass beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection. If I were to live to encounter them, I would surely kill them as ‘Ād were killed.”

The Commander of the Faithful, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, fought them together with the Companions who were with him. The early generations of the Muslim community and its imams agreed that they should be fought. They did not dispute fighting them as they disputed fighting at the Battle of the Camel and at Siffīn.

During the fighting of the civil strife, the Companions fell into three groups: those who fought alongside ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him; those who fought alongside his opponents; and those who abstained from fighting and fought neither side. As for the Khawārij,

---

## Page 14104

none of the Companions were among them, nor did any Companion forbid fighting them. In the Sahīh, Abū Sa‘īd reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A faction will break away at a time of division among the Muslims, and the party with the stronger claim to the truth will kill them.”

Another wording reads: “the closer of the two parties to the truth.”

This authentic hadith establishes that ‘Alī and his companions were closer to the truth than Mu‘āwiya and his companions. It also establishes that the ruling concerning that faction which passed out of Islam differs from the ruling concerning either of the two parties. Indeed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded that this breakaway faction be fought and emphatically reiterated that command. He did not command fighting either of the two parties as he commanded fighting this faction.

Rather, it is authentically reported from him in the Sahīh, in the hadith of Abū Bakra, that he said of al-Hasan:

“This son of mine is a leader, and through him Allah will reconcile two great parties of Muslims.”

He thus praised and commended al-Hasan for the reconciliation Allah brought about through him between the two parties when he abandoned fighting, although allegiance had already been pledged to him. He chose the better course and spared bloodshed, relinquishing authority in the process. Had fighting been commanded, the Prophet would not have praised and commended al-Hasan for abandoning what Allah had commanded and doing what Allah had forbidden.

Scholars take two approaches to fighting those among the people of the qiblah who warrant being fought:

Some regard all the fighting at Harūrā’, the Battle of the Camel, and Siffīn as falling under the category of fighting rebels. They likewise classify Abū Bakr’s fighting against those who withheld zakat, as well as fighting all the others who were fought among those professing allegiance to the qiblah, as stated by those who discussed this

---

## Page 14105

among the followers of Abū Hanīfa and al-Shāfi‘ī, and those followers of Ahmad and others who agreed with them. They all agree that the Companions are not morally corrupt but upright.

They therefore maintain that rebels remain upright despite their fighting, and that their error is like that of scholars exercising independent legal judgment in subsidiary matters. A group, including Ibn ‘Aqīl and others, disagreed and held that rebels are morally corrupt. These scholars considered those whom they counted as rebels in their own time and judged them morally corrupt. Undoubtedly, they do not include the Companions in this judgment. Only some adherents of deviant doctrines among the Mu‘tazila and similar groups declare the Companions morally corrupt, just as some adherents of deviant doctrines among the Khawārij and the Rāfida declare them unbelievers. This is not the position of the imams and jurists of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah.

Nor do they say that their property retains the same inviolability as before. Whatever property remains in its original form is returned to its owner, while no compensation is due for what was destroyed during the fighting. Indeed, the majority of scholars hold that neither side is liable for compensation. As al-Zuhrī said: “Civil strife broke out while the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, were still numerous. They unanimously agreed that no compensation was due for any loss of property or bloodshed occasioned by an interpretation of the Quran.”

Is it permissible to use their weapons in fighting them when there is no necessity to do so? There are two views within Ahmad’s school. One permits it; prohibition is al-Shāfi‘ī’s position, while permission is Abū Hanīfa’s position.

They disagreed over killing their captives, pursuing their retreating fighters, and finishing off their wounded

---

## Page 14106

if they have a force to which they can retreat.

Abū Hanīfa permitted this, while al-Shāfi‘ī prohibited it; the latter is also the well-known position within Ahmad’s school. Another view within his school permits pursuing their retreating fighters at the outset of the fighting.

If, however, they have no such force, their captives are not to be killed, nor their wounded finished off. Sa‘īd and others narrated that Marwān ibn al-Hakam said: “On the day of the Battle of the Camel, a herald went out on ‘Alī’s behalf, proclaiming: ‘No retreating fighter is to be killed, nor any wounded man finished off. Whoever closes his door is safe, and whoever lays down his weapons is safe.’”

Someone following this approach might mistakenly suppose that these Tatars are rebels acting on an interpretive judgment and should be subject to these same rulings, just as some have included those who withheld zakat and the Khawārij under this ruling. We shall explain the error of this supposition, if Allah Most High wills.

The second approach is that fighting those who withhold zakat, the Khawārij, and others like them is not the same as fighting the participants in the Battles of the Camel and Siffīn. This is the position explicitly transmitted from the majority of the early imams, and it is what they mention when setting out the creed of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah. It is the position of the scholars of Medina, such as Mālik and others, and of the imams of hadith, such as Ahmad and others. They explicitly distinguished between the two in several places, even regarding property. Some of them permitted taking the property of the Khawārij as spoils. In the report transmitted by Abū Tālib, Ahmad gave an explicit ruling concerning some Harūriyya who held a share in a village and then went out

---

## Page 14107

to fight the Muslims and were killed by the Muslims. Their land then becomes booty for the Muslims: one fifth is divided into five shares, while the remaining four fifths belong to those who fought and are divided among them. Alternatively, the ruler may levy land tax on the Muslims and leave the land undivided, just as ‘Umar conquered the Sawād by force and made it an endowment for the Muslims. Thus, Ahmad treated land captured from the Khawārij in the same way as property captured from the disbelievers.

In short, this approach is unquestionably correct. Both the scriptural evidence and scholarly consensus distinguish between these two cases, as does the conduct of ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him. He fought the Khawārij on the explicit instruction of the Messenger of Allah, rejoiced in doing so, and was opposed in this by none of the Companions. As for the fighting at Siffīn, his aversion to it and his condemnation of it were manifest.

Concerning those who fought at the Battle of the Camel and others, he said: “They are our brothers who rebelled against us; the sword has purified them.” He offered funeral prayers for the slain of both sides.

As for the Khawārij, the two Sahīh collections report that ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib said: “I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

‘Near the end of time, a people will emerge, young in years and foolish in judgment, who utter some of the finest words spoken by mankind. Their faith will not go beyond their throats. They will pass out of the religion as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will be rewarded on the Day of Resurrection.’”

Sahīh Muslim also reports from Zayd ibn Wahb that he was in the army that

---

## Page 14108

accompanied ‘Alī on the march against the Khawārij. ‘Alī said:

“O people, I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

‘A people will emerge from my nation who recite the Quran. Your recitation will be nothing compared with theirs, your prayer nothing compared with theirs, and your fasting nothing compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, thinking that it supports them, whereas it stands against them. Their prayer does not go beyond their collarbones. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. If the army that encounters them knew what had been decreed for them through the words of Muhammad, their Prophet, they would cease striving. Their distinguishing sign is that among them is a man with an upper arm but no forearm. On his upper arm is something like a nipple, bearing a few white hairs.’”

He said: “Are they, then, to march against Mu‘āwiyah and the people of Syria, leaving these men behind among your children and possessions? By Allah, I certainly hope that these are the people described, for they have shed blood forbidden to them and raided people’s grazing livestock. So march in the name of Allah.”

He said: “When we met in battle, the Khawārij were led that day by ‘Abd Allah ibn Wahb. He said to them: ‘Cast down your spears and draw your swords from your belts. I adjure you as they adjured you on the day of Harūrā’.’ They turned back, threw away their spears, and drew their swords, while our men thrust at them with their spears.”

He said: “They closed in on one another, and only two of our men were killed that day.”

‘Alī said: “Search among them for the man with the malformed arm.” They searched but did not find him. He rose, leaning on his sword, and came to some men pressed against one another.

He said: “Move them aside.” They found him underneath, next to the ground. ‘Alī proclaimed Allah’s greatness and then said: “Allah has spoken the truth, and His Messenger has delivered the message.”

He said: “‘Ubaydah al-Salmānī rose and approached him, saying: ‘O Commander of the Faithful, by Allah, besides whom there is no god but

---

## Page 14109

Him, did you hear this hadith from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?’

He replied: ‘Yes, by Allah, besides whom there is no god but Him.’ He made him swear three times, and each time he swore to him.”

The Muslim community is agreed on condemning the Khawārij and judging them misguided. Their disagreement concerns only whether they are disbelievers. There are two well-known positions on this in the schools of Mālik and Ahmad, and there is also disagreement within al-Shāfi‘ī’s school regarding their disbelief.

Thus, under the first approach, there are two opinions concerning them in Ahmad’s school and elsewhere. The first is that they are rebels. The second is that they are disbelievers, like apostates: it is permissible to initiate fighting against them, kill their captives, and pursue those who flee. Anyone among them who is apprehended is called upon to repent, like an apostate; if he repents, he is spared, otherwise he is killed.

Likewise, two positions are transmitted from Ahmad concerning those who withhold zakat and fight the ruler over it: do they become disbelievers despite acknowledging that it is obligatory?

All of this demonstrates that al-Siddīq’s fighting against those who withheld zakat and ‘Alī’s fighting against the Khawārij were not like the fighting at the Battles of the Camel and Siffīn. The statements of ‘Alī and others concerning the Khawārij imply that they are not disbelievers like those who apostatize from Islam itself. This is the position explicitly transmitted from the imams, such as Ahmad and others. Nevertheless, the rulings concerning them are not the same as those concerning the participants in the Battles of the Camel and Siffīn. Rather, they constitute a third category. This is the soundest of the three positions concerning them.

---

## Page 14110

Among those whom the Companions fought—despite their acknowledgment of the two testimonies of faith, prayer, and other matters—were those who withheld zakat. As reported in the two Sahīh collections:

“Abu Hurayrah reported that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said to Abū Bakr: ‘O successor to the Messenger of Allah, how can you fight the people when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah. Once they say this, their lives and property are protected from me, except as its rightful requirements demand”?’

“Abū Bakr replied: ‘Did he not tell you, “except as its rightful requirements demand”? Zakat is one of its rightful requirements. By Allah, if they withheld from me even a young female goat that they used to give to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I would fight them for withholding it.’

“‘Umar said: ‘As soon as I saw that Allah had opened Abū Bakr’s heart to fighting, I knew that this was right.’”

The Companions and the imams after them agreed that those who withhold zakat are to be fought, even if they perform the five daily prayers and fast the month of Ramadan. These people had no plausible grounds for doubt, and were therefore apostates. They are to be fought for withholding it, even if they acknowledge its obligation, as Allah has commanded.

It is reported that they said: ‘Allah commanded His Prophet to collect zakat in His words, “Take charity from their wealth,” but this obligation lapsed with his death.’ Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded that those who would not desist from drinking wine be fought.

As for the other principle—ascertaining their circumstances—it is known that these

---

## Page 14111

people first passed through Syria in the year ninety-nine. They granted the people a guarantee of safety and had it read from the pulpit in Damascus. Despite this, they took captive what is said to have been a hundred thousand or more Muslim children. In Jerusalem, the hill of al-Sālihiyyah, Nablus, Homs, Dārayyā, and elsewhere, they perpetrated killing and captivity on a scale known only to Allah. Indeed, it is said that they took nearly a hundred thousand Muslims captive. They proceeded to violate the most virtuous Muslim women in mosques and elsewhere, including al-Aqsā Mosque, the Umayyad Mosque, and others. They razed the congregational mosque in al-Uqaybah to the ground.

We ourselves observed their army and saw that most of them did not pray. We saw neither a caller to prayer nor an imam in their army. They seized the Muslims’ wealth and children and destroyed their homes on a scale known only to Allah.

Those associated with their rule were none but the worst of creation: either a heretical hypocrite who did not inwardly believe in Islam; one of the worst adherents of religious innovation, such as the Rāfidah, Jahmiyyah, Ittihādiyyah, and their like; or one of the most wicked and openly sinful people.

In their own lands, despite having the means, they do not perform pilgrimage to the Ancient House. Although some among them pray and fast, establishing prayer and paying zakat are not their prevailing practice. They fight for the dominion of Genghis Khan. Whoever submits to their authority, they regard as

---

## Page 14112

an ally, even if he is an unbeliever; whoever rejects their authority, they regard as an enemy, even if he is among the finest Muslims. They do not fight for Islam, nor do they impose jizyah and subjection. Indeed, many of the Muslims among them, including their highest-ranking emirs and ministers, aspire to no more than for a Muslim to enjoy the same standing among them as the polytheists among the Jews and Christians whom they revere. Thus, their foremost commander among those who came to Syria, while addressing the Muslim envoys and seeking their goodwill by declaring, “We are Muslims,” said: “These are two great signs that came from Allah: Muhammad and Genghis Khan.”

This, then, is the furthest their foremost commander goes in seeking the Muslims’ goodwill: equating the Messenger of Allah—the noblest of creation in His sight, the master of the children of Adam, and the Seal of the Messengers—with an unbelieving, polytheistic king, among the worst polytheists in unbelief, corruption, and aggression, of the same kind as Nebuchadnezzar and his like.

These Tatars held an exalted belief concerning Genghis Khan: they believed him to be the son of Allah, much as the Christians believe concerning the Messiah. They say that the sun impregnated his mother: she was in a tent, and the sun descended through an opening in the tent and entered her, causing her to conceive. Everyone who professes a religion knows that this is a lie. This is evidence that he was born of fornication, and that his mother committed fornication, concealed it, and made this claim to ward off its disgrace.

Despite this, they regard him as the greatest messenger in Allah’s sight, venerating what he instituted and prescribed for them according to his own conjecture and desire, to the point that

---

## Page 14113

they say of the wealth they possess, “This is provision from Genghis Khan,” and thank him for their food and drink. They consider it lawful to kill anyone who opposes what this accursed unbeliever instituted for them—this enemy of Allah, His prophets, His Messenger, and His believing servants.

Thus, this man and others like him among their commanders, even after embracing Islam, aspired to no more than placing Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on the same level as this accursed man. It is well known that Musaylimah the Liar caused the Muslims less harm than this man did, yet he claimed to share Muhammad’s messengership. On that account, the Companions deemed it lawful to fight him and his apostate followers. What, then, of someone who, in his outward profession of Islam, places Muhammad on a par with Genghis Khan?

In reality, despite their outward profession of Islam, they exalt the cause of Genghis Khan above that of the Muslims who follow the law of the Quran. They do not fight those who follow what Genghis Khan instituted as they fight the Muslims; rather, they fight the Muslims still more fiercely. Those unbelievers offer him obedience and submission, bring him wealth, and acknowledge his authority as deputy. They disobey his commands only as someone who rebels against a ruler disobeys that ruler.

Yet they wage war against the Muslims and show them the utmost enmity. They demand that the Muslims obey them, surrender their wealth, and submit to what that unbelieving, polytheistic king laid down for them—a king resembling Pharaoh, Nimrod, and their like. Indeed, he wrought even greater corruption on earth than either of them.

Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people into factions, oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons

---

## Page 14114

and keeping their women alive. Indeed, he was one of the corrupters.”

This unbeliever likewise exalted himself in the land, oppressing the adherents of all faiths—Muslims, Jews, Christians, and those polytheists who opposed him—by killing the men, taking the women captive, seizing wealth, and destroying crops and offspring. Allah does not love corruption. He turns people away from the ways of the prophets and messengers that they had followed until they embrace the pagan way and unbelieving law he devised.

Thus, they profess Islam while exalting the religion of those unbelievers above the religion of the Muslims. Their obedience and allegiance to them far exceed their obedience to Allah and His Messenger and their allegiance to the believers. Disputes among their leading men are adjudicated according to the judgment of pagan ignorance, not the judgment of Allah and His Messenger.

Likewise, their senior ministers and other leading figures place Islam on a par with Judaism and Christianity, holding that all these are paths to Allah, comparable to the four schools of law among the Muslims. Some prefer Judaism or Christianity, while others prefer Islam. This view is widespread and predominant among them, even among their jurists and worshippers, particularly the Jahmiyyah among the Pharaonic monists and others like them, for philosophy has come to dominate their thinking. This is the doctrine of many, or most, of those who engage in philosophy, and it is also held by

---

## Page 14115

many, or most, Christians, and many Jews as well. Indeed, it would not be far-fetched to say that most of their leading scholars and worshippers subscribe to this doctrine. I have personally seen and heard more of this than there is room to recount here.

It is a self-evident teaching of the Muslims’ religion, unanimously agreed upon by all Muslims, that whoever considers it permissible to follow a religion other than Islam, or a law other than the law of Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is an unbeliever. His disbelief is like that of someone who believes in part of the Scripture and disbelieves in another part, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, saying, ‘We believe in some and disbelieve in others,’ and wish to take a way in between—”

“Those are truly the disbelievers, and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.”

The Jews and Christians are included in this, as are those who engage in philosophy: they believe in some and disbelieve in others. Those Jews and Christians who embrace philosophy are thus unbelievers on two counts.

Most of their ministers belong to this category. The man whose counsel they follow is, at best, of this sort: he was a Jew who engaged in philosophy, then professed affiliation with Islam while retaining his Judaism and philosophy, and added Rāfidī Shiism to these. This, then, is their greatest man of the pen, while that other man was their greatest man of the sword. Let the believer take heed of this.

In short, there is no form of hypocrisy, heresy, or religious deviation that is not encompassed by following the Tatars;

---

## Page 14116

for they are among the most ignorant of all people, the least knowledgeable about religion, the furthest from following it, and the most given to following conjecture and their own desires.

They divide people into four categories: yāl, bā‘, dāshmand, and tāt—that is, their friend, their enemy, the scholar, and the common person. Whoever submits to their rule of ignorance and their unbelieving practices is their friend. Whoever opposes them is their enemy, even if he is one of Allah’s prophets, messengers, or close servants. They call everyone associated with learning or religion a “dāshmand”: the jurist, ascetic, priest, monk, Jewish dannān, astrologer, sorcerer, physician, scribe, and accountant. They even include the custodian of idols. Thus, they include in this category untold numbers of polytheists, People of the Book, and followers of religious innovations, and treat the people of knowledge and faith as just one category.

Indeed, they make the Qarmatians—godless esotericists, heretics, and hypocrites such as al-Tūsī and his like—the rulers over everyone associated with learning or religion among the Muslims, Jews, and Christians. Likewise, their foolish minister, given the title al-Rashīd, exercises authority over these groups and gives precedence to the worst of the Muslims, such as the Rāfidīs and the godless, over the best of the Muslims—the people of knowledge and faith. This went so far that the office of chief judge came to be held by someone closer to heresy, religious deviation, and disbelief in Allah and His Messenger, whose willingness to accommodate the wishes of the unbelievers and hypocrites among the Jews, Qarmatians, godless, and Rāfidīs was greater than that of others.

## Page 14117

and he outwardly observes only as much of Islamic law as he must because of the Muslims there. This vile, ignorant man cited His words as evidence:

contain nothing implying that the religion of the disbelievers is true or that the Prophet approves of it. Rather, they indicate his disavowal of their religion. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said of this surah:

Likewise, He says in another verse:

“If they reject you, then say, ‘To me are my deeds, and to you are yours. You are free of responsibility for what I do, and I am free of responsibility for what you do.’”

Thus, His words,

“For you is your religion, and for me is my religion,”

are like His words,

“To us are our deeds, and to you are yours.”

He followed this with its necessary implication and consequence, saying:

“You are free of responsibility for what I do, and I am free of responsibility for what you do.”

Even if it were supposed that this surah contained something implying that they were not commanded to abandon their religion, it is necessarily known from the religion of

and taking their women captive.

Adherents of heresy and godlessness also joined the Rāfidah, including the “Nusayriyyah,” the “Ismāʿīliyyah,” and others like them among the godless “Qarāmitah” and others in Khurāsān, Iraq, Syria, and elsewhere. upper arms is like a woman’s breast or a piece of flesh. They will emerge at a time of division among the people.’”

Abū Sa‘īd said: “I testify that I heard this hadith from Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and I testify that Alī ibn Abī Tālib fought them while I was with him. Among the gravest grounds on which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, condemned these Khārijites, who pass out of the religion, was that they kill the people of Islam and leave the idolaters alone.
