## Page 14150

move about because of old age or weakness. Among them are children who have not yet reached puberty, widows, and people with disabilities. Others are engaged in sacred learning and reciting the Quran, or provide a general benefit to the Muslims and have a share in the public treasury.

Among them are also those in charge of lodges and hospices, who devote themselves exclusively to worship and receiving visitors: jurists, scholars, and other wayfarers. Others are the orphaned children of soldiers and others martyred in the path of Allah Most High, who have not left them enough to meet their needs. There are also those who request permission to bring uncultivated land into use and do so, or reclaim high-lying ahrās so that they may retain them after their reclamation. They have brought them into cultivation over many years, and their tenure has become established according to the prevailing customs in such matters.

Do these circumstances justify their receiving what they have been granted—what the Muslim kings and their deputies allocated to them in the public interest, and which has remained in their possession until now—or not? What is the ruling concerning someone who declares them ineligible despite their possessing these qualifications, and seeks favour with the sultan by striving to cut off their stipends, thereby causing the closure of the lodges and most of the lodges and hospices that benefit wayfarers and others devoted exclusively to worship, and in which the public observances of Islam are maintained? Is he thereby sinful and disobedient, or not?

Must these people be required to prove their entitlement, even though these allocations have remained in their possession by authorization of those in authority?

If they were required to do so, would they have to establish it before one particular judge

---

## Page 14151

who is a stranger from their region and openly hostile to them, despite the presence of several other judges in their region, or not?

What is the ruling concerning those among them who cannot establish their entitlement because they lack the means to produce legally admissible testimony, given the prevailing practice whereby witnesses nowadays will testify only for a fee satisfactory to them, which a poor person may be unable to afford? The same applies to women, whose circumstances are generally unknown to the witnesses.

If the ruler asks a judge about the entitlement of those mentioned, and he replies, “Of these people and others in similar circumstances, only the blind, those with disabling impairments of their limbs, and the chronically incapacitated are entitled—no one else. Disregard everyone else,” without knowing their actual circumstances, is he thereby sinful and disobedient, or not? What must he do in this matter?

If the ruler asks him whether those in the lodges and hospices are entitled to their allocated stipends, and he replies that these lodges and hospices are “shops”—although their residents undoubtedly include righteous people, scholars, bearers of the Noble Book, and those devoted exclusively to Allah Most High—does he thereby cause them harm, or not?

What is the ruling on this sweeping statement about them, made without knowing them all or having any comprehensive knowledge of their actual circumstances, if it proves to be unfounded and false? Would his narrations and other reports thereby cease to be accepted, or not?

May those he has slandered bring a claim against him over this attack upon them, which leads kings to cut off their stipends, and require him to substantiate it? If he cannot substantiate it, may they then demand of him

---

## Page 14152

that he bear the legal consequences, or not?

If he is unable to establish this, does that impugn his probity and discredit him, such that he is removed from religious offices, or not?

May someone who behaves in this manner toward this group lead them in prayer when they detest him so intensely, given the reported saying:

“Let no man lead people in prayer when most of them dislike him”?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

These questions require the establishment of a comprehensive principle governing the funds of the public treasury, founded upon the Book and the Sunnah laid down by the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and his rightly guided caliphs. As ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and the rulers after him established practices. Adhering to them affirms the Book of Allah, puts obedience to Allah into practice, and strengthens one in obeying Him. No one has the right to change them or to entertain the views of those who oppose them. Whoever follows their guidance is rightly guided; whoever seeks victory through them is granted victory. Whoever opposes them and follows a path other than that of the believers, Allah will leave him to what he has chosen and cast him into Hell—what an evil destination!”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also said:

“I enjoin you to listen and obey, for whoever among you lives after me will see much disagreement. Adhere, then, to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me. Hold fast to it and bite firmly onto it with your molar teeth. Beware of newly introduced matters, for every religious innovation is misguidance.”

The rulers and other Muslims are obliged in these matters to act

---

## Page 14153

in accordance with what is required of them, as Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you are able; and when I forbid you something, avoid it.”

We shall explain this briefly as follows:

The funds whose basis is established in the Book of Allah and whose distribution is entrusted to the rulers fall into three categories. The first is war booty. This belongs to those who participated in the battle, except for one-fifth, which is allocated as Allah states:

“Know that whatever you take as spoils, one-fifth of it is for Allah, the Messenger, close relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveller, if you believe in Allah.”

War booty is what is taken from the unbelievers through fighting. Such are the provisions concerning war booty and its fifth.

The second category is fay’ (property acquired without fighting). This is what Allah Most High mentions in Sūrat al-Hashr, where He says:

“As for what Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you spurred neither horses nor riding camels to obtain it.”

His words, “you spurred neither,” mean that you neither set them in motion, nor put them to work, nor drove them onward. Of a camel moving at a particular gait, one says wajafa, with the present tense yajifu and the verbal noun wujūf; awjaftuhu means “I urged it onward.”

This, then, is the fay’ that Allah restored to His Messenger: whatever came into Muslim possession without spurring horses or riding camels. This expression refers to

---

## Page 14154

fighting—that is, you did not fight to obtain it. Whatever they fought to obtain belonged to the fighters, while whatever they obtained without fighting is fay’, because Allah restored it to the Muslims. He created His creatures to worship Him and made wholesome things lawful for them, so that they might eat wholesome food and do righteous deeds. The unbelievers worshipped others besides Him and thus became undeserving of that wealth. He therefore permitted the believers to worship Him, to enslave the unbelievers themselves, and to reclaim their wealth. When Allah restores that wealth from them to the believers, it has returned—that is, it has reverted to those entitled to it.

This fay’ includes the poll tax collected from non-Muslims under Muslim protection, the levies of one-tenth and one-twentieth collected from them, and the wealth stipulated in peace agreements with the unbelievers, such as the payments they remit, and other such revenues. It also includes whatever they vacate and abandon out of fear of the Muslims, such as the property of Banū al-Nadīr, concerning which Allah revealed Sūrat al-Hashr, saying:

“It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first gathering. You did not think they would leave, and they thought their fortresses would protect them from Allah. But Allah came upon them from where they had not expected and cast terror into their hearts. They destroyed their homes with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take heed, O people of insight.”

“Had Allah not decreed exile for them, He would have punished them in this world; and in the Hereafter they will have the punishment of the Fire.”

These were the people whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, expelled. They had lived east of the Prophet’s city, Medina. He expelled them after besieging them, and their property was among what Allah restored to His Messenger.

---

## Page 14155

and He explained how fay’ was to be allocated, saying:

“Whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah, the Messenger, his close relatives, orphans, the needy, and the stranded traveller, so that it does not circulate solely among the wealthy among you. Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.”

“For the poor emigrants who were driven from their homes and their wealth, seeking Allah’s bounty and pleasure and supporting Allah and His Messenger. It is they who are truly sincere.”

“And those who had already settled in the city and embraced the faith before them love those who emigrated to them, harbour no envy in their hearts for what the emigrants were given, and give them preference over themselves, even though they themselves are in need. Whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul—it is they who will be successful.”

“And those who came after them say, ‘Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not place in our hearts any rancour towards those who believe. Our Lord, You are indeed Most Kind, Most Merciful.’”

These are the Emigrants, the Helpers, and those who come after them until the Day of Resurrection. For this reason, Mālik, Abū ‘Ubayd, Abū Hakīm al-Nahrawānī—one of Ahmad’s followers—and others said that anyone who reviles the Companions has no share in fay’.

Fay’ also includes the levy that ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, imposed on lands he conquered by force but did not distribute, such as the lands of Egypt and Iraq—except for a small portion—the Syrian mainland, and elsewhere.

According to the vast majority of imams, such as Abū Hanīfa, Mālik, and Ahmad, no fifth is to be set aside from this fay’. Setting aside a fifth of it is advocated only by al-Shāfi‘ī and some

---

## Page 14156

of Ahmad’s followers, who also transmitted this as a position reported from him. Ibn al-Mundhir said: “No one before al-Shāfi‘ī is known to have held that a fifth must be set aside from fay’ as it is from war booty.”

According to most scholars, this fay’ was not the personal property of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, during his lifetime. Al-Shāfi‘ī and some of Ahmad’s followers, however, held that it was his property.

As for its allocation after his death, the scholars agreed that it should fund the stipends of soldiers who fight the unbelievers, since strengthening them subdues the unbelievers, from whom fay’ is then obtained. They disagreed over whether it may also be spent on other Muslim public interests or is reserved exclusively for the fighting men. There are two positions reported from al-Shāfi‘ī and two views within Imam Ahmad’s school. The well-known position in Ahmad’s school, which is also the position of Abū Hanīfa and Mālik, is that it is not reserved exclusively for the fighting men, but may be spent on all public interests.

Under either position, anyone whose service benefits those entitled to fay’ collectively is to receive from it. Al-Shāfi‘ī said: “The imam should single out the fighting men in the towns—that is, those who have reached puberty—and enumerate the children, meaning those below that age, and the women.” Later he said: “Then, each year, he should give the fighting men their stipends and give the children and women enough to meet their needs for that year.”

He said: “A stipend from fay’ is only for someone who has reached puberty and is capable of fighting.” He also stated that none of those he had met disputed that slaves have no entitlement to these stipends, nor do the Bedouins who are recipients of zakat.

He said: “If any fay’ remains, the imam should allocate it to those stationed in fortresses, to acquiring more horses and weapons, and to everything that

---

## Page 14157

strengthens the Muslims. If they have no further need of it and all their public interests have been provided for, he should distribute the remainder among them in proportion to their entitlement to that wealth.”

He said: “From fay’, he should pay the stipends of officials, governors, and everyone engaged in its administration—whether a governor, judge, clerk, or soldier—whose services are indispensable to those entitled to fay’.”

This is difficult to reconcile with his statement that no child, insane person, slave, woman, or person too weak to fight is to receive anything from fay’, because it is for the fighting men.

If this revenue is designated for public interests, it should be allocated to everyone whose services benefit the Muslims collectively, such as the fighting men and those who administer their affairs: military commanders, officials responsible for the registers, judges, and those who teach them the Quran, give them fatwas, teach them hadith, lead them in prayer, and call them to prayer.

It should also be spent on securing their frontiers and maintaining their roads and fortresses, and should be given to those among them who are in need. Priority should be given to the most important purposes, then the next most important. Thus, those whose services the Muslims need take precedence over those in need who provide no such benefit. This is explicitly stated by the jurists generally among the followers of Ahmad, al-Shāfi‘ī, Abū Hanīfa, and others.

Abū Hanīfa’s followers stated that he should spend it on public interests that secure the frontiers, including bridges and causeways; provide Muslim judges with enough to meet their needs; and pay the stipends of the fighting men from it. Those in need are to receive from zakat and similar funds. Whatever remains beyond

---

## Page 14158

the needs of the Muslims is to be distributed among them.

However, the view of al-Shāfiʿī and some of Ahmad’s followers is that wealthy people whose services bring no benefit to the Muslims have no entitlement to it when funds remain beyond the Muslims’ needs—as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb (may Allah be pleased with him) did when wealth became abundant and he distributed it among the Muslims generally. All categories of Muslims, rich and poor alike, thus had an allotted stipend in ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb’s register. Those registered, however, belonged to two categories: fighting men, who were adult males; and dependants, who were children and women not eligible for combat.

Nevertheless, the poor must be given priority over wealthy people whose services bring no benefit. No wealthy person is to receive anything until a surplus remains after the poor have been provided for. This is the view of the majority, including Mālik and Ahmad, according to the sounder of the two reports from him. Al-Shāfiʿī’s view, as noted above, is that the surplus is reserved exclusively for the poor.

As for “the third category of wealth,” it consists of the obligatory alms levied as zakat on Muslims’ property: zakat on agricultural produce, namely the tenths and half-tenths collected from grain and fruit; zakat on livestock, namely camels, cattle, sheep and goats; zakat on trade goods; and zakat on gold and silver.

This wealth is to be spent on the recipients Allah Most High mentions in His words:

“Zakat is only for the poor and the needy, those employed to administer it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, freeing those in bondage, those in debt, the cause of Allah, and the stranded traveller—an obligation ordained by Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

The Sunan collections report: “A man asked the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) to give him some of the zakat funds.

---

## Page 14159

He replied: ‘Allah has not left the distribution of zakat to a prophet or anyone else. Rather, He has divided it into eight shares. If you belong to one of those categories, I shall give you.’”

The Muslims agree that zakat may not be distributed outside the eight categories mentioned in this verse, as the Quran indicates. With this principle established, we shall state another:

The funds of the public treasury in times such as these fall into several categories. One consists of fay (wealth acquired without fighting), zakat, or the prescribed fifth. The ruling concerning these has already been explained. Another consists of funds that have rightfully entered the public treasury from other sources, such as the estate of a Muslim who dies without an heir. Some cases within this category are disputed, while others are agreed upon.

Another category consists of funds received without right, or on the basis of an interpretation, which must be returned to those entitled to them whenever possible, but which cannot now be returned. This includes funds confiscated from officials and others who accepted gifts or took wealth belonging to the Muslims to which they had no entitlement. The ruler recovered these funds from them or their estates but did not know who was entitled to them. It also includes proceeds from newly introduced levies that could not be returned to their owners, and similar funds.

According to most scholars, funds that cannot be returned to their rightful owners—for example, because their identities are unknown—are to be spent on the interests of the Muslims. Likewise, if someone holds wealth whose owner he does not know—such as a repentant usurper, a repentant betrayer of trust, a repentant dealer in usury, or anyone else who has come into possession of wealth that he neither owns nor knows the owner of—then he

---

## Page 14160

is to spend it on those in need and on the interests of the Muslims. With these two principles established, we say:

Those in need—such as the poor, the needy, those burdened by debt, and stranded travellers—may, indeed must, be given from zakat and from funds whose owners are unknown, by agreement of the Muslims. According to most scholars, they are also to be given from whatever fay remains after indispensable public needs have been met, as explained earlier. This applies whether or not they are pursuing learning that is a communal obligation, and whether or not they reside in retreats or lodges. However, those distinguished by knowledge or piety are to be given priority over others.

The most deserving within this category are those whom Allah mentions in His words:

“For the poor who are restricted in Allah’s cause and cannot travel about the land. Those unaware of their condition think them wealthy because of their restraint. You will recognize them by their signs: they do not beg from people insistently.”

Thus, anyone whose pursuit of knowledge and religious devotion has restricted him in Allah’s cause and prevented him from earning a living deserves priority over others. Muslim judges and scholars are to be given enough from these funds to meet their needs, and the stipends of fighting men and their offspring are to be paid from them, especially those of Banū Hāshim—the Tālibids, the Abbasids, and others. These must be provided for from the prescribed fifth, fay, and funds for public interests, because zakat is forbidden to them.

The poor person in the legal sense mentioned in the Quran and Sunnah, who is entitled to receive zakat, funds for public interests, and the like, is not the same as the faqīr in the conventional sense, who adheres to a form of dress

---

## Page 14161

of a particular kind and to a particular path. Rather, anyone who lacks enough to provide for himself and his dependants is among the poor and needy.

The scholars have differed over whether the poor person is in greater need than the needy person, whether the reverse is true, or whether the poor person is one who refrains from asking while the needy person asks. These are their three views. They agree that anyone who has no wealth and is unable to earn a living should be given enough to meet his needs, whether he dresses as a faqīr in the conventional sense, as a soldier or fighting man, as a legal witness, or as a merchant, craftsman or farmer. Charity is not reserved for any one of these groups.

Rather, everyone among them whose needs are not fully met is entitled to it: the craftsman whose craft does not provide him with enough; the merchant whose trade does not provide him with enough; the soldier whose allotment does not provide him with enough; the faqīr or Sufi whose stipend from an endowment does not provide him with enough; and the legal witness or jurist whose income does not provide him with enough. The same applies to someone living in a retreat or lodge who cannot meet his own needs. All these people are entitled to assistance.

Whoever among all these people is a pious believer is an ally of Allah. For Allah’s allies are described as follows:

“There will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.”

“Those who believe and are mindful of Allah.”

This applies whatever group they belong to among those who face the qiblah in prayer. Whoever among them is a hypocrite or openly promotes an innovation contrary to the Quran and Sunnah, whether in beliefs or acts of worship, deserves punishment. Part of his punishment is to be denied such assistance until he repents.

---

## Page 14162

As for heretics—such as those who believe in divine indwelling, those who regard all things as permissible, those who consider the leader they follow superior to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and those who believe that inwardly they are not obliged to follow the Law of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; or that once they attain spiritual knowledge and realization, they are no longer bound by commands and prohibitions; or that someone who has attained such knowledge and realization may practise Judaism or Christianity without being obliged to adhere to the Quran and Sunnah—and others like them: these are hypocrites and heretics. If any one of them is exposed, he must be put to death, by agreement of the Muslims. They are numerous in these times.

Alongside providing for the poor—indeed, for the wealthy as well—the authorities must require these people to follow the Quran and Sunnah and obey Allah and His Messenger. They must not allow anyone to depart from this, whatever claims he may make, even if he claims to fly through the air or walk on water.

According to al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, a poor person who is able to earn a living, and is not kept from doing so by work that benefits Muslims generally, may not be given zakat. Abū Hanīfah, however, permitted this. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person or for a strong person able to earn a living.”

Zakat may not be given to someone to use for hosting meals and offering hospitality to the poor, nor may it be used to lay out meals, whether for visitors or anyone else. Rather, it must be given to the poor person in need as his own property, so that, if he wishes, he may spend it on himself and his dependants in his own home, pay off his debts with it, and spend it

---

## Page 14163

to meet his needs. No Muslim objects to distributing charitable funds and surplus funds allocated to public interests among the poor and needy. Anyone reported to hold such an objection must either be among the most ignorant of religious knowledge or among the most disbelieving in the religion—indeed, in all religions and revealed laws—or the report attributed to him must be false or distorted. Anyone with even a moderate degree of knowledge and religious commitment would recognize this and would not prohibit it.

Yet right and wrong have become mixed together in these regular government allocations. Many needy, devout, and learned people are not given enough to support themselves. They are ravaged by hunger, yet do not beg, while those who know them have nothing to give them. Many others consume people’s wealth unjustly and turn others away from Allah’s path. Some receive stipends many times greater than their needs; others receive stipends despite being wealthy and having no need of them. Some secure appointments at mosques and elsewhere and take the stipends attached to them, making exceptions for those to whom they give a paltry sum. Some people in religious lodges and retreats receive funds to which they are entitled, but also take more than their rightful share, while withholding all or part of the share due to others who have a stronger claim than they do. This is found in many places.

No Muslim doubts that striving to distinguish those who are entitled from those who are not, to assign offices and stipends to those most entitled to them, and to treat people justly in this regard

---

## Page 14164

and putting this into practice as far as possible are among the finest deeds of those in authority—indeed, among their most binding duties. Allah commands justice and kindness, and justice is obligatory upon everyone in every matter.

Just as reviewing the circumstances of fighting troops, treating them equitably, increasing the stipends of those who deserve an increase, reducing those of those who deserve a reduction, and providing for those unable to engage in jihad from another source are among the finest and most binding duties of those in authority, so too is reviewing the circumstances of all other recipients of stipends from fay’ (revenues acquired without fighting), charitable funds, funds allocated to public interests, and endowments. They must treat these recipients justly, give each eligible person enough to meet his needs fully, and prevent those who have entered the ranks of eligible recipients without being entitled from competing with them for their stipends.

If someone who is not known to be wealthy claims poverty and requests charitable funds, the ruler may give him some without requiring proof, after informing him that there is no share in them for a wealthy person or a strong person able to earn a living:

“For two men asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for charity. Seeing that they were able-bodied, he looked them up and down and said, ‘If you wish, I will give you, but there is no share in it for a wealthy person or a strong person able to earn a living.’”

But if he states that he has dependants, is proof required? Scholars hold two well-known views on this, both of which are found in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. If the ruler adopts the view that proof is required, there is no disagreement among scholars that the witnesses providing it need not be witnesses whose probity has been formally attested; rather, they must not have received remuneration

---

## Page 14165

for giving testimony. Their testimony is therefore rejected if they receive remuneration for it, especially given the known prevalence of false testimony. Hence, the customary practice in Syria has been that witnesses paid for their testimony do not testify on matters requiring judgment, such as tithes, sound judgment, probity, competence, entitlement, and similar matters. Rather, they testify to matters perceived by the senses, such as what they have heard and seen. Testimony on matters requiring judgment is open to interpretation and suspicion, and payment makes it easier to testify about them without due care. This differs from matters perceived by the senses, where adding anything constitutes an outright lie, something only a person prepared to give blatantly false testimony would venture to do. Such people are fewer than the others. Rather, if one of these people brings witnesses known to be truthful from among his neighbours, acquaintances, and those intimately familiar with his circumstances, their testimony is accepted.

The blanket assertion that all those residing in religious lodges and retreats are ineligible is manifestly false. Likewise, the blanket assertion that everyone in them is entitled to what he receives is also false. Neither assertion is correct. Among them are eligible recipients who receive their due, those who receive more than their due, those who are given less than their due, and those who are not eligible at all. Even in the food they share, one may be given better food than another despite being wealthier than him. This runs contrary to the customary practice of those who act justly, who distribute food equitably, as is done in lodges administered by just people.

For the ruler to command these people to comply with everything mentioned is among the finest acts of worship and the greatest obligations.

---

## Page 14166

As for the statement attributed to some judges—that only the blind, those disabled in their limbs, and the infirm among these people are eligible—no Muslim has ever said such a thing. Nor can one imagine a judge of the sort ordinarily appointed to judicial office saying this, unless he were among the most ignorant or wicked of people. Clearly, this impugns his probity and must be taken as evidence against it. Likewise, if the person attributing this statement to a judge has lied about him, he should receive a punishment that deters him and others like him from fabricating allegations against people.

The ruler need not wait for those concerned to lodge a complaint before punishing someone who fabricates lies against people and speaks about them and their entitlement in a manner contrary to Islam. Rather, punishment in such cases is permissible without anyone lodging a complaint, just as the ruler may punish someone who speaks about religion without knowledge, transmitting reports and issuing fatwas without knowledge. Such people are subject to punishment. All these people may therefore be punished without a complaint being lodged. Indeed, lying about people and speaking unjustifiably about religion and about people are widespread practices among many.

Whoever says that only the blind, the infirm, and those disabled in their limbs are eligible is mistaken by the agreement of the Muslims.

Likewise, whoever says that the various categories of public treasury funds are the entitlement of certain groups, including the poor, and that the ruler must allocate enough from the public treasury to meet their needs, is mistaken. Rather, they are undoubtedly entitled to receive zakat. As for fay revenues and public-interest funds, they are entitled only to what remains after

---

## Page 14167

provision has been made for public interests. Even if they receive insufficient zakat to meet their needs, and the public treasury’s funds are entirely committed to public interests, supporting those among them who cannot earn a living remains a collective obligation. Muslims collectively must feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and leave no one among them in need. The ruler must provide for this from communal funds remaining after indispensable public needs have been met.

As for someone who receives funds for performing a public service, Muslims agree that he may receive them when he is in need. But may he receive them when he is wealthy—for example, a judge, witness, mufti, accountant, Quran teacher, or hadith scholar? May such a person receive a stipend from the public treasury for this work despite being wealthy? Scholars hold two well-known views on this.

Likewise, the claim that the ruler must give greater attention to those in need than to those performing public services indispensable to people’s religious and worldly affairs—such as jihad, governance, and scholarship—is unsound for several reasons.

First, scholars have explicitly stated that those providing a public benefit must be given priority when distributing fay revenues and funds designated for public interests.

As for zakat funds, two categories receive them:

Those who receive them because of their need, such as the poor, the needy, those who have incurred debts for their own needs, and stranded travelers.

And those who receive them because of the benefit they provide, such as zakat collectors and those who incur debts to reconcile disputing parties; likewise, those who provide a public benefit, such as combatants and those who direct their affairs, and in the cause of

---

## Page 14168

Allah. Neither category has a greater entitlement than the other; both are indispensable.

Second:

The corrupt intentions alleged against many who serve public interests through jihad, public office, and scholarship are counterbalanced by the sinfulness and heresy found among many of those in need. Just as some of those in need are righteous friends of Allah, so too are some fighters and scholars. Allah’s friends are the believers who fear Him, whatever category they belong to. Those friends of Allah who engage in jihad and scholarship are superior to those who do not, for the foremost friends of Allah among the Emigrants and the Helpers were such people.

As for the claim:

“Nowadays, many fighters and scholars merely use jihad, fighting, and scholarly pursuits as a worldly livelihood through which they protect their status and wealth. They sin through their fighting and scholarly pursuits, besides committing other sins and evils that there is no room to recount here. A fighter striving to make Allah’s word supreme, or a teacher whose aim is that learning should serve purely to draw near to Allah, is rarely found, if at all. Undoubtedly, sincerity and adherence to the Sunnah are more prevalent among those who do not consume people’s wealth than among those who take money through such activities; indeed, even heresy…”

We counter this with a truer statement: many residents of religious lodges and retreats, and those who make an outward show of poverty before people, merely use this as a worldly livelihood. This is accompanied by unbelief, sinfulness, and evils that there is no room to recount here, such as claims of divine indwelling and union among

---

## Page 14169

worshippers—claims more prevalent among them than among scholars and those engaged in jihad. The same applies to seeking nearness to Allah through innovated acts of worship. It is well known that every group includes both the righteous and the wicked, the utterly truthful and the heretical. It is obligatory to maintain allegiance to Allah’s God-fearing friends from every group and to hate the unbelievers and hypocrites from every group. A sinful Muslim is accorded allegiance in proportion to his faith and enmity in proportion to his sinfulness. For the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah is that a sinful Muslim is entitled to reward and liable to punishment, unless Allah pardons him. Those sinful people whom Allah wills must enter Hell, although no person of faith will remain there forever. Rather, the hypocrites will remain there forever, just as those who openly profess unbelief will.

Third:

Most soldiers, scholars, and others who receive funds for serving the Muslims’ interests are also in need. Indeed, most have no income apart from their stipend. Someone who receives funds on grounds of both service and need has a stronger claim than someone who receives them solely on grounds of need.

Fourth:

When a grant serves the Muslims’ interests, no consideration is given to whether the recipient’s intention is sound or corrupt. If the ruler were to give to needy people unable to fight, while withholding payment from the fighting men until they set right their intentions toward the Muslims, the unbelievers would overrun the Muslim lands; for making grants conditional

---

## Page 14170

on what is in people’s hearts is impracticable. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah indeed supports this religion through a wicked man and through people who have no share in the Hereafter.”

He also said:

“I give to some men and leave others without giving, although those I leave are dearer to me than those I give to. I give to some men because of the anxiety and distress in their hearts, while leaving others to the contentment and goodness in their hearts.”

He also said:

“I give one of them a gift, and he goes away carrying it under his arm as fire.” They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, why, then, do you give to them?” He replied, “They insist on asking me, and Allah does not allow me to be miserly.”

In the year of Hunayn, he distributed the spoils of Hunayn among those whose hearts were to be won over from the people of Najd and the freed men of Quraysh: ‘Uyaynah ibn Hisn, al-‘Abbās ibn Mirdās, al-Aqra‘ ibn Hābis and others like them; and Suhayl ibn ‘Amr, Safwān ibn Umayyah, ‘Ikrimah ibn Abī Jahl, Abū Sufyān ibn Harb, his son Mu‘āwiyah, and others like them whom he had set free in the year of the conquest. He gave nothing to the Emigrants and the Helpers.

He gave to these men to win their hearts over to Islam, and winning them over served the Muslims’ common interests. Those to whom he gave nothing were better in his estimation: they were foremost among Allah’s God-fearing friends and the best of Allah’s righteous servants after the prophets and messengers. Among those to whom he gave were some who apostatized from Islam before his death, and most of them were wealthy, not poor.

Had giving on grounds of need taken precedence over giving for the common good, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not have given to these wealthy chiefs, whose clans obeyed them, while withholding grants from those with him among

---

## Page 14171

the Emigrants and the Helpers, who were needier and better than they were. On similar grounds, the Khawārij attacked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

The first of them said to him, “O Muhammad, be just, for you have not been just!” He also said, “This is a distribution that was not intended to seek the countenance of Allah Most High.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then said:

“Woe to you! Who would be just if I were not just? You would indeed be lost and ruined if I were not just.”

One of the Companions said to him, “Let me strike this man’s neck.” He replied:

“From this man’s offspring will emerge people whose prayer, fasting and recitation will make any of you consider his own insignificant by comparison. They will recite the Quran, but it will not go beyond their throats. They will pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

Another narration states:

“If I live to encounter them, I will certainly kill them as ‘Ād were killed.”

These people rebelled during the rule of the Commander of the Faithful, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him. He killed all those among them who fought him, despite their abundant fasting, prayer and recitation. They were thus excluded from the Sunnah and the Muslim community. They were people of worship, scrupulousness and asceticism, but without knowledge. This led them to hold that grants should go only to those in need, and that giving to wealthy chiefs who commanded obedience was not proper for any purpose other than Allah’s sake, as they claimed.

This arose from their ignorance, for grants are to be allocated according to what serves Allah’s religion. The more obedient a person is to Allah and the more beneficial he is to Allah’s religion, the more deserving he is of a grant. And a grant

---

## Page 14172

needed to establish the religion, subdue its enemies, make it prevail and raise it high is of greater value than giving to someone who does not serve these purposes, even if the latter is needier.

As for the assertion that these restrictions accord with al-Shāfi‘ī’s school but not Mālik’s, and what has been reported of ‘Umar’s position, assessing this requires knowledge of the imams’ positions on this matter and the caliphs’ practice in distributing grants.

The basis of this issue is that scholars hold three views concerning land conquered by force. The first—which is al-Shāfi‘ī’s position—is that it must be divided among those entitled to the spoils, unless the ruler obtains their willing consent to make it an endowment. Al-Umm states that if a judge rules that it is to be made an endowment without their willing consent, his ruling is to be overturned, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, divided Khaybar among those entitled to the spoils.

However, the majority of the imams disagreed with al-Shāfi‘ī on this. They regarded ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb’s decision to make land conquered by force communal property as sound and permissible, and held that ‘Umar retained it without obtaining the willing consent of those entitled to the spoils. There is no dispute that ‘Umar did not divide any of the lands he conquered by force in Syria, Iraq, Egypt and elsewhere among those entitled to the spoils; he divided only the movable property.

But Mālik and a group of scholars—this being the second view—held that it was reserved exclusively for those who had been at al-Hudaybiyyah. Ismā‘īl ibn Ishāq, the leading Mālikī scholar, wrote a work on this in which he disputed al-Shāfi‘ī’s position on this issue and addressed his arguments. Positions corresponding to both views have been transmitted from Imam Ahmad, but the well-known position in his school is the

---

## Page 14173

third view, held by the majority, including Abū Hanīfah and his followers, al-Thawrī, and Abū ‘Ubayd: the ruler should adopt whichever course best serves the Muslims’ interests, whether dividing the land or retaining it undivided. If he considers it best to divide it, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, divided Khaybar, he may do so. If he considers it best to leave it as fay (communal property) for the Muslims, he may do so, as ‘Umar did. It is also reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did this with half of Khaybar: he divided one half and retained the other to meet contingencies. He also conquered Mecca by force without dividing it among those entitled to the spoils. Thus, land conquered by force may either be divided or left undivided. A substantial work has been written on this subject.

With this understood, Egypt was among the territories conquered by force, and ‘Umar did not divide it among those entitled to the spoils, as the leading scholars of the Hanafī, Mālikī, Hanbalī, and Shāfi‘ī schools explicitly stated. Its circumstances subsequently changed, however, just as those of Iraq changed. The Abbasid caliphs changed Iraq’s taxation from a fixed land-tax assessment to a share of its produce. This is permissible according to one of the two scholarly views. Likewise, the land tax was lifted from Egypt some time ago—I do not know when this began—and ownership of the land became vested in the Muslims. This is permissible according to one of the two scholarly views.

As for ‘Umar’s policy regarding fay, he recognized every Muslim’s right to a share in it, but gave priority to the poor and those who benefited the Muslims. As ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “No one is more entitled to this wealth than anyone else. Rather, account is taken of a man’s proven service, and a man’s contribution,

---

## Page 14174

and a man’s early acceptance of Islam, and a man’s need.” He therefore gave priority in stipends on these grounds, and his practice was to award larger stipends according to religious merit. Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, however, gave equal stipends to those whose needs were equal, even if some were superior to others in religious merit.

He said:
“They embraced Islam for Allah’s sake, and their reward rests with Allah. These worldly goods are merely a means of subsistence.”

It is also reported that he said:
“They are equal in their faith”—meaning that their need for worldly goods is the same—“so I give to them on that basis, not because of their early acceptance of Islam or religious merit, for their reward remains with Allah.” Thus, when their worldly needs were equal, he gave them equal stipends.

It is reported that, towards the end of his life, ‘Umar said:
“If I live until next year, I shall certainly put everyone on an equal footing.”

That is, one māya; in other words, a single category.

His preference in allocating stipends rested on the four grounds he mentioned:

“A man’s proven service”: this refers to someone who strives in fighting the enemy. “A man’s contribution”: this refers to someone who serves the Muslims’ interests—their rulers, teachers, and others like them. “A man’s early acceptance of Islam”: this refers to someone who was among the earliest Muslims, for he awarded them larger stipends than others. “A man’s poverty”: he gave priority to the poor over the wealthy.

This is clear: when there are people in need, how could some of them be denied a share while it is given to a wealthy person who has no need and provides no benefit? This is especially so when the public treasury’s funds are insufficient to provide for all Muslims, rich and poor alike. How, then, can it be permissible to give to a wealthy person who

---

## Page 14175

provides no public benefit, while depriving a poor person in need—even a poor person who benefits others?

It is reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him,
“gave from the property of Banū al-Nadīr to the poor among the Emigrants, to whom it had been allocated. He gave none of it to the Ansār because they were well-off, except that he gave to some of the Ansār because of their poverty.”

The Sunan collections report:
“When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, received funds, he would give a married man two shares and an unmarried man one share.”

He thus gave the married man more than the unmarried man, because he needed to support both himself and his wife. The hadith was narrated by Abū Dāwūd and by Abū Hātim in his Sahīh. Imam Ahmad also narrated it, as transmitted by Abū Tālib, and said, “It is a good hadith.” Its wording, as reported from ‘Awf ibn Mālik, is:
“When the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, received fay’ revenues, he would distribute them that same day, giving a married man two shares and an unmarried man one share.”

The report from ‘Umar was narrated by Ahmad and Abū Dāwūd. In Abū Dāwūd’s wording, Mālik ibn Aws ibn al-Hadathān said:

‘Umar once mentioned fay’ revenues and said:
“I have no greater right to these fay’ revenues than you, nor does any one of us have a greater right to them than another. We are, however, accorded our respective standing in the Book of Allah: a man’s early acceptance of Islam, a man’s proven service, a man’s contribution, and a man’s need.”

In Ahmad’s wording, he said:

‘Umar used to swear three oaths:
“By Allah, no one has a greater right to this wealth than anyone else, and I have no greater right to it than anyone else. By Allah, there is no Muslim who does not have a share in this wealth, except an enslaved person. We are, however, accorded our respective standing in the Book of Allah: a man’s proven service to Islam, and a man’s

---

## Page 14176

early acceptance of Islam, a man’s contribution to Islam, and a man’s need. By Allah, if I live long enough, I will ensure that the shepherd on the mountain of San‘ā’ receives his share of this wealth while tending his flock where he is.”

These are the words of ‘Umar, in which he states that every Muslim has a right to this wealth and mentions giving priority to those in need. There is no disagreement among Muslims that it is impermissible to give to wealthy people who provide no benefit while depriving the poor. This contradicts the words of the Most High:

“So that it may not circulate solely among the rich among you.”

If he makes fay’ revenues circulate only among the wealthy, that is precisely what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and what this verse actually prohibits.

As for the transmitter’s account of Mālik’s position, he states that al-Mudawwana says: “The poll tax levied on people under Muslim protection and the land tax on territories acquired by force or by treaty both constitute jizya in Mālik’s view, and he considers jizya to be fay’ revenues.”

He said:

“This fay’ is given to the people of each territory which they conquered by force or acquired by treaty. It is divided among them, with some receiving more than others. Those in need are given priority until they have enough. None is sent elsewhere unless another people are afflicted by need, in which case it is transferred to them after its own people have received enough to free them from need.”

He also said:

Mālik said: “As for the jizya levied on land, I do not know how it used to be handled, except that ‘Umar left the land as it was and did not divide it among those who conquered it. I consider that whoever encounters such a matter should seek clarification about it

---

## Page 14177

from someone he trusts. If he finds a scholar, he should seek his ruling; otherwise, he and those present should exercise their own judgment.”

Reclaiming uncultivated land is permissible without the ruler’s permission according to al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, Abū Yūsuf, and Muhammad. Abū Hanīfa, however, stipulated that the ruler’s permission is required.

Mālik said: “If it is far from settled areas, where people do not compete over it, the ruler’s permission is unnecessary. If it is near settled areas, where people compete over it, his permission is required.”

However, if the land reclaimed is subject to land tax, does reclamation confer ownership without liability for land tax, or does the person hold it while remaining liable for that tax? Scholars hold two opinions on this, both transmitted from Ahmad.

When a fighting man is killed or dies, his wife and young children are provided with stipends. According to Ahmad’s school, one of al-Shāfiʿī’s two opinions, and other scholars, his wife is supported until she remarries, his young daughter until she marries, and his young son until he reaches puberty. The son is then enrolled among the fighting men if he is fit for combat. Otherwise, if he is needy and among those eligible to receive zakat and the surplus of fay’ revenues and public-welfare funds, he is given from these; if not, he receives nothing.

---

## Page 14178

He—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

If the public treasury is properly administered, so that its wealth is spent only on rightful purposes and is not withheld from those entitled to it, then anyone who directs some of its assets or their usufruct toward an authorized purpose of the treasury—such as building or repairing a road—without the ruler’s permission has overstepped his authority, since responsibility for administering it belongs to the ruler. The ruler must then do what best serves the public interest: if reversing that action is more beneficial to the Muslims, he reverses it; if allowing it to stand is more beneficial, he lets it stand.

The same applies when someone acts concerning property belonging to an endowment or an orphan, without the administrator’s permission, in a manner that is otherwise lawful—for example, by using its assets to build a shop or house on land belonging to the endowment or orphan.

But if the administration of the public treasury is in disorder, the jurists have said:

If someone directs some of its assets or their usufruct toward a public benefit, without grounds for suspecting improper motives in that action, and the action genuinely serves the public interest, then the ruler should neither reverse it nor hold the person who acted financially liable. Nevertheless, it is not permissible to disobey the ruler, whether he is righteous or wicked, unless he commands disobedience to Allah.

A ruling or distribution he makes is effective if it accords with what is right, whether he is righteous or wicked. But if someone acts

---

## Page 14179

in a way that gives grounds for suspecting improper motives—for example, by taking the money for himself on the interpretation that “I have an entitlement from the public treasury, but I am not given my due”—then this … (1).

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Some people own properties inherited from their fathers and grandfathers, from which the ruler is entitled to a one-third share—that is, one third of the yield. A contractor purchased the ruler’s one-third share, then forcibly seized all their property. Is he entitled to do so or not?

He answered:

He has no right, on the grounds mentioned, to dispossess people of the properties they hold. Nor is it permissible on those grounds to deprive Muslims of their established possession of what rightfully belongs to them. Land subject to land tax, such as the Sawād and other lands, was transferred from a land-tax assessment to an assessment based on a share of the yield—as Abū Ja‘far al-Mansūr did with the Sawād of Iraq—while remaining in the possession of its holders.

Such land passes from its holders to their descendants and to others through inheritance, bequests and gifts, and likewise through sale, according to the sounder of the two scholarly opinions. Its legal status in the buyer’s possession is the same as in the seller’s possession. Such land is not subject to the rules of an endowment that cannot be sold, given away or inherited. Those who prohibited selling the land of the Sawād were mistaken in this respect, believing it to be like an endowment that may not be

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A blank in the original.

---

## Page 14180

sold, even though such land may be inherited and given away; there is no disagreement on this. Rather, the public treasury’s holdings in these lands should be sold, as should its share of the yield, which is equivalent to land tax.

Another view is that these should not be sold, because doing so would squander the rights of the Muslims.

He was asked:

If the Tatars enter Syria and plunder the property of Christians and Muslims, and the Muslims subsequently plunder the Tatars and strip their dead of their possessions, is the property taken from them, including the possessions stripped from their dead, lawful or not?

He answered:

One fifth of everything taken from the Tatars is to be set aside, and it is permissible to benefit from it.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Regarding a poor man living away from home who regularly observes the five daily prayers: if he receives a stipend from the ruler that provides his subsistence and spares him from begging, is he sinful? Would he be granted leniency?

The Answer

He answered:

Yes, if the ruler gives someone like this enough to meet his needs from the funds of

---

## Page 14181

the public treasury, that is permissible. Neither all nor even most of the funds held by the Islamic fiscal administration are unlawful, so as to warrant such a judgment. Rather, they include zakah funds, state revenues, and funds devoted to the public welfare in amounts known only to Allah. They also include funds that are unlawful or doubtful. If he knows that what he has been given comes from unlawful funds, he may not accept it; but if he does not know its provenance, accepting it is not forbidden to him. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Regarding a man whom the ruler has awarded a revenue grant that includes some illicit levies: may he use these for his own subsistence, assign them to his soldiers, or spend them on fodder for his horses and pay for his retainers?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Funds collected from the various revenue sources are not free of doubt, but they are not all wholly unlawful. Some are unlawful, while others are collected rightfully, and some are less objectionable than others. Thus, levies on al-Sāhil and its revenue grants are less objectionable than those imposed on sales of real estate and other such commodities, or on the yarn market and similar markets. There is no uncertainty about these latter levies: they constitute manifest injustice.

The same applies to the revenue-farming arrangement known as damān al-ifrāj, since its proceeds may be collected either from forbidden sexual acts or from lawful marriages. In the latter case, this is injustice; in the former, it is assistance in the immoral practices that

---

## Page 14182

are known as “maghānī al-ʿArab,” and the like. In some forms, this involves farming the revenues of taverns. This is utterly reprehensible, unlike the levies at Sāhil al-Qiblah, where many people may nevertheless suffer injustice. However, if holders of extensive revenue grants have been granted more than their entitlement, it is not unjust for the ruler to order that some of the surplus be taken back. His grant originally consists of zakah, but unjust exactions have been added to it.

Accordingly, anyone whose revenue grant includes something of this kind should reserve the lawful, wholesome portion for his own food and drink, then the next best for other people, and the portion below that for feeding camels. The funds used for feeding horses should be better than those used for camels, since horses are nobler. He should allocate the next portion to the drummers, trumpeters, bāziyāt, and others like them.

For Allah says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

Everyone must therefore fear Allah as much as he is able. Whatever evil cannot be eliminated should be reduced as far as possible, for Allah sent the messengers to secure and perfect benefits, and to eliminate and reduce harms.

---

## Page 14183

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about property whose rightful recipient is either entirely unknown or uncertain.

Answer

This is a matter of widespread relevance, for people may come into possession of property they know is unlawful for them because of the rights of others. It may have been acquired unjustly, through forcible seizure and related wrongdoing, theft, or embezzlement; or it may have been received through an invalid transaction involving usury or gambling, while the identity of its rightful recipient is unknown.

Sometimes it is known that the rightful recipient is one of two people, but not which one. Examples include an inheritance known to belong to one of two wives—the one who remained married, rather than the divorced wife—and an item claimed by two people which its possessor attributes to one of them. The position of Imam Ahmad, Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, and the majority of the early generations is that such property should be given to those most entitled to it.

Al-Shāfiʿī’s position is that it must be safeguarded in all cases and must never be spent. Thus, regarding seized property, borrowed items, and deposits held in trust whose owners are unknown, he says that they must be kept until their owners appear, like other lost property. Regarding an item known to belong to one of two people, he says that the matter must be suspended until they reach a settlement.

The position of Ahmad and Abū Hanīfah concerning property whose owner is unknown is that it should be spent on its owners’ behalf for beneficial purposes:

---

## Page 14184

such as giving charity to the poor. Where the owner’s identity is uncertain, Ahmad holds that lots should be drawn, while Abū Hanīfah holds that the property should be divided. A thousand useful questions of practical relevance follow from this principle.

This also provides an answer to the hypothetical case posed by Abū al-Maʿālī in his book “al-Ghiyāthī” and taken up by those who followed him: if unlawful property were to encompass the earth and no means of obtaining lawful property remained, people would be permitted as much food, clothing, and housing as they needed; and need is broader than necessity. He explained that this situation could arise if unjust rulers seized property without right and distributed it among the people, and that his own time was close to this hypothetical situation—so what of later times?

Yet what he proposed is an impossible hypothesis that cannot arise, because of the “principle of Islamic law” I have mentioned. For prohibited things fall into two categories: things prohibited in themselves, such as impure substances, including blood and carrion; and things prohibited because of another person’s rights, though their kind is permissible, such as food, housing, clothing, riding animals, money, and other things.

The prohibition of all these things comes down to injustice, for they become prohibited only for two reasons:

(The first is taking possession of them without their owner’s willing consent and without the Lawgiver’s permission. This is outright injustice, such as theft, breach of trust, and overt forcible seizure. This is the category most widely recognized as prohibited.

---

## Page 14185

The second is taking possession of such property without the Lawgiver’s permission, even if its owner consents. This includes prohibited contracts and receipts of property, such as usury, gambling, and the like.

Whoever comes into possession of it must return it to the person entitled to it. If that proves impossible, an unknown person is treated as nonexistent. This is indicated by the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning lost property:

“If you find its owner, return it to him; otherwise, it is Allah’s property, which He gives to whomever He wills.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus explained that when lost property is known to belong to someone whose rights are protected by Islamic law, and has left his possession without his consent, but its owner cannot be found, Allah has given it to the person whom He enabled to acquire it through the lawful procedures for collecting lost property.

Likewise, Muslims agree that when someone dies without any known heir, his property is spent on the public interests of the Muslims. Yet most people must have some distant residuary heir; his identity, however, is unknown, with no prospect of discovering it, so he is treated as nonexistent. This is evident, and there are not two conclusive proofs by analogy like those we have mentioned from the Sunnah and consensus. For whatever cannot possibly be known or is entirely beyond our ability is, as far as we are concerned, equivalent to what does not exist. We are therefore charged only with what we know and are capable of doing.

When knowledge or ability is lacking—as in the case of someone who is insane or incapable—there is no difference, as far as our obligations are concerned, between an act we have not been commanded to perform and one we have been commanded to perform in general. Likewise, there is no difference, as far as our obligations are concerned, between property that has no owner to whom we have been commanded to deliver it and property that we have been commanded, in general, to deliver to its owner, when we lack knowledge of him or the ability

---

## Page 14186

to do so. Property and actions are alike in this respect.

This category is prohibited only because another person has a right to it. If that person does not exist, is wholly unknown, or is entirely beyond reach, his claim upon it lapses altogether. Likewise, when there is hope of identifying him or being able to deliver it to him, his claim is suspended until his identity becomes known or delivery becomes possible. This is exactly the case with lost property, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, indicated by saying:

“If its owner comes forward; otherwise, it is Allah’s property, which He gives to whomever He wills.”

For if the owner ceased to exist, ownership would pass from him by consensus. The same therefore applies when knowledge of his identity is permanently unavailable or when delivering the property to him is permanently impossible. The former case is clear. An example of the latter is property that kings have taken from its owners—through levies and the like—which we know with certainty we cannot restore to them. Spending it on purposes that serve its owners’ interests, such as jihad on their behalf, is better than leaving it in the hands of oppressors to consume. When it is spent, it is lawful for those who receive it rightfully, just as it is unlawful for those who consume it wrongfully.

The second proof, “analogical reasoning”—in addition to the Sunnah and consensus already mentioned—is that such property must either be withheld, destroyed, or spent. Destroying it constitutes corruption:

“And Allah does not love corruption.”

It also amounts to wasting it.

---

## Page 14187

and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade wasting wealth. The schools of Ahmad and Mālik do, however, permit financial penalties, sometimes through confiscation and sometimes through destruction. This is Ahmad’s position concerning the belongings of someone who misappropriates war booty, and the position of Ahmad and those Mālikīs who share his view concerning wine vessels, the premises of wine sellers, and other such things. Punishment through the destruction of certain property in some circumstances is comparable to punishment through taking certain lives in some circumstances.

This is permissible when making an example of the offender serves the benefit for which such punishment was prescribed, as with taking a life or a limb. Just as taking a life is forbidden except in retribution for a life or for spreading corruption—as Allah Most High says:

“Whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption in the land”

—and as the angels said:

“Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption and shed blood?”

—so too is destroying property permissible only as retaliation or because of its owner’s wrongdoing. Thus, we have permitted destroying the buildings and plantations of those at war with us in retaliation for their doing the same to us, without disagreement. We have likewise permitted what we have permitted on account of its owner’s wrongdoing.

For this reason, I know of no one who has said that legally protected property whose owner is unknown should be destroyed. Such conduct is merely reported of certain mistaken individuals seeking to practise religious scrupulousness: one cast some of his wealth into the sea, or abandoned it on land, and the like. In such people one finds good intentions and sincere scrupulousness, but not sound conduct.

As for withholding it permanently, forever, with no anticipated endpoint—indeed, knowing that there is no

---

## Page 14188

hope of identifying its owner or being able to deliver it to him—this is like destroying it. Destruction is forbidden precisely because it prevents people from benefiting from the property, and withholding it does the same. Indeed, withholding it is worse in two respects:

First, it torments people by keeping what they need beyond their use.

Second, experience shows that such property will inevitably fall into the hands of some oppressor if those committed to justice and truth do not spend it. Withholding it therefore assists oppressors and, in reality, hands it over to them. Thus, one denies it to those who uphold the truth and gives it to those who uphold falsehood. Whether or not this is intended makes no difference here: whoever places someone among beasts of prey has effectively killed him; whoever throws meat among wild beasts has effectively devoured it; and whoever withholds great sums of wealth, leaving them for oppressors to seize, has effectively given that wealth to them.

Since destroying it is forbidden, and withholding it is worse than destroying it, spending it becomes obligatory. As it has no specifically designated use, it should be spent on all charitable and devotional causes through which one draws near to Allah. For Allah created His creatures to worship Him and created wealth for them to help them worship Him; it should therefore be spent in Allah’s cause. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 14189

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

About a man entitled to payment from the public treasury, either for his contribution to jihad or for holding public office, who was directed to collect part of his entitlement from certain unjust exactions.

He replied:

Do not collect this yourself or assist in collecting it, for that is wrongdoing. Rather, seek your entitlement from the funds already collected and held by them, even if those funds have been gathered from this and other sources. For money accumulated in the public treasury and not returned to its owners is better spent on the interests of its owners and the Muslims than on purposes that do not benefit its owners or that harm them. I have written about a similar issue elsewhere.

Moreover, the money becomes mixed with other funds, so the ruling prohibiting that particular property no longer applies to it, while spending on someone in this position is an obligation upon the Muslims. Officials sometimes commit injustice in collecting funds and sometimes in spending them. It is therefore unlawful to assist them in unjust collection, or for anyone to take what he is not entitled to.

As for collection and expenditure that admit of legitimate juristic judgment, these are to be treated as matters of juristic judgment. But where taking and giving admit of no such judgment, they must not be assisted.

---

## Page 14190

but if the recipient is entitled to an amount equal to what is taken, he may receive it from any funds that may lawfully be disbursed, such as property whose owner is unknown when its disbursement becomes obligatory. If they refuse to return it to its rightful recipient, is it preferable to leave it in the hands of the wrongdoers, or to strive to spend it on the interests of its owners and the Muslims, provided that the person striving to do so disapproves of its original seizure, did not assist in taking it, and indeed sought to prevent it?

This is an important question that deserves careful attention; otherwise, one may fall into committing prohibited acts or neglecting obligations. Assisting injustice is a prohibited act. Yet if obligations cannot be fulfilled without the expenditure just mentioned, refraining from it amounts to neglecting those obligations. If the only alternatives are to leave the money in the wrongdoer’s hands or spend it on beneficial purposes, then forbidding such expenditure assists in increasing injustice by leaving it in the wrongdoer’s hands. Just as injustice must be eliminated, it must be reduced when eliminating it altogether is impossible. This is a principle of great importance, and Allah knows best.

Another principle is that doubtful funds should be directed towards uses furthest removed from direct personal benefit, giving priority to the most remote. Thus, regarding a cupper’s earnings, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—instructed that they be used to feed slaves and a water-drawing animal. The most direct benefit is that obtained through food, drink, and the like; next comes clothing in contact with the outside of the body; then buildings that provide shelter while remaining separate from it; then incidental benefits such as riding and the like. Such is the ranking of the ways one benefits from one’s provision. This is also the practice of our fellow jurists.

---

## Page 14191

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

A man gave a slave to a king. The recipient then died, and another king succeeded him. May the latter free that slave?

He replied:

Slaves purchased with Muslim public funds are assets of the public treasury, like horses and weapons purchased with Muslim public funds or presented as gifts to Muslim rulers. If the second king disposes of them by freeing them or giving them away, his action has the same standing as that of the first. Does the second king’s disposal of them through emancipation or gift take legal effect just as the first king’s does? Yes. This is the position of all the imams. Allah knows best.

He was also asked:

A boy was taken captive from dār al-harb (the abode of war) before reaching puberty and was purchased by Christians. He grew up, married, had Christian children, and then died. Evidence established that he had been captured before puberty, but it was not known who had taken him captive—whether someone belonging to the People of the Book or a Muslim. Are his children to be regarded as Muslims or not?

---

## Page 14192

He replied:

If his captor was a Muslim, the child is deemed Muslim. If his captor was an unbeliever, or neither possibility has been established by proof, he is not deemed Muslim. His children follow his status in either case. Allah knows best.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

From Ahmad ibn Taymiyya to Sarjawān, the eminent leader of the people of his faith, and those under his care among religious leaders, eminent priests and monks, princes, secretaries, and their followers.

Peace be upon those who follow right guidance.

They were singled out for the taking of the covenant: Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad.

Allah Most High named them in His Book, saying—mighty and majestic is He:

“He has ordained for you of

## Page 14193

religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: establish the religion and do not become divided in it. Difficult for the polytheists is that to which you call them. Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns to Him.”

And the Most High said:

We ask Him to bestow His noblest blessings and peace especially upon the last of the messengers: their spokesman when they come before their Lord, their leader when they assemble, the intercessor for creation on the Day of Resurrection, the Prophet of mercy and the Prophet of battle, who united the virtues of the prophets. His coming was foretold by Allah’s servant, His spirit, and His word which He conveyed to the truthful, pure virgin whom no man had ever touched: Mary, daughter of ʿImrān.
